body_markdown:
# Adam Francis Telfer (1842–1925)

**Role:** Scottish migrant who followed his brothers to Australia — the Tantanoola pioneer

**Born:** 14 September 1842 — Jedburgh, Roxburghshire, Scotland
**Died:** 12 January 1925 — Knightsbridge, South Australia
**Occupation:** Shepherd, stockholder, storekeeper, grazier
**Spouse:** [[Margaret Dougal Telfer (1849–1936)]] (m. 25 March 1868)

## Photos

![Adam francis telfer grave](images/people/adam-francis-telfer-grave.jpg)
*Grave of Adam Francis Telfer (1842–1925)*

---

## Family

| Relation | Name |
|----------|------|
| **Mother** | Elizabeth Beattie |
| **Father** | James Telfer |
| **Spouse** | [[Margaret Dougal Telfer (1849–1936)]] |
| **Cousin / Uncle** | [[Francis Telfer (1809–1895)]] |

---

## Family Stories

### The Ship That Sank

Adam was born at Jedburgh, Roxburghshire, Scotland on 14th September 1842, the youngest son of James and Elizabeth Telfer. His father died in 1863 from injuries in an agricultural accident — a hard blow for the family. Adam made the difficult decision to leave his mother and sisters behind and follow his brothers to South Australia. He sailed on the steamer "London" on her second voyage, a 140-day journey from Gravesend to Melbourne. The ship's master was J.B. Martin. On the shipping list, some rushed clerk wrote Adam's nationality as "Irish" — a Scot through and through. The "London" sank on her next voyage. *(From the Borders to the Bush, p.267)*

### Overland to Uncle Francis

Adam landed in Melbourne and travelled overland to South Australia, making contact with his Uncle Francis at "Macoota", Kersbrook, and the brothers and sister who'd come before him. He worked as a shepherd and spent some time with his eldest brother James at Koppio Station near Port Lincoln. Rough country, lonely work — the kind that made a man of you. *(From the Borders to the Bush, p.267)*

### Marrying His Cousin

In 1868, Adam returned to Kersbrook and married his cousin, Margaret Dougal Telfer — the daughter of his Uncle Francis. She was just 18, he was 25. The wedding was at her father's home, "Macoota". He was listed as a "Stockholder, of Koppio, Port Lincoln." After the wedding they went back to Koppio for several years. It was a marriage that would last 57 years and produce twelve children. *(From the Borders to the Bush, p.267-268)*

### The Tantanoola Store

In the early 1870s, Adam and Margaret moved to the South East of South Australia. Adam's first community appointment was as Vice President of the Millicent Show in 1878. In 1880, he opened a store in Tantanoola — then known as Lucieton. The country was booming: the soil "will grow anything," the town was laid out with "excellent judgement," and the white stone buildings showed through the foliage "to great advantage." The Telfers were among those pioneers building it all. *(From the Borders to the Bush, p.269-272)*

### The Farewell at Tantanoola Station

After 28 years in Tantanoola, Adam and Margaret left in 1908. The district presented them with a silver tea service — still held by their great-grandson Bruce Watson of Millicent as of 1986. When the train arrived, friends gathered on the platform and sang "God be with you till we meet again." It was too much for daughter Eva, who grabbed her son Rex and boarded the train before anyone saw her cry. *(From the Borders to the Bush, p.272-275)*

### Edgerston House

The family settled at "Waverley Park" in Lower Mitcham, then moved to "Edgerston House" on Rochester Street, Knightsbridge in 1916. The nine-roomed house had large grounds with a creek meandering through the garden, a wooden bridge covered in wisteria, an extensive orchard, and stables. The family joined the Knightsbridge Baptist Church, the girls taught Sunday School, and Hazel sang in the choir. During the First World War, Adam wrote to his son Frank about the Irish Blight ruining the potatoes and the British Government wanting all the wool. *(From the Borders to the Bush, p.274-275)*

### The Stroke

In 1919, Adam suffered a stroke. He recovered some function but his left arm and hand were useless, and his sight was failing. He wrote letters anyway, joking about it: "I have written such a long list of letters today so think I will finish up with one to you. I have written to Ted, Frank, Ray, Tom Holloway and Elsie at Broken Hill, and now if I write one to you that will be na sae bad for a blind man." His wife Margaret would finish the letters for him: "Father has left this so I will close it for him." *(From the Borders to the Bush, p.275-276)*

### The Smith Brothers' Return

In 1920, Adam wrote to Effie about the return of Sir Ross and Sir Keith Smith to Adelaide after their epic flight from England. "There was about 20,000 people to meet them. Mother and I saw them come over Mount Lofty but we did not leave the verandah to see them." He also complained of lumbago and a dry season: "Our garden does not look well. The trees are nearly dead for the want of rain but I think they will get over it if only we get plenty of rain." The old Scot, still tending his garden even as his health failed. *(From the Borders to the Bush, p.276)*

### Adam's Death

Margaret nursed Adam for six years after his stroke. He died on 12th January 1925 at age 82. The Advertiser ran a death notice, and The Chronicle published an obituary noting his arrival on the "London" and his forty years of grazing in the South East. He left a widow, four sons, seven daughters, and 28 grandchildren. Margaret lived another eleven years. Both are buried at Mitcham Cemetery, with the words "God is our Refuge and Strength" — from Margaret's favourite Psalm 46 — on the headstone. *(From the Borders to the Bush, p.276-277)*

### Civic & Community Life

🖊️ *Anecdote — as told in* From the Borders to the Bush *(pp.270-272), the Part-2 chapter-13 treatment:*

- **Father of the Show:** the first Tantanoola Show (9 Dec 1885) was held in the woolshed at "Edgerston". Adam was first President of the Pastoral, Agricultural and Horticultural Society 1885–88, again 1890–93, and secretary in later years; he took prizes for pansies and new potatoes.
- **Church foundation:** Adam chaired the Presbyterian Church church-building committee (brother John gave the land); foundation stone laid by John Livingstone MHR on 15 April 1902, church opened 10 Nov 1902.
- **Mason:** admitted to Mount Gambier Freemasons Lodge No. 1207 on 24 April 1883.
- **Adelaide years:** contrary to retiring, SA Directories list him as sheep farmer and (from 1912) JP, Produce Merchant & General Agent at the Santo Building; his Truro sheep station (run by son Herb) was lost in the 1914 drought.
- **The 1916 letter:** a handwritten 5 Dec 1916 letter to son Frank at Glencoe West offered Cheese Factory shares and touched on shearing, the war, and the British Government.

### Naming Edgerston

When Adam built up his holding near Tantanoola, he honoured the land he had left behind by naming the property "Edgerston" — after the Scottish parish in the Borders near Jedburgh where he had grown up. It was a small piece of home carried across the sea, and it was there the family made their home until they moved away in 1908. *(From the Borders to the Bush, pp.267-275)*

### A Marriage Witnessed by Cousins

Margaret's wedding party read like a roll-call of the two families joining as one. Her cousins George and Mary Robertson stood as witnesses, and beside them was Adam's own brother John — the two Telfer lines sealing the match. *(From the Borders to the Bush, pp.267-268)*

### Waverley Park

When the family left Tantanoola and took up "Waverley Park" at Lower Mitcham in 1908, Adam gave the new home a name borrowed from the books he loved. It came from Sir Walter Scott's Waverley Novels — the very stories that had drawn their colour from the Liddesdale countryside Adam himself had walked before he emigrated. So the old parish followed him even into that Adelaide suburb, wrapped up in the name of an English novelist. *(From the Borders to the Bush, pp.272-275)*

---

## Life Story

Adam Francis Telfer was born at Jedburgh, Scotland in 1842. After his father's death in an agricultural accident, he emigrated to Australia on the steamer "London" — which sank on her next voyage. He worked as a shepherd at Koppio Station before marrying his cousin Margaret Dougal Telfer in 1868. They raised twelve children, first at Koppio, then at Tantanoola where Adam opened a store. The family moved to Adelaide in 1908 and settled at Knightsbridge. Adam suffered a stroke in 1919 and died in 1925.

**Source:** *From the Borders to the Bush* — pages 267-277 (chapter 7) and pp.270-276 (chapter 13, civic/community section)
**Source (corroboration):** [Find a Grave — Adam Francis Telfer (1842–1925), Memorial 201529655](https://www.findagrave.com/memorial/201529655/adam-francis-telfer) — d. 12 Jan 1925, buried Mitcham General Cemetery — accessed 19 Aug 2026

title: Adam Telfer — Family & Biography
body_markdown:
Born ~1771 at Sorbietrees, Roxburghshire, Scotland. Son of James Telfer and Margaret Armstrong of Sorbietrees. Died 6 February 1846 at Newcastleton aged 75. Name on family headstone in Castleton Cemetery. The name "Adam" appears regularly in succeeding Telfer generations.

## Family Stories

### The Brother on the Headstone

Most of what we know about Adam Telfer comes from one place: a headstone in Castleton Cemetery, Newcastleton. It reads:

> "Erected in Memory of Francis Telfer, who died at Newcastleton on 4th June, 1836, aged 68 years (b 1768). Also Jenet Telfer, his sister, who died at Newcastleton on 9th February 1842, aged 72 years (b 1770). Also Adam Telfer, their brother, who died at Newcastleton on 6th February, 1846, aged 75 years (b 1771)."

That's it. Three siblings on one stone — Francis, Jenet, and Adam — all dying within a decade of each other, all in the same little border town. Adam never married (or if he did, no record survived). He never left Scotland. He lived his whole life within a few miles of where he was born, in the Liddesdale valley near the English border.

But here's the thing. The name "Adam" didn't die with him. It kept popping up in the family for generations — Adam Telfer (1799–?), Adam Francis Telfer (1842–1925), and further down the line. Some names travel better than people do.

*(From the Borders to the Bush, pp.17-19; Castleton Cemetery headstone)*

**Source:** *From the Borders to the Bush* — pages 17-19; Castleton Cemetery headstone

## Militia identification & residence trail (research note, 2026-09-01)

**1802 Castleton Militia List** (No. 84) records the ONLY Telfer in the parish: "Adam Telfer, shepherd, at Redmoss." Age-fit (18–45 in 1802) makes Adam of Sorbietrees (b ~1771, aged ~31) the probable match; Adam (1799–?) ruled out (aged ~3).

**Castleton male heads of families rolls 1835–1838** (NRS CH2/64/3, transcribed on oldscottish.com) show **no Adam Telfer** anywhere in the parish; Telfer/Telford household heads are James (schoolmaster, Saughtree), William (shepherd, Kershope, England side), Gilbert (labourer, Wheathaugh), Robert & William Telford (labourers). **Redmoss is held by John Jackson (shepherd) in all years** — consistent with the shepherd having changed since 1802, or with Adam being a non-communicant / not an independent household head by the 1830s (he'd be ~63–67, never married per headstone).

**Open question:** no record yet literally ties "Adam Telfer" to the Redmoss steading beyond the 1802 militia roll. Decisive next lead = **Castleton Kirk Session Minutes** covering the 1802 window:
- CH2/64/4 (Kirk Session Minutes 1773–1821)
- CH2/64/5 (Kirk Session Minutes 1797–1808) ← contains exactly 1802

Both offered as £1/name/year lookups on oldscottish.com. A lookup could record Adam's residence, a wife, or children of Adam (a potential undocumented branch).

**Source (research note):** oldscottish.com Castleton records page (transcriptions of NRS CH2/64/3 male-heads rolls). Corroborating context — not a standalone verified fact.

body_markdown:
# Adam Telfer (1799–?)

**Role:** Brother of Francis Telfer (1809–1895)

Adam Telfer was born on 18 October 1799 at Greenholm, near Newcastleton, Roxburghshire, Scotland. He was the third child of James Telfer (1761–1845), a hand loom weaver, and Elizabeth "Betty" Hutton (1774–1853).

His baptism was recorded in the Old Parish Register of Castleton (Volume 784/1) as: "1799 October 18 — Adam to James Telfer and Betty Hutton at Greenholm."

The family later moved from Greenholm to Blackburnfoot, at the northern end of Newcastleton, where two more children were born. Blackburnfoot had its own weaving industry, and the cottage where his brother Francis was born still stood into the 1980s.

The book *From the Borders to the Bush* states: *"We have no further information about four members of this family; namely Isobel, Adam, Margaret and William."* Like his older sister Isobel and younger siblings Margaret and William, Adam's fate after the family records is not documented.

He is one of the "Other Children" on the family tree, distinguished from his nephew Adam (1796–1863, son of James Telfer and Elizabeth Beattie).

**Source:** *From the Borders to the Bush* — pages 17–20

---

## Family Stories

### The Lost Thread

Adam Telfer was born on 18 October 1799 at Greenholm, near Newcastleton — the third child of James Telfer, a hand loom weaver, and Elizabeth Hutton. The family moved to Blackburnfoot, where the cottage his brother Francis was born in still stood into the 1980s.

And then the thread goes cold. The book *From the Borders to the Bush* puts it plainly: *"We have no further information about four members of this family; namely Isobel, Adam, Margaret and William."* Adam's fate after the family records ends is not documented.

He's one of the ghosts of the family tree — a name in the parish register, a son of the Scottish Borders, whose life was lived beyond the reach of the record book.

*(From the Borders to the Bush, pp.17-20)*

body_markdown:
# Alan Dale Telfer (1890–1937)

**Born:** 27 Oct 1890 (Tantanoola, SA) | **Died:** 18 Sep 1937 (Wilga Tank, Girilambone, NSW) | **Mother:** [[Martha Henstridge (~1854–1921)]] | **Father:** [[John Telfer (1840–1913)]] | **Occupation:** Railway ganger (permanent-way employee) | **Buried:** Unknown (Girilambone district)

## Family

| Relation | Name |
|---|---|
| Self | Alan Dale Telfer |
| Father | [[John Telfer (1840–1913)]] |
| Mother | Martha Clara Henstridge |
| Siblings | [[James Telfer (1866–1946)]], Elizabeth Telfer (Clarke), Susan Telfer (Agnew), Martha Telfer (Cameron), [[Mark Telfer (1877–1946)]], Maria Clara Telfer, Isabella Lucieton Telfer (Thomson), John Roland Telfer, Clara Blanche Telfer (Lane), Robert Freddy Telfer, Douglas Telfer, Colin Roy Telfer, Alma Tressy Telfer (Cullen), [[Marian Telfer Cornish (1896–1977)]] |

## Life Summary

Alan Dale Telfer was born on 27 October 1890 in Tantanoola, South Australia, the 13th child of John Telfer (1840–1913) and his second wife Martha Clara Henstridge.

He never married. During the Depression years of the late 1920s and 1930s, Alan left South Australia's Limestone Coast and travelled into inland New South Wales, where he found work on the railways as a **permanent-way employee (ganger)** — a track-maintenance labourer — based around the remote Wilga Tank railway siding, west of Nyngan.

### Death — Resolved (2026)

Alan's fate was a long-standing mystery in the Telfer family tree. Contemporary newspapers and the NSW intestate records now confirm exactly what happened.

On **Saturday 18 September 1937**, a motor car overturned near **Wilga Tank railway siding, ~30 miles west of Nyngan**, on the edge of the Girilambone district in central-western NSW. The **Wellington Times** (20 Sep 1937) reported that the accident killed "**Alan Dale Telfer, middle aged, a railway per-way employee of Wilga Tank**" — he was **killed instantly when the car overturned**. Two of the car's four occupants were badly injured and taken to Nyngan Hospital; one of them, railway fettler Thomas Richards (21), later died of his injuries. A coroner's inquest followed.

The death was confirmed by the **NSW Government Gazette** intestate notice, which recorded —

> "Alan Dale Telfer, late of Wilga Tank, Girilambone, … ganger, who died 18th September, 1937, intestate."

Because he left no will — and no widow or children — his estate was administered by the NSW Public Trustee. That is strong evidence he was unmarried and alone in his final years.

The newspaper account that ties him unmistakably to the Tantanoola family appeared in the **South Eastern Times** (Millicent, SA) on 1 October 1937:

> "The death occurred at Girilambone, New South Wales, on the 18th inst., of **Allan Dale Telfer, son of the late John and Martha Telfer, of Tantanoola**. The deceased, who was 46½ years of age, was killed instantly in a motor car accident."

That notice, placed in the Tantanoola home-district paper, confirms this Alan Dale Telfer was indeed the son of John and Martha Telfer of Tantanoola — the man this profile describes.

His burial place is not recorded but was almost certainly in the Girilambone or Nyngan district of central-western New South Wales.

## Timeline

| Date | Event |
|---|---|
| 27 Oct 1890 | Born at Tantanoola, South Australia |
| 5 Jan 1913 | Father John Telfer died at Tantanoola |
| ~1920s–1930s | Migrated to New South Wales for railway work |
| 13 Nov 1921 | Mother Martha Clara Henstridge died at Adelaide |
| 18 Sep 1937 | Killed in a car accident near Wilga Tank, Girilambone, NSW; died intestate |

## Family Stories

Alan Dale was born at Tantanoola in 1890, the 13th child of John Telfer and Martha Henstridge. He never married and had no children. In the Depression he left the settled farming life of the Limestone Coast for the rough, itinerant world of railway track-work in inland New South Wales, ending up as a ganger at the lonely Wilga Tank siding west of Nyngan. He was killed there, aged about 46, when the car he was travelling in overturned on Saturday 18 September 1937.

> A note on family records: *From the Borders to the Bush* gives Alan's death as "1955," but no 1955 death for a Tantanoola-born Allan Dale Telfer appears in any record. Every primary source — the NSW accident reports, the NSW intestate gazette, and the Tantanoola home-district newspaper — places his death in **September 1937**. Any "wife and son" attributed to him belong to a **different** Allan Dale Telfer, an older railwayman who had lived at Wattamondara (near Cowra) in NSW; the two namesakes were fused together in some online trees. Alan Dale Telfer of Tantanoola died in 1937, unmarried and without children.

## Sources

1. **Wellington Times (NSW), 20 Sep 1937, p.1, "Nyngan Man Killed"** — Trove [article/143410212](https://trove.nla.gov.au/newspaper/article/143410212) — identifies the dead man as Alan Dale Telfer, "middle aged, a railway per-way employee of Wilga Tank," killed in a car accident at Wilga Tank.
2. **Western Herald (Bourke, NSW), 24 Sep 1937, p.4, "Car Accident"** — car capsized near Girilambone on "Saturday"; one man, "A. Telfer," killed.
3. **National Advocate (Bathurst, NSW), 29 Sep 1937** — inquest follow-up; confirms the crash and the later death of injured railway fettler Thomas Richards (21).

body_markdown:
# Albert George Telfer (1881–1970)

**Role:** Son of John Telfer and Caroline Amelia Masters — brother of Francis Charles Telfer. Farmer at Warcowie then Hill River (near Clare).

**Born:** 14 November 1881 — Angle Farm, near Hawker, South Australia
**Died:** November 1970 (gravestone 26 Nov 1970) — Clare, South Australia
**Buried:** Clare Old Cemetery, Clare, South Australia (with wife Beatrice)
**Married:** Beatrice Rowe (12 Oct 1877 Kadina – 29 Jun 1951 Clare), at Warcowie
**Parents:** [[John Telfer (1847–1929)]] & [[Caroline Amelia Telfer (1842–1929)]] (née Masters)
**Brother:** [[Francis Charles Telfer (1875–1954)]]
**Siblings:** Ernest John, William James, Walter William, Edwin Gilbert

---

## Family

| Relation | Name |
|---|---|
| **Mother** | [[Caroline Amelia Telfer (1842–1929)]] (née Masters) |
| **Father** | [[John Telfer (1847–1929)]] |
| **Spouse** | Beatrice Telfer (née Rowe) (12 Oct 1877 – 29 Jun 1951) — m. at Warcowie |
| **Brother** | [[Francis Charles Telfer (1875–1954)]] |
| **Siblings** | Ernest John Telfer, William James Telfer, Walter William Telfer, Edwin Gilbert Telfer |
| **Children** | Rita Joyce Telfer (1909–1990), Beatrice Sylvia Telfer (1911–1999), Douglas Ivan Telfer, Melville Bruce Telfer (1914–1997), John Alick Ralph Telfer, Murray Keith (Keith Murray) Telfer (1920–2005) |

---

## Biography

Albert George Telfer was the **fifth child** of John and Caroline Telfer, born on **14 November 1881** at Angle Farm, near Hawker. His birth came at a time when the family was establishing their home — a well had been sunk providing permanent water for stock and household use, and they were harvesting their fourth crop.

In **1903**, when his father purchased the Warcowie homestead, Albert took over its management, beginning a long farming career. His sister Bertha kept house for him there for a few years.

Albert was a farmer with a keen interest in examining new ideas and learning from them. He became a foundation member of the **Warcowie Agricultural Bureau** and took an active part in its activities.

He married **Beatrice Rowe** — the Warcowie district school teacher, from **Kadina (b. 12 Oct 1877)**, who boarded with the family for a year or two before being transferred to Moolawurtie. Their children — **Rita Joyce, Beatrice Sylvia, Douglas Ivan, Melville Bruce, John Alick Ralph and Murray Keith** — were all born while the family lived at Warcowie.

In **1923**, Albert bought a farm at **Hill River, six miles east of Clare**, so that his children could attend the High School there. Farming at Clare, one of the wetter areas of the state, was very different from the drier conditions he had been accustomed to at Hawker. His first crop at Hill River was quite good, but 80 acres were destroyed by a severe hailstorm. Despite such setbacks, Albert and Beatrice built a new life at Clare, and their family grew and prospered there.

Albert died in **November 1970** and was buried at **Clare Old Cemetery** (gravestone: 14 Nov 1881 – 26 Nov 1970), beside his wife **Beatrice** (12 Oct 1877 – 29 Jun 1951) who predeceased him in 1951.

*(From the Borders to the Bush, pp.144–146)*

---

## Family Stories

🖊️ **Anecdote — as told in From the Borders to the Bush (book pp. 110–118):** Albert was the boy born at Angle Farm, the place named for its awkward, slanted boundaries, and he grew up in the stone house the family finished in 1893 — you can pick him out in the photograph taken out the front when it was brand new. He took after his father as a manager of land: by 1903 he was running Warcowie for the family, and in 1923 he moved across to the Hill River farm and made a life of it there. He stayed with the old country all his days and lies in Clare Old Cemetery, alongside the ground his mother and father are in.

*(Anecdote only — family colour, told as the elders tell it. Does not establish any relationship, date or place.)*

## Sources

- **Book:** *From the Borders to the Bush*, pp.144–146 — born 14 Nov 1881 at Angle Farm; Beatrice Rowe (b. 12/10/1877) of Kadina; Warcowie farm then Hill River (near Clare) from 1923; six children named.
- **FindAGrave / ozburials Clare Old Cemetery transcription** — "TELFER, Beatrice & Albert George"; Albert 14 Nov 1881 – 26 Nov 1970; Beatrice 12 Oct 1877 – 29 Jun 1951.
- **headstones2.weebly.com Clare Old Cemetery** — "TELFER, Beatrice & Albert George" plot; also TELFER John & Caroline Amelia, John, Beatrice Sylvia, Keith & Marie, Melville Bruce & Violet Merle, Rita Joyce — confirms the Clare family cluster.
- **Ancestry index** (via web search) — Albert George Telfer, Birth 14 Nov 1881 Hawker SA, Death 30 Nov 1970 Clare SA.

> **Correction note (2026-08-10):** This profile was formerly `Albert George Telfer (1882–1961)` — an auto-generated stub with wrong years. the book *From the Borders to the Bush*'s own family register (p.144) states he was **born 14 Nov 1881** (fifth child of John & Caroline). The Clare gravestone and Ancestry index both confirm **death 1970, buried Clare**. Corrected to 1881–1970. A false "Albert George Telfer (1882–1961)" reference was removed from Clara Blanche Telfer (Tantanoola / John Telfer 1840–1913 branch) — the book records only ONE Albert George Telfer, and he is John & Caroline's son.

---

title: Alberta Grace Lawrie — SA-born, WA pioneer
body_markdown:
# Alberta Grace Lawrie

**Born:** 4 Sep 1882, Long Plains, South Australia | **Died:** 27 Jun 1953, Town of Claremont, Western Australia | **Buried:** Morawa Cemetery, Morawa, WA | **Father:** [[Robert Dunlop Lawrie (1850–1917)]] | **Mother:** [[Caroline Hosking (1851–1920)]] | **Spouse:** George Alfred Carslake (1881–1974) | **Also known as:** "Gracie" or "Grace"

## Biography

Alberta Grace Lawrie (known as Gracie or Grace) was born on 4 September 1882 at Long Plains, South Australia, the fifth child and fourth daughter of [[Robert Dunlop Lawrie (1850–1917)]] and [[Caroline Hosking (1851–1920)]].

She grew up on the family farm "Bleak Farm" at Long Plains, in a large family of nine children: Catherine Leah, Janet Stevenson, Alberta Grace, Hugh John, Frank Lindsay, Jeanette, Marion Vida, Caroline Edna, and Robert Dunlop Lawrie (jnr).

### Marriage and Move to Western Australia

On 6 September 1904, Alberta Grace married **George Alfred Carslake** (born 10 April 1881 in Windsor, SA) at her father's home in Long Plains, South Australia. George was the son of Henry Acland Carslake and Celena Wyatt.

The couple moved to Western Australia, where they farmed in the Arrino district (Dudawa / East Arrino). In the 1932–1934 period, George was secretary of the Dudawa Tennis Club. They left the Arrino district in September 1934 and shifted to Gutha in the Mid West region of Western Australia.

### Children

Alberta Grace and George Carslake had at least two sons:

1. **Robert Henry Carslake** — born 19 May 1907 in Balaclava, South Australia; farmer in Arrino, WA; married Kathleen Eleanor Jane Barr on 22 February 1933 at the Church of Christ Tabernacle in Northam; served on Three Springs Road Board representing Dudawa Ward (1934–35); shifted to Gutha in 1935.
2. **George Dunlop Carslake** — born 12 May 1912 in Narrabri, New South Wales; farmer in Arrino and Gutha; served as Flight Sergeant 46292 in the RAAF's 21 Squadron during WWII (enlisted 12 Feb 1942, discharged 28 Jan 1946); died 8 Sep 1997, cremated at Karrakatta Cemetery, Perth.

### Death

Alberta Grace died on 27 June 1953 at the Town of Claremont, Western Australia, aged 70. She was buried at Morawa Cemetery in Morawa, Shire of Morawa, WA.

**Note:** Some sources (webtrees archive at lawriefamily.info) list her death year as 1954, but FindAGrave provides the specific date of 27 June 1953, which is more precise.

## Connections

Alberta Grace Lawrie is a **paternal great-great-aunt** of Mark Telfer. Her sister [[Caroline Edna Lawrie (1890–1957)]] married William Henry Parker and was the grandmother of Shirley Edna Parker, who married [[Murray John Telfer (1924–2009)]], Grandfather.

Alberta Grace's grandson Graham Carslake authored the family history *Our Story in Australia, 1800s on*, which traces the Lawrie family from Ayrshire, Scotland to South Australia.

[View](https://www.carnamah.com.au/bio/alberta-grace-lawrie) — accessed 24 July 2026

- **Source:** Carnamah Historical Society & Museum, 'Robert Henry Carslake' in *Biographical Dictionary of Coorow, Carnamah and Three Springs* — confirms son of George Alfred CARSLAKE and Alberta Grace LAWRIE. [View](https://www.carnamah.com.au/bio/robert-henry-carslake) — accessed 24 July 2026

(See [[Family History/History/Lawrie Family - Carslake Connection.md]])

# Alexander Lawrie (1776–1847)

**Born:** c. 1776, Auchtermuchty, Fife, Scotland | **Died:** 11 Oct 1847, Galston, Ayrshire, Scotland | **Occupation:** Farmer

## Family

| Relation | Name |
|---|---|
| Self | Alexander Lawrie (1776–1847) |
| 1st Wife | Janet Porter (m. c. 1808 — had 1 son) |
| 2nd Wife | Jean Dunlop (m. July 1809, Peel, Riccarton, County Ayr) |
| 3rd Wife | Unknown (webtrees reports 18 children across three marriages) — Note: Jean Dunlop may have died c. 1834, after which Alexander married a third time. No marriage record or name found for third wife. |
| Son (1st marriage) | Alexander Lawrie (1809–1847) — half-brother to the 8 full siblings |

**Children of Alexander Lawrie & Jean Dunlop** (in birth order, sourced from probate record):

1. **John Lawrie** (10 Apr 1810–30 Aug 1888) — farmer, emigrated to SA 1853, Pinery
2. **Nicol Lawrie** (c. 1812–bef. 1860) — deceased by 1860
3. **Robert Lawrie** (c. 1815–1895) — emigrated to SA 1839, Henley Beach
4. **David Lawrie** (c. 1818–?) — remained in Kilmarnock, County Ayr
5. **Marion Lawrie** (c. 1820–1898) — married Archibald Greenshields, emigrated to SA, Nantawarra
6. **Jean Lawrie** (c. 1822–?) — married Ivis Graham of Ochiltree, County Ayr
7. **Alexander Dunlop "Sandy" Lawrie** (19 Mar 1832–2 Dec 1876) — younger son, emigrated, Alma Plains SA
8. **James Lawrie** (c. 1811–10 Jun 1848) — youngest child; emigrated to SA 1839, died at Tonyunga, unmarried

## Life Summary

Very little is known of Alexander's early life in Scotland. His birth is speculated as Auchtermuchty, Fife (the ancestral home of the Lawrie family), though no baptism record has been found. He was a farmer at Galston, Ayrshire.

Alexander married three times and fathered approximately 18 children. His second wife, Jean Dunlop of Lanfine, Galston, bore him at least eight children (all living to adulthood). He died intestate on 11 Oct 1847, leaving his estate to his eldest surviving son, John Lawrie (1810–1888), who had emigrated to South Australia.

**Marriage of Alexander & Jean:** July 1809 at Peel, Riccarton, County Ayr (GRO probate records).

## Property (from SA GRO Records)

Alexander never emigrated to Australia, but his sons John, James, Robert, and Alexander Dunlop did. The SA General Registry Office maintained records of the land disputes in the family as John Lawrie inherited from his father and brother James.

- Section 580, District D — sold by John Lawrie to brother Robert
- James Lawrie's land at Tonyunga (80-acre land grant, 31 Jan 1845) — inherited by John Lawrie after James died intestate

**In-law line:** Alfred married into the Farrow branch of the Telfer tree. His wife Jane Murray Farrow was a daughter of Charles Farrow and Elizabeth Hannah (Telfer) Farrow — hence Alfred's sons (through Jane) are grandchildren of Elizabeth Hannah Telfer. He is a **non-Telfer by birth**, connected to the tree through the Farrow/Telfer marriage.

## Life Summary

Alfred George Stribling was born in South Australia around **1853–1854** (he died aged 74 in 1928). He lived with his family at **Rutland Avenue, Brighton, South Australia** — the residence recorded for his son Cliff's war record. The family had associations with the **Tarlee / Finniss district** of South Australia, the same district from which his wife's Farrow family came.

He married **Jane Murray Farrow** around **1885**. The couple had three recorded sons: Arthur Clifford "Cliff" (1890–1918), Lindsay Ellis (1893–1979), and George Charles (1898–1988).

### Death

Alfred died on **27 January 1928** at Brighton, City of Holdfast Bay, South Australia, aged about 74. He was buried at **North Brighton Cemetery**, City of Holdfast Bay, South Australia. His wife Jane, who died in 1934, is interred with him on a joint family headstone.

**Born:** 21 July 1880, OB Flat, South Australia | **Died:** 24 April 1965, Adelaide, South Australia | **Parents:** Wilhelm August Sporer & Bertha Augusta Bottroff | **Spouse:** [[James Telfer (1866–1946)]] (m. 24 Oct 1917) | **Daughter:** Vida Templer (1919–2021)

## Life Summary

Alma Ida Sporer was born on 21 July 1880 at OB Flat, South Australia, the daughter of Wilhelm August Sporer and Bertha Augusta Bottroff.

She married James Telfer, eldest son of [[John Telfer (1840–1913)]] and Martha Allen, on 24 October 1917 at St Martins Church, Mount Gambier. James, then 49, was a newspaper agent and later shopkeeper; Alma was 37. Together they established a general store at Glencoe West which housed the local Post Office. Their only child, Vida, was born on 8 March 1919.

Alma died on 24 April 1965 at Adelaide, South Australia, and was buried in the Lake Terrace Cemetery, Mount Gambier, beside her husband James (d. 1946).

## Family Stories

Alma Ida Sporer married James Telfer at Mount Gambier in 1917, and together they ran the general store at Glencoe West — a store that also served as the local Post Office and sold groceries, hardware, drapery and other goods needed by the farming community. James was an Elder at the local Presbyterian Church. They had one daughter, Vida. James died in 1946; Alma died in 1965.

*(From the Borders to the Bush, pp.235–236)*

## Family Stories

### A Christmas Gift — Ernie's Book

Charlie's brother Ernie (Ernest John Telfer) wrote a book about his missionary work titled *Amongst Australian Aborigines*. A copy was given to Charlie and Amy as a Christmas gift, inscribed "Charlie & Amy, with love & Christmas wishes, from Eva." The book later passed to their son Murray and his wife Shirley at Ungarra. *(Inscription in front of "Amongst Australian Aborigines" by E.J. Telfer, 1939)*

Amy Ellen Provis married Francis Charles Telfer at Stokes in 1909 and together they raised ten children on a pioneering farm at Ungarra on the Eyre Peninsula. Life was brutally hard for her — no electricity, no running water, no refrigeration, no washing machine. She cooked on a wood stove, baked all the family's bread using homemade yeast made from hops, potatoes, flour and water, and made butter that she had to drive 18 miles into Tumby Bay in a sulky with one horse before the heat of the day. The money from the butter bought whatever groceries she could manage. She did the family laundry with a copper that had to be stoked with wood, two tubs, a scrubbing board and homemade soap, and ironed with a box iron full of hot coals. She carried water from the sheds in four-gallon kerosene tin buckets for all household needs. With a baby every couple of years, she somehow kept the household running through it all. Her daughters remembered that there was no entertainment as such in those days, "but plenty of hard work and just enough rest to keep us going." *(From the Borders to the Bush, pp.130–131)*

On **6 April 1909**, she married [[Francis Charles Telfer (1875–1954)]] at Stokes, South Australia. The wedding was reportedly covered by a local newspaper article — "Family Wedding at Jamestown" — which mentions the celebration.

Together they raised **ten children** on family farms, moving from the mid-north toward the Eyre Peninsula over the decades. Amy passed away in October 1951, predeceasing her husband Francis by about three years.

Her name appears in Murray John Telfer's profile as "Amy May" in some vault records, but her registered birth name is **Amy Ellen Provis**.

---

## Parents: The Provis & Thorpe Families

**George Provis** (Amy's father) — married **Emily Ellen Thorpe** on 15 June 1882. Emily's parents were **Charles Robert Thorpe** (1832–1893) and **Amelia White** (1833–1916).

## Life Summary

Arnold Cuthbert Lawrie — known as "Cuth" — was born on 22 June 1895 at Telowie, South Australia, the son of John and Elizabeth (née Nunan) Lawrie of Nelshaby, near Port Pirie. He was a compositor in the printing trade and a skilled artisan.

He married Hazel Rose Telfer on 28 June 1924. During the early years of their marriage they lived in Adelaide, but the Great Depression forced them to leave the city and seek work in the country. They moved to Ceduna on the Far West Coast, where Cuth was employed at the gypsum works.

As economic conditions improved, the family left the West Coast and moved to Murray Bridge, where Cuth resumed his trade as a compositor at the *Murray Valley Standard* newspaper.

He was a keen sportsman — an excellent footballer, cricketer and tennis player. He loved fishing and would travel to Streaky Bay and Smoky Bay where there was an abundance of fish. He would shoot rabbits to help supplement the family's food.

# Arthur Clifford Stribling (1890–1918)

**Role:** Son of Alfred George Stribling and Jane Murray (Farrow) Stribling — Telfer in-law line (Farrow branch, grandson of Charles Farrow & Elizabeth Hannah Telfer)
**Born:** 4 February 1890 — South Australia
**Died:** 25 April 1918 (aged 28) — wounded in action near Villers-Bretonneux, France, died of wounds the same day (Second Battle of Villers-Bretonneux)
**Buried:** Blangy-Tronville Communal Cemetery, Département de la Somme, Picardie, France — Grave 22

**Parents:** Alfred George Stribling and Jane Murray Farrow Stribling, of Rutland Avenue, Brighton, South Australia

**Aunts/uncles (Farrow siblings of his mother):** [[Amy Farrow Stribling (1868–1945)]], [[George Hope Farrow (1872–1919)]], Charles Farrow Jr, Mary Bayes Farrow (1875–1938, m. Lillecrapp), plus others.

## Life Summary

Arthur Clifford "Cliff" Stribling was born **4 February 1890** in South Australia, the eldest son of **Alfred George Stribling** and **Jane Murray (Farrow) Stribling**. He was a **farmer from Tarlee, South Australia** prior to enlisting — the same Tarlee/Finniss district from which his mother's Farrow family came.

### Military Service (World War I)

Cliff enlisted in the Australian Imperial Force and served in the **50th Infantry Battalion (B Company)** as **Private, Service No. 2731**. He embarked with the **6th Reinforcements** from Adelaide on **23 October 1916** aboard HMAT **"Port Melbourne" (A16)** for Devonport, England.

He was hospitalised with illness for eight weeks on arrival and did not join his battalion on the Western Front near **Ploegsteert, Belgium** until mid-July 1917. After a foot injury hospitalisation from January to March 1918, he rejoined his battalion near **Arras** in late March 1918.

### Death

Cliff was **wounded in action near Villers-Bretonneux and died of these wounds on 25 April 1918**, aged 28 — during the Second Battle of Villers-Bretonneux. He was buried at **Blangy-Tronville Communal Cemetery, France, Grave 22**, one of sixteen Australians interred in the village cemetery. He is commemorated on the **Australian War Memorial Roll of Honour, Panel 151**.

### School Renaming (local commemoration)

In **September 2017** the school in **Blangy-Tronville**, France, was **renamed in honour of Arthur Clifford "Cliff" Stribling** — a South Australian soldier interred with fifteen other Australians in the village cemetery. (Australian War Memorial / Virtual War Memorial Australia commemorative note.)

# Bertha Telfer (Alcorn)

**Role:** Adopted daughter of John & Caroline Telfer — missionary, "first white woman" in remote NW-Australian postings
**Born:** ~1872 (aged 93 at death in 1965)
**Died:** 10 August 1965 — Serene Nursing Home, Lockleys, South Australia
**Buried:** West Terrace Cemetery, Adelaide (Portion Road 5 Ext)
**Spouse:** James Alcorn (official, Broome pearl fisheries); one son Frank

## Life Summary

Bertha was the adopted daughter of John and Caroline Telfer. As a child her mother died and her father — a Swiss immigrant named Moelling — could not care for his four children, so Bertha was taken in and raised by the Telfer family. She studied at Rev Lockhart Morton's College in Adelaide preparing for missionary service and was accepted by the United Aborigines Mission in December 1908. At the Burnt Bridge Mission on the Macleay River in 1906, she gave addresses alongside Mrs Rudder and Mrs Ingram. She was a tiny woman with enormous courage — the book *Amongst Australian Aborigines* describes her going to many places where a white woman had never been before, full of fun, with a simple faith. She would "just say a little prayer and the dear Lord will look after me." She later worked at La Grange Bay mission station in northwestern Australia (near Broome), a particularly remote posting. Around 1915–17 while at Sunday Island in the Buccaneer Archipelago near Broome, she met and married James Alcorn, an official with the Broome pearl fisheries. They had one son, Frank. After returning to South Australia and spending time at Willow Plains and Warcowie, they moved to New Guinea where Jim had a government job. They later lived at Clare and then Norwood, where they ran a small shop. After Jim's death, Bertha lived at Edwardstown in a granny flat built onto Frank's property until she became too feeble. She spent her remaining years at the Serene Nursing Home at Lockleys and died on 10 August 1965, aged 93. *(From the Borders to the Bush, pp.127–129; Amongst Australian Aborigines, OCR ref line 16719: "Miss Bertha Telfer" at La Grange Bay, NW Australia)*

## Family Stories

🖊️ **Anecdote — as told in From the Borders to the Bush (book pp. 127–129):** Bertha was a tiny thing by anybody's measure — not the sort you'd picture knocking about the roughest end of the country. But when the call went out for a woman to take God's word into the far north-west, where no white woman had ever set foot, it was Bertha who crossed the sand. She didn't just preach; she swung a hammer and put up mission buildings with her own hands, one after another, out where there was nothing but heat and distance. And at La Grange Bay they found the most unlikely duty for her — she'd play her little organ for the prisoners, gentle music in a place that had never had any. Her faith was the plain, trusting sort, and it carried her through when stronger-looking folk wouldn't have lasted a month. She married James Alcorn toward the end of the Great War and settled into a quieter life, but she was the first white woman in that country, and nobody could take that from her.

*(Anecdote only — family colour, told as the elders tell it. Does not establish any relationship, date or place.)*

# Caroline Amelia Telfer (1842–1929)

**Lifespan:** 10 June 1842 – 24 August 1929

**Branch:** Masters → Telfer (married into)

**Role:** School teacher at Tarlee; matriarch of Willow Plains

## Photos

![Caroline amelia telfer portrait c1910](images/people/caroline-amelia-telfer-portrait-c1910.jpg)
*Caroline Amelia Telfer (née Masters) — studio portrait, circa 1910*

![Telfer family reunion c1920](images/people/telfer-family-reunion-c1920.jpg)
*Telfer family reunion, circa 1920 — a large multi-generational group portrait of about 25 people. John Telfer (1847–1929, aged ~73) and Caroline Amelia Telfer (1842–1929, aged ~78) seated centre with white beard and lace collar; their children and grandchildren stand around them in a studio setting with textured wallpaper backdrop on the left and dark curtain on the right*

## Biography

Caroline Amelia Masters was born 10th June 1842 in Brownsover, Warwickshire, England — daughter of [[Charles Masters (1809–1866)]] and [[Martha Williams Masters (1814–1896)]]. She emigrated to South Australia with her family on the *Templar*, arriving **24 November 1845**.

The family farmed at Flaxman's Valley, Angaston. Her father Charles farmed there until about 1865, after which Martha (with the help of her children) carried on.

### The School Teacher

Caroline and her sister Mary Ellen first tried opening a school at Gilberton, near the Forrester's Arms Hotel — a staging camp for bullockies. The railway bypassed the hotel and the town of Tarlee sprang up at the rail head instead, so the venture failed.

In 1870 she tried again, granted a licence by the Tarlee District Council. She taught in the original section of the Baptist Church with 41 pupils — 18 boys and 23 girls. The Tarlee school history records her "dedication and persistence that would do a present day teacher proud." She taught there until 17th August 1874.

### Marriage and Family

She married [[John Telfer (1847–1929)]] on 22nd September 1874 in the Tarlee Baptist Church (her schoolroom for four years). She was 32, he was 27. John's brother George and Caroline's sister Mary Ellen were witnesses.

On the marriage certificate she signed as C.A. Masters. In later years she dropped the "Amelia" because she didn't want her initials to be C.A.T. Telfer. From then on she was C.M. Telfer.

### The Move North

When the government opened the Northern Districts for farming, it was Caroline who urged John to apply. After his successful application they moved to Arkaba, where she gave birth to six sons in a one-roomed wood and iron hut with a hessian partition. The first of these, Ernest John, was the first white baby born at Willow Plains.

She and John died within hours of each other in August 1929 — she on the 24th, he on the 23rd — and are buried together at Clare Cemetery.

## Family Stories

*See [[John Telfer (1847–1929)]] for full stories, including the uncle's matchmaking, the pupil's poem for baby John Ernest, the adopted children, the C.A.T. initials, Caroline's brick oven, and Cocky the wonder bird.*

*(From the Borders to the Bush, pp.109-118)*

body_markdown:
# Charles Farrow (1836–1884)

**Role:** Husband of Elizabeth Hannah Telfer
**Born:** ~1836 (exact date unknown)
**Died:** 3 December 1884 — Pneumonia (aged 48)

Charles Farrow married Elizabeth Hannah Telfer (1836–1916) in 1856 (per FindAGrave). The book *From the Borders to the Bush* narrative records his death as 3 December 1884 from pneumonia (aged 48) — 32 years before Elizabeth's death in 1916. (The chapter header shows 1828–1876, but the narrative text is the authoritative source.)

His father was **Joseph Farrow (1814–1899)**, confirmed by FindAGrave ([[Joseph Farrow (1814–1899)]]). His mother is not identified on the FindAGrave record — Charles was born ~1836, twelve years before his father married Mary Ellen Bayes in 1848, so his mother was likely Joseph's first wife (unknown). Charles's daughter Mary Bayes Farrow (1875–1938) was named after Joseph's known wife Mary Bayes, indicating the Bayes name runs in the family.

Together he and Elizabeth had a large family including Jane Murray, Peter, John, Charles Jr, Esther Hannah, Elizabeth, Margaret, Sarah, Edith, James, Robert, William, Eva Agnes, George Hope, and Mary Bayes Farrow.

**Source:** *From the Borders to the Bush* — Chapter on Elizabeth Hannah Telfer

## Family Stories

🖊️ **Anecdote — as told in From the Borders to the Bush (book pp. 59–60):** Just nineteen years old, our Charles did something that even surprised the old hands. He walked into a deal with John Ridley — the very man who'd invented the stripper — and bought a hundred and fifty-two acres for three hundred and nineteen pounds. He christened the place Hope Farm. But land doesn't come with a roof, so every week he'd set out on foot from Kersbrook and trudge nearly forty-five miles to the farm, raise four days' worth of stone walls for his cottage, and then turn around and walk all the way back home — because come Sunday, he was determined to be in church.

*(Anecdote only — family colour, told as the elders tell it. Does not establish any relationship, date or place.)*

🖊️ **Anecdote — as told in From the Borders to the Bush (book pp. 59, 61):** Now here's a story that'll make you lose your nerve just hearing it. One day, coming up that long road towards Hope Farm, Charles stopped at a spring well to catch his breath — the one everyone called Tuppeny Well. And wouldn't you know it, a great bull had taken it into its head that this patch was his, and he pinned our Charles there. There wasn't a tree in sight to scramble up, so Charles did the only thing a man could — he shinned up the whip-post, the tall stockwhip pole, and sat up there while the beast glowered below. He waited up that post until full dark settled in, then dropped down and walked the last six miles to the farm with his heart in his throat the whole way.

*(Anecdote only — family colour, told as the elders tell it. Does not establish any relationship, date or place.)*

🖊️ **Anecdote — as told in From the Borders to the Bush (book pp. 60):** In March of 1865 the cottage they'd raised went up in flames — everything they'd scrimped and saved for, gone in one angry night of fire. But Charles Farrow was not a man to sit and grieve the ashes. He set to at once and built a bigger house, this time with a proper iron roof that would stand up to the weather and the years. And stand it has — that very house is still there today, sheltered and sound. When the family gathered back in Tarlee for the reunion in 1984, they all walked through it, and you could feel Charles in every stone and every beam.

*(Anecdote only — family colour, told as the elders tell it. Does not establish any relationship, date or place.)*

🖊️ **Anecdote — as told in From the Borders to the Bush (book pp. 60, 62):** If you want to know what mattered to our Charles, look no further than the church. In June of 1868 a band of folk gathered right there in the Farrow home to do something bold — to form a church of their own at Tarlee. Charles didn't just lend his parlour; he gave his whole self. For sixteen years he sat on the council as chairman and stood before the people as deacon and lay preacher, word of God on his lips till the end of his days. That Meeting you see standing in Tarlee owes its very beginning to a house on the Farrow farm.

*(Anecdote only — family colour, told as the elders tell it. Does not establish any relationship, date or place.)*

Charles Farrow married Elizabeth Telfer and the couple settled at Finniss Point, where they were close neighbours of the Flavel uncles who looked out for the young Telfer generation. It was these same uncles who knew of the high esteem in which the Tarlee schoolmistress Caroline Masters was held, and who steered young John Telfer her way — a chain of connections that ran right through the Farrow household at Finniss Point. Charles also stood as a witness at his sister-in-law Jane's second marriage to Frederick Parker, alongside his niece Jane Farrow, at the Wesleyan Church in Kapunda on Christmas Day 1871.

*(From the Borders to the Bush, pp.93, 110)*

### Children
- **Jane Murray Farrow Stribling (1857–1934)** — confirmed via FindAGrave memorial 147662212. Married Stribling, found in Tarlee area.
- **George Hope Farrow (1872–1919)** — confirmed via FindAGrave memorial 196572529. Died aged 47.
- **Mary Bayes Farrow Lillecrapp (1875–1938)** — confirmed via FindAGrave memorial 201506962. Named Mary Bayes, reinforcing the Bayes family connection.

Cites GenSA death reg FARROW/Charles/03-Dec-1884/age 48/Gilbert/142/330; GenSA marriage 25/190; death notice (*Express & Telegraph* 6 Dec 1884); obituary (*Kapunda Herald* 5 Dec 1884). — accessed 06 Aug 2026. [Link](https://www.wikitree.com/wiki/Farrow-2277)

Transcribed by Lorraine Larment (photographs by Marylin and Steve Jones). — accessed 12 Aug 2026. [Link](http://www.ozburials.com/CemsSA/tarlee.htm)

Confirmed by two independent source groups (Find a Grave 184343881 + WikiTree citing GenSA death registration 142/330 and two contemporary newspaper notices). the book *From the Borders to the Bush*'s chapter header "1828–1876" is a confirmed typographical error.

## Family Stories

Clarice May — known as May — was the eldest daughter of Francis Charles and Amy Telfer. She contributed a first-hand account of her father's pioneering life to the family history. She recalled how he drove his horses and wagon down from Hawker to the Eyre Peninsula to take up land, and described the gruelling childhood she and her siblings endured: walking three and a half miles to school each day, then coming home to feed hay into the chaff cutter by lantern light — "the prickles and mice it contained was not funny" — bagging up ten to twelve bags of chaff every night, tending sheep, milking cows, turning the milk separator, and pumping water by hand for the garden. She married Verbin Reginald Fatchen in 1935 and raised a large family. *(From the Borders to the Bush, pp.130–131)*

# David Parker (1822–1888)

## **Note — two sons named Hugh Parker**

David Parker **did** have two sons named **Hugh Parker**, both with his first wife Isabella Kelly. A prior data-hygiene correction (see below) removed the two bare `Hugh Parker` refs on the grounds that "no dedicated records exist"; that conclusion was **reversed on 26 Aug 2026** when evidence was found. The two sons are:
1. **[[Hugh Parker (1859–1861)]]** — born Nov 1859, Virginia SA; died 13 Dec 1861 (aged ~2), Peachy Belt SA. *Lead — parent link from WikiTree + SA death reg (Port Gawler 14/144); exact-date burial at Two Wells (FindAGrave).*
2. **[[Hugh Parker (1864–1891)]]** — born 31 Oct 1864, Virginia SA; died 23 Nov 1891 (aged 27), Hundred of Pirie SA; buried Port Pirie Cemetery. *VERIFIED — WikiTree + FindAGrave + father's 1888 death notice ("leaving seven sons and one daughter", which only counts with Hugh included).*

Both were named after David's own father, **Hugh Parker**. The name was reused after infant #1 died in 1861, a common practice of the era. These are **sons**, not the grandson Hugh Kelly Parker (1896–1959).

**What happened (original 26 Aug 2026 correction, now superseded):** the bare frontmatter refs `Elizabeth Parker`, `Frederick Robert Parker`, `Hugh Kelly Parker`, and two `Hugh Parker` were removed. `Hugh Kelly Parker` (1896–1959) is a grandson (via David Parker 1856–1906), not a son; `Elizabeth Parker` (1879–1957) is a granddaughter (daughter of William Humphrey Parker & Hannah Baker); `Frederick Robert Parker` resolved to a different family (~1838–1928, son of George Parker, husband of Jean Telfer). The two bare `Hugh Parker` refs were dropped as "no dedicated records exist" — but research (26 Aug 2026) proved records **do** exist and both were genuine sons; they are re-added above.

## Life Summary

David Parker was born on 29 June 1822 at Ragged Hill Farm, Tarbolton, Ayrshire, Scotland. He was christened on 13 July 1822 at Tarbolton, with parents listed as Hugh Parker and Christian Fulton.

He married Isabella Kelly on 9 August 1846 in Barony, Lanarkshire, Scotland. In the 1851 Scotland Census, he was recorded as a Victualler living at Wallace Street, Wallacetown, St Quivox, Ayrshire, with wife Isabella and infant son William H (age 1).

The family emigrated to South Australia in 1852 aboard the ship **Martin Luther** (arriving 4 May 1852 in Adelaide), travelling with wife Isabella and three children.

After Isabella's death on 6 July 1867, he married Clementina Minto on 20 June 1871 at Hailes House, Hackney, Adelaide.

With Isabella he also had two sons named **Hugh Parker**: the first (born Nov 1859) died in infancy in December 1861, and the name was given to a second son born in 1864, who survived to age 27 but died in 1891 — both named in honour of David's own father, Hugh Parker. See [[Hugh Parker (1859–1861)]] and [[Hugh Parker (1864–1891)]].

He died on 4 April 1888 at his residence "Wheatlands", Hundred of Pirie, South Australia, aged 65, and was buried at Port Pirie Cemetery.

# Dinah Flavel (1821–1844)

**Role:** Second wife of [[Francis Telfer (1809–1895)]] — mother of his daughter Jean
**Born:** 10 June 1821 — Pytchley, Kettering Borough, Northamptonshire, England
**Died:** 20 March 1844 (aged 22) — Chain of Ponds, Adelaide Hills, South Australia
**Buried:** West Terrace Cemetery, Adelaide, South Australia

## Family

| Relation | Name |
|----------|------|
| **Spouse** | [[Francis Telfer (1809–1895)]] (m. 4 November 1839) |
| **Daughter** | Jean Telfer (7 Aug 1840 – 15 Jul 1892) — m. A.F. Telfer |

## Life Summary

Dinah Flavel was born on 10 June 1821 at Pytchley, Northamptonshire, England — the daughter of Joseph Flavel (1797–1840) and Mary Bayes. Little is known of her childhood in England.

She married Francis Telfer on 4 November 1839 — just months after the death of his first wife Jean Murray. The marriage took place at Holy Trinity Church, Adelaide, South Australia. Dinah was 18 years old; Francis was 30 with three young children from his first marriage.

Dinah gave birth to a daughter, Jean, on 7 August 1840 at Chain of Ponds in the Adelaide Hills. She died just over three years later, on 20 March 1844 at Chain of Ponds, barely 22 years old. She was buried at West Terrace Cemetery, Adelaide.

Her brief life was marked by the frontier conditions of early South Australia — a young English immigrant who married a widowed Scottish farmer with young children, had a daughter, and died before reaching age 23.

## Timeline

| Date | Event |
|------|-------|
| 10 Jun 1821 | Born — Pytchley, Northamptonshire, England |
| ~1838 | Emigrated to South Australia |
| 4 Nov 1839 | Married [[Francis Telfer (1809–1895)]] at Holy Trinity Church, Adelaide |
| 7 Aug 1840 | Daughter Jean born at Chain of Ponds, SA |
| 20 Mar 1844 | Died (aged 22) — Chain of Ponds, SA |
| | Buried — West Terrace Cemetery, Adelaide |

## Family Stories

### The Flavel Family Voyage

Dinah travelled to South Australia aboard the *Prince George* with her parents Joseph and Mary Flavel and her six siblings, alongside the Telfer family. Her brother William Flavel later wrote about arriving at Port Misery — walking barefoot through the sandhills where the summer heat was so fierce he "had to run from one bush to another till I got clear of the sand." Barely four months after Francis's first wife Jean Murray died, Dinah married him and became stepmother to three young children — James (7), Esther (5), and Elizabeth (4). She was just 18.

*(From the Borders to the Bush, pp.23–25)*

## Sources

- **Source:** Donald Telfer, *From the Borders to the Bush* (ISBN 0 7316 6387 X), pp. 21–25 — extract via vision_analyze 19 June 2026
- **Source (marriage date 4 Nov 1839):** [Geneanet — Christopher STEELE family tree, Francis Telfer](https://gw.geneanet.org/steelorama?lang=en&n=telfer&p=francis) — "Married November 4, 1839" to Dinah Flavel, Adelaide, SA. Accessed 18 Aug 2026.

- **Source (marriage occurred pre-1842 register):** [Jaunay — SA Births, Deaths & Marriages before civil registration](http://www.jaunay.com/earlybdm.php) — lists "Francis TELFER Dinah FLAVEL" as a pre-June-1842 church marriage. Accessed 18 Aug 2026.
- FindAGrave: [Dinah Flavel Telfer (1821–1844)](https://www.findagrave.com/memorial/166265805) — memorial 166265805, West Terrace Cemetery. Accessed 18 June 2026.
- WikiTree: [Flavel-64](https://www.wikitree.com/wiki/Flavel-64) — profile for Dinah Flavel. Accessed 18 June 2026.

> **Marriage-date correction (18 Aug 2026):** The marriage date was corrected from **4 May 1839** to **4 November 1839** under the verifier's hands. Corroborated by 3+ independent source groups — Geneanet compiled tree (read live), RootsWeb moadfamily compiled tree, the family book *A Telfer Family Tree* (per Swing 1), and the Jaunay SA pre-civil-registration marriage index confirming the marriage occurred pre-1842. The prior "4 May" value had no primary/compiled support and is an apparent May/Nov transcription error. Some records suggest a Douglas Telfer whose ashes were interred at St John's Cemetery, Gordon (New South Wales) on 29 November 1967, while other records point to a Reverend Douglas Telfer operating in Canada. # Elizabeth Beattie (1802–1891)

**Role:** Wife of James Telfer (1796–1863) — mother of the South Australian Telfer immigrants

## Family

---

## Family Stories

### The Mother Who Stayed Behind

Elizabeth Beattie was born in 1802 and married James Telfer, the eldest son of James Telfer (1761–1845) and Betty Hutton. The couple settled in the Jedburgh area of Roxburghshire, Scotland, where they raised their family. James worked as a farm labourer — a hard life in the Scottish Borders.

### Raising a Family

Elizabeth and James had at least five children who survived to adulthood: James (born 1829), twin daughters Elizabeth and Margaret (1832), Robert (1837), John (1840), and Adam Francis (1842). The 1841 Census shows the family living at Castleton, with James working the land and Elizabeth managing the household.

### Tragedy and Change

In 1863, James Telfer died from injuries sustained in an agricultural accident. This left Elizabeth a widow in her sixties with most of her children grown. The loss of her husband changed everything. One by one, her children made the decision to leave Scotland and seek a new life in South Australia.

James Jr arrived first, followed by Robert, John, and Adam Francis. Even her daughter Elizabeth, now married to John Charles Dillon, made the journey. Elizabeth Beattie stayed behind — the old country was all she knew, and at her age, the voyage was too much. She lived out her remaining years in Scotland, likely with family who remained, passing away in 1891 at around 89 years of age. She never saw her children or grandchildren in Australia again.

*(From the Borders to the Bush, pp.19–20)*

## Sources

- *From the Borders to the Bush* by Hope Simmons (1989), pp.19–20
- 1841 Census, Castleton, Roxburghshire, Scotland
- Statutory Death Index — James Telfer (1863), agricultural accident
- Castleton Parish Records — baptism records

🖊️ **Anecdote — as told in From the Borders to the Bush (book pp. 269–272, 280–285):** Bessie was the one who made the family tree flower. She came from Edgerston and married William Beaton, and look what she sent out into the world: eight children, and six of them into teaching careers. William ran the post office, sat as Chairman and Clerk of the Council, and helped start the Tantanoola Football Club in the years it mattered. And it was Bessie's own hand that pegged the prize boards at the Show — her scones, her verbenas, her pastry, even ironed shirts took a ribbon, just like her mother's. She watched two wars take her boys. Harold and Frank served and came back, though the war marked them. And Colin she never saw home again; the Japanese took him at Changi and he died on the Burma Railway at twenty-nine, and it broke her. She went to her rest at Tantanoola in 1948, a queen of that town's day.

## Life Summary

Elizabeth Beattie Telfer, known as "Betty" in the family, was the second child and eldest daughter of James and Elizabeth Telfer. She emigrated to South Australia with her brothers James and Robert on the *Oliver Lang* in 1854, landing in Melbourne and travelling overland to SA. She married John Charles Dillon in 1856.

## Family Stories

Elizabeth Beattie Telfer — known in the family as Betty — was born in 1832 at Castleton in Scotland. She was the only daughter among the five children of James and Elizabeth. In 1854, she emigrated to South Australia with her brothers James and Robert on the ship *Oliver Lang*, landing in Melbourne and then travelling overland to Uncle Francis Telfer at "Macoota" in the Adelaide Hills.

Betty married John Charles Dillon on 18 December 1856 at the home of her uncle Francis Telfer, at "Macoota", Chain of Ponds. John had come from Ireland. They made their home in the South East of South Australia and had a large family of ten children — five sons and five daughters — though tragically, one son was stillborn and twin girls lived only 15 minutes.

The Dillon family spread through the South East region. The connection between the Telfers and Dillons runs deep — Betty was the bridge between the two families, and her descendants are still found in the Mount Gambier district today.

Betty died in 1896, aged 64. John Charles Dillon died in 1906 at the age of 79.

Elizabeth is also remembered through the Dillon family stories (in her husband John's profile, retold from *From the Borders to the Bush*, pp. 214–219) — the account of her coming out to South Australia on the *Oliver Lang* in 1854, her wedding to John Charles Dillon at Kersbrook on 18 December 1856, and the lighter tales of the wild Irish woman, the Sunday School chase, the Millbrook Reservoir and the rosemary miracle.

*(From the Borders to the Bush, pp. 214–215)*

# Elizabeth Hannah Telfer (1836–1916)

**Role:** Second daughter of Francis Telfer — matriarch of the Farrow line at Hope Farm, Tarlee
**Born:** 7 June 1836 — Dumfriesshire, Scotland
**Died:** 11 October 1916 (aged 80) — Tarlee, South Australia
**Buried:** Tarlee Cemetery (beside husband)
**Spouse:** Charles Farrow (~1836 – Dec 1884) — m. 28 March 1856
**Ship:** *Prince George* — arrived Port Adelaide 26 December 1838 (aged 2)

## Family

| Relation | Name |
|----------|------|
| **Father** | [[Francis Telfer (1809–1895)]] |
| **Mother** | Jean Murray (1810–1839) |
| **Husband** | Charles Farrow (~1836 – Dec 1884) |
| **Sister** | [[Esther Jane Telfer (1834–1909)]] |

### Children (all born at Hope Farm, Tarlee)

| Child | Spouse |
|-------|--------|
| Jane Murray Farrow | Alfred Stribling |
| Esther "Ettie" Farrow | Richard Pelling Latter |
| Elizabeth Telfer Farrow | Thomas Holloway |
| Joseph Francis Farrow | Annie Louise Downton |
| Charles Farrow Jr | Ethel Mary Sambell |
| Amy Farrow | Sidney Stribling |
| John James Telfer Farrow | Emily Smithers |
| George Hope Farrow | Caroline Stanton |
| Mary Bayes Farrow | Alfred Edward Lillecrapp |
| Eva Agnes Farrow | Walter Hookings |

## Life Summary

Elizabeth was born in Dumfriesshire, Scotland to Francis Telfer and Jean Murray. She was just two years old when the family sailed for South Australia on the *Prince George*, arriving at Port Adelaide on 26 December 1838. Her mother Jean died at the Emigration Depot barely a month later.

She grew up at Chain of Ponds and Kersbrook in the Adelaide Hills. On 28 March 1856, aged 19, she married **Charles Farrow** at her family's home on Section 6146, Parra Wirra. The ceremony was performed by Rev. William Vercoe, witnessed by A.B. Murray and P.M. Murray — Elizabeth's uncles.

They settled at **Hope Farm**, Finniss Point, near Tarlee — 152 acres Charles had bought from John Ridley for £319/4. Charles had walked from Kersbrook to Tarlee weekly carrying food, then built a small stone cottage by hand with an axe.

Elizabeth was described as a "very kind and most gracious lady, always quick to help anyone in need." She was a foundation member of Tarlee Baptist Church. After Charles died of pneumonia in 1884, she ran the farm with her sons for over three decades.

Her father Francis Telfer came to stay with Elizabeth at Hope Farm before his death on 2 September 1895, and was buried at Tarlee Cemetery.

She died on 11 October 1916, aged 80, and was buried beside Charles.

## Family Stories

### The Bull at Tuppeny Well

Not long after Charles bought Hope Farm, he was walking there on a hot Monday. About two miles south of Tarlee on the eastern side of the main road was a shallow well called "Tuppeny Well" — the owner charged tuppence to water bullocks and horses. An irate bull came up for a drink. There were no trees nearby, so Charles climbed a six-to-seven-foot whip post used to draw water and sat there until dark when the bull wandered off. Then he walked the remaining six miles home.

*(From the Borders to the Bush, p.59)*

### The Fire of 1865

On Saturday, 25 March 1865, fire destroyed the Farrow cottage. The roof was gone, part of the front wall collapsed, and most of their belongings. Amos Flavel's diary recorded it: *"Mr Farrow helping put out the fire but the roof was destroyed & part of the front wall of the house & a very great deal of other things."*

Charles rebuilt — a larger house with a galvanized iron roof and guttering. It was still standing when the Tarlee reunion was held on 2 December 1984.

*(From the Borders to the Bush, pp.59–60; Amos Flavel Diary, 25 Mar 1865)*

### The Water Walk

During a long dry summer, the rainwater tanks at Hope Farm ran dry. With three small girls to care for, Elizabeth would tie baby Elizabeth Telfer Farrow to the kitchen table leg with a leather strap, take Jane (age 5) and Esther (age 3), and walk 14 miles to Deep Creek to carry back water for the family's daily washing.

*(From the Borders to the Bush, p.61)*

### Charles's Last Night

On 2 December 1884, Charles returned home from his rounds travelling the district with his draught stallion for mating. He was wet through from heavy showers. He told his son Charles Junior to put the horses away: *"I am feeling very ill."*

That night he became much worse. Elizabeth woke Charles Junior to ride to Kapunda for the doctor. The doctor arrived around 4am and promised to return that afternoon. Charles Farrow died just before the doctor got back — pneumonia, in the days before penicillin.

*(From the Borders to the Bush, p.62)*

### Tarlee Baptist Church

In June 1868, the Farrow home hosted the founding meeting of Tarlee Baptist Church. Charles was appointed Deacon and lay preacher, serving for over 16 years. The Minute Book recorded after his death:

> *"This Church deeply mourns the death of Brother Farrow Senior and desires to record the Church's appreciation of his devoted labours in the cause of Christ among us."*

*(From the Borders to the Bush, p.63)*

### Ashley Cooper's 80th Birthday

Ashley Cooper, born in 1908, was the grandson of Elizabeth's daughter Esther Farrow. He worked for the Adelaide Steamship Company as an auditor, travelled to coastal shipping centres, and during WWII was transferred to Perth to oversee merchant ships used as troop carriers. He travelled extensively in the Flinders Ranges — Parachilna, Beltana, Moralana — and wrote a book on the history of Beltana. He suffered a stroke but kept typing one-fingered. He celebrated his 80th birthday in March 1988.

*(From the Borders to the Bush, p.68)*

## Sources

- **Note:** the *From the Borders to the Bush* header lists Charles Farrow as (1837–1876) and the family tree as (1828–1876), but the narrative clearly states he died in December 1884 — 32 years before Elizabeth's 1916 death. The detailed story (Dec 1884, pneumonia) is taken as accurate over the header dates. Born ~1836 based on being age 19 when buying the farm in Nov 1855.
- **Source:** Donald Telfer, *From the Borders to the Bush* (ISBN 0 7316 6387 X), pp. 58–75 — extract via OCR 19 June 2026

- **Oz Burials:** [Tarlee Cemetery — Elizabeth Farrow, 11 Oct 1916 (aged 80)](http://www.ozburials.com/CemsSA/tarlee.htm) — headstone transcription
- **Find a Grave:** [Elizabeth Telfer Farrow (1836–1916) — Memorial 184343892](https://www.findagrave.com/memorial/184343892/elizabeth-farrow) — confirms birth 3 Jun 1836, death 11 Oct 1916

## Life Summary

Elizabeth "Betty" Hutton was born in 1774 and married James Telfer around 1795 in the Castleton / Liddesdale area of the Scottish Borders. She and James raised at least eight children at the family farm in Castleton parish, Roxburghshire.

Her maiden surname is confirmed by the Scottish Statutory Death Index registrations for her children — William Telfer's death entry records mother's maiden surname as "Hutton". This same surname appears in the WikiTree profile for her son Francis Telfer (Telfer-400), linking her as the mother of the Australian immigrant branch.

Betty outlived her husband by eight years. She died in April 1853 and was buried alongside James at Old Castleton Cemetery in Newcastleton.

> **Source:** [FindAGrave — Elizabeth "Betty" Hutton Telfer](https://www.findagrave.com/memorial/170769934/elizabeth_betty-telfer) — accessed 27 May 2026

---

## Family Stories

### The Woman at the Heart of the Clan

Elizabeth "Betty" Hutton was born in 1774 in the Scottish Borders and married James Telfer sometime around 1795. She would go on to be the mother of eight children — six sons and two daughters — and the matriarch of a family that spread from the Liddesdale valley to the other side of the world.

### Life at Greenholm

Betty and James began their married life at Greenholm, a small farming area in Liddesdale near Newcastleton, Roxburghshire. There she gave birth to their first six children between 1796 and 1805: James, Isobel, Adam, Margaret, Robert, and John. Life for a hand-loom weaver's wife was demanding. The cottage was small, the winters were harsh, and there were always hungry mouths to feed. Betty managed her household, raised the children, and kept the family running while James worked the loom and tended the sheep.

### The Move to Blackburnfoot

Sometime around 1805, the family moved a short distance north to a place called Blackburnfoot at the northern end of Newcastleton. The area had its own small weaving industry, which suited James's trade. It was there that Betty's last two children were born — Francis in February 1809, and William in April 1811. Blackburnfoot has since vanished — demolished when the railway line was built through Liddesdale in the 1840s — but it held the childhood home of the man who would one day cross the world.

### The Widow's Years

James Telfer died in December 1845 at the age of 84, leaving Betty a widow after about 50 years of marriage. She outlived him by eight years, dying at Castleton on 4 April 1853 at the age of 79. She was laid to rest beside him in Old Castleton Cemetery. Their headstone reads simply: *"Elizabeth Hutton his spouse"* — a quiet marker for a woman who raised eight children through the hard Border winters, who watched most of them scatter, and whose son Francis would help build a new Telfer legacy in South Australia.

*(From the Borders to the Bush, pp.17–20)*

## Family Stories

### A Quiet Life in Liddesdale

Elizabeth Oliver was born around 1807 and married Robert Telfer, one of the younger brothers of Francis Telfer who would later emigrate to South Australia. Unlike Francis, Robert and Elizabeth stayed in Scotland, living in Newcastleton in the Liddesdale valley where the Telfers had been for generations.

### The 1841 Census Snapshot

The 1841 Census for Newcastleton gives us a rare clear window into Elizabeth's life. The entry reads: "Robert Telfer 36, and Betty 34 with children, Elizabeth 7, James 5, Jean 3, and John 2, also James aged 75, and Betty Hutton 65 of Newcastleton."

So in 1841, Elizabeth (recorded as "Betty") was living with Robert at age 34, with four young children under eight. Also in the household were Robert's elderly parents — James Telfer (75) and Betty Hutton (65) — making it a multi-generational home. This tells us that Elizabeth not only raised her own children but likely helped care for her aging in-laws as well.

### A Short Life

Elizabeth died in 1846 at around 39 years old, leaving Robert a widower with four children to raise — the oldest just twelve. She never lived to see the next chapter of the Telfer story, when some of the next generation would follow Uncle Francis to Australia. Her children — Elizabeth, James, Jean, and John — carried on the family name in Scotland, and some of their descendants would later make the journey to the new world.

*(From the Borders to the Bush, p.18)*

## Sources

- 1841 Census, Newcastleton, Roxburghshire — records Robert Telfer (36), Elizabeth/Betty (34), and children Elizabeth (7), James (5), Jean (3), John (2), plus parents James Telfer (75) and Betty Hutton (65)
- *From the Borders to the Bush* by Hope Simmons (1989), p.18
- Castleton Parish Records, OPR 784/1 — baptism records for Telfer children

Elizabeth (known in family records as **Elizabeth Telfer** Farrow, child #3 of the ten Farrow children) was born at Hope Farm, Tarlee on 22 August 1861. She married **Thomas Holloway** (1856–1922) on 23 March 1883. Her descendants form the Holloway–Serle–Marks–Grosser family line recorded in the family's 2017 supplement tree.

🖊️ **Anecdote — as told in From the Borders to the Bush (book pp. 60):** In the dry years you did what you had to, and no one did it better than the family's Elizabeth. One summer the water all but vanished, and she needed to do the week's wash. So she strapped baby little Elizabeth to a table leg with a good stout leather strap so the mite couldn't wander into trouble — then she took off with five-year-old Jane and three-year-old Esther tagging along, and walked the full mile and a quarter down to Deep Creek. Between hanging on to two little girls and hauling the wash water back up that hill, that woman earned her keep a hundred times over. That's the kind of arm our grandmothers had.
