# Ernest John Telfer (1878–1953)

**Role:** Son of John Telfer and Caroline Amelia Masters — brother of Francis Charles Telfer, missionary, author
**Born:** 2 Sep 1878 — Willow Plains (near Hawker), South Australia
**Died:** 9 Jul 1953 — Waverley, New South Wales
**Buried:** Rookwood General Cemetery, Rookwood, NSW (Zone F, Independent Section K, Grave 1760)
**Parents:** [[John Telfer (1847–1929)]] & [[Caroline Amelia Telfer (1842–1929)]] (née Masters)
**Brother:** [[Francis Charles Telfer (1875–1954)]]
**Siblings:** William James, Albert George, Walter William, Edwin Gilbert
**Spouse:** Florence Nicholas (m. 24 Feb 1909)
**Children:** John Ernest, Jessica Veronica, Lloyd Wilbur, Gweneth Miranda

![Rev ej telfer portrait](images/people/rev-ej-telfer-portrait.png)
*Rev. E.J. Telfer — portrait frontispiece from "Amongst Australian Aborigines" (c.1939)*

![Rev EJ Telfer group 199](images/people/Rev-EJ-Telfer-group-199.jpg)
*Rev. E.J. Telfer (seated left) with Miss V.E. Turner, Mr. T. Graham, Mr. J. Jago, Mr. G.L. Aitken, and Mr. H. Rotherham — group photo from "Amongst Australian Aborigines" (c.1939), p.199*

---

## Family

| Relation | Name |
|---|---|
| **Mother** | [[Caroline Amelia Telfer (1842–1929)]] (née Masters) |
| **Father** | [[John Telfer (1847–1929)]] |
| **Brother** | [[Francis Charles Telfer (1875–1954)]] |
| **Siblings** | William James Telfer, Albert George Telfer, Walter William Telfer, Edwin Gilbert Telfer |
| **Spouse** | [[Florence Nicholas|Florence Nicholas Telfer]] (m. 24 Feb 1909) |
| **Children** | John Ernest, Jessica Veronica, Lloyd Wilbur, Gweneth Miranda |

---

## Life Summary

Ernie was the first white baby born at Willow Plains, the family's pioneering property near Hawker, on **2 September 1878**. He was born in a galvanised iron room and tent — the only shelter the family had at the time. His uncle, Walter "Watt" Telfer, once described young Ernie as "a larrikin," suggesting a spirited nature.

He trained for ministry at Rev. Lockhart Morton's College (Angas College) in Adelaide. On 8 February 1901 he was accepted by the Council of the United Aborigines' Mission as a missionary for the Macleay River district of New South Wales. His induction was held at Pitt Street Congregational Church, Sydney, on 2 April 1901.

In April 1906 he was set apart to pioneer mission work through scattered Aboriginal camps across New South Wales. In late 1907 came the call to go West — he travelled to Western Australia with Peter Wandy, a native helper originally from Coolgardie, stopping in South Australia en route to enlist support.

On 24 February 1909 he married Miss Florence Nicholas of Boulder City, Western Australia. The following day they commenced work at the Dulhi-Gunyah (meaning "little child's home") Orphanage in East Perth. While Ernie travelled inland, Mrs Telfer remained in charge of the orphanage.

In May 1910 he undertook a gruelling overland journey of over 2000 miles to Derby, travelling by steamer to Carnarvon and then by bicycle, accompanied by his cousin Eustace Radford. They crossed waist-deep rivers carrying their bicycles and gear, were shadowed by crows in the heat, and camped in the bush.

In March 1911, Ernie and Florence resigned from the UAM staff. Shortly afterwards Ernie entered the Baptist ministry, accepting the pastorate at Terowie, South Australia from 1912 to 1916. He later held charges in Tasmania and New South Wales, the last of which was at Waverley, NSW.

In 1949 he became the inaugural President of the Australian Aborigines' Evangelical Mission.

His book *Amongst Australian Aborigines — Forty Years of Missionary Work* was published in 1939 (preface dated 1 May 1939) and told the story of the United Aborigines' Mission.

He also served as the family's photographer for many key events.

---

## Family Stories

### The First White Baby at Willow Plains

Ernie Telfer's birth on **2 September 1878** was an event — the first white child born on the pioneering Telfer property at Willow Plains, near Hawker. His mother Caroline had only a one-room galvanised iron hut with a tent attached. A stone fireplace and open fire served for cooking, washing, and boiling the kettle. When a visitor once asked his mother how she managed, she replied: "You could do it for one day. And for another day? Yes, I suppose so! Then just one day at a time." *(From the Borders to the Bush, pp.127, 141–142, 178)*

### The Blowfly Incident

While having a lone lunch in the bush, Ernie became irritated by a blowfly. When the fly settled on a stone five yards away, he picked up his 12-gauge muzzle-loaded shotgun and blazed away. Afterward he was disappointed he couldn't find the fly to see where he'd hit it. *(From the Borders to the Bush, p.141)*

### The Teapot Bet

As a young man, Ernie was known as a bit of a larrikin. A neighbour's daughter, in retaliation for his teasing, placed a hot teapot against his arm while it was resting on the table. Ernie didn't flinch or bat an eye. Her attention was distracted for a few minutes until she picked up the teapot again — with Ernie's arm still against it and a two-inch blister sticking up half an inch. *(From the Borders to the Bush, p.141)*

### The Book That Told the Mission's Story

Ernie's book *Amongst Australian Aborigines — Forty Years of Missionary Work*, published in 1939, tells the story of the United Aborigines' Mission from its early days at La Perouse through its expansion across Australia. Written mostly as chapters for the "United Aborigines Messenger" magazine, the book gives a rare glimpse into Ernie's own work while referring to himself only as "the writer." A copy of this book, inscribed to his brother Charlie and sister-in-law Amy, ended up with Murray and Shirley Telfer at Ungarra and found its way into the family history collection. *(Amongst Australian Aborigines, p.7; inscription in front of book)*

---

## Life Summary

Esther Cowan was born on 31 March 1783 in Langholm, Dumfriesshire, Scotland, the third daughter of James Cowan (a baker by trade) and Jean Hinshelwood. She was baptised on 6 April 1783.

On or after 21 May 1806, Esther married [[John Murray (1779–1849)|John Murray]] in Ewes, Dumfriesshire. John was a widower — his first wife Janet Little had died earlier that year. John and Esther settled at Langshawburn in Eskdalemuir parish, where John worked as a shepherd and agricultural labourer.

Esther and John had at least ten children together, including [[Jean Murray (1810–1839)|Jean]] (who married Francis Telfer and emigrated to South Australia in 1838), Pultney Malcolm Murray (who also emigrated to SA and became a prominent colonist), and William Murray (who also emigrated to SA).

After John's death in 1849, Esther continued living at Langshawburn. She died there on 4 August 1856 at age 73 and was buried at Eskdalemuir Churchyard alongside her husband.

## Life Summary

Esther was the second child born to Charles Farrow and Elizabeth Hannah Telfer at Hope Farm, Finniss Point, near Tarlee. She married **Richard Pelling Latter** on 2 March 1882. Her descendants form the Latter–Cooper–Wishart family line recorded in the family's 2017 supplement tree.

## Family Stories

🖊️ **Anecdote — as told in From the Borders to the Bush (book pp. 63–65):** A story of the family's Dick — Richard Latter, who married Esther. He worked for Jas Martin & Co over in Gawler, making farming machinery that was the talk of the colonies. But in 1908 he did something that must have sounded like a tall tale then — he packed a shipment of harvesters onto a ship bound all the way round the world to Argentina. When they landed, he stayed on to put every one of those machines back together and run them through their trial, proving to the Argentine farmers they'd been built to work. He wrote letters home from Buenos Aires about all of it, and thank goodness for that — his grandson Ashley Cooper still holds those letters today, so we can hear Dick's own voice telling us about it.

body_markdown:
# Esther Jane Telfer (1834–1909)

**Role:** Daughter of Francis Telfer — matriarch of the Smith line
**Born:** 21 May 1834 — Isle of Skye, Scotland
**Died:** 12 March 1909 (aged 75) — Nyngan, New South Wales
**Buried:** Nyngan Cemetery (Church of England section)
**Spouse:** John Smith (~1827 – 5 May 1895)
**Ship:** *Prince George* — arrived Port Adelaide 26 December 1838 (aged 4)

## Photo

> ![Esther Jane Smith nee Telfer portrait](images/people/Esther_Jane_Smith_nee_Telfer_portrait.jpg)

**Esther Jane Smith (née Telfer)** — formal studio portrait, likely late 1880s–early 1900s. She is seated in a dignified pose, dark high-necked gown with lace cuffs, a beaded necklace, and a rich fur-trimmed cape with fringed edging. Her hair is swept up in an elaborate chignon with small floral/beaded adornments. Hands rest over a book on a small draped side table against a painted studio backdrop. Captioned "Esther Jane Smith (nee Telfer)." *(photograph supplied by Mark Telfer; date of portrait not recorded)*

> ![John Smith Ebenezer farm Natimuk](images/people/John_Smith_Ebenezer_farm_Natimuk.jpg)

**Their new home "Ebenezer"** — the John Smith family farm at **Sherwood Dam near Mount Arapiles, Natimuk, Victoria** (c. 1878–1889). A pug-and-thatch construction named "Ebenezer." The three women in the garden are not named in the source caption; the dress (dark gowns, white aprons, straw boaters) is typical 1890s–1900s farmwear. The children attended Arapiles School. Book caption: "They called their new home Ebenezer." *(From the Borders to the Bush, p.35; photograph supplied by Mark Telfer)*

## Family

| Relation | Name |
|----------|------|
| **Father** | [[Francis Telfer (1809–1895)]] |
| **Mother** | Jean Murray (1810–1839) |
| **Husband** | John Smith |

### Children

| Child | Born | Died | Married |
|-------|------|------|---------|
| Jane Sophie Smith | South Australia | Apr 1913 (aged 47) | Benjamin Harper |
| Margaret Dougal Smith | Burra, S.A. | 30 Oct 1961 (aged ~93) | Thomas Parkins |
| Esther Telfer Smith | 27 Sep 1870, Tungkillo S.A. | 5 May 1896 (aged 25) | Thomas Henry Kent |
| John James "Jack" Smith | 1871, Tungkillo S.A. | — | Idona Caston Murray |
| Francis Telfer "Frank" Smith | 14 Feb 1874, Mt Gambier S.A. | 9 Jul 1945, Nyngan | Ellie Forbes, Catherine Gibson |
| Elizabeth Anne Smith | 1878, Millicent S.A. | — | — |

## Life Summary

### Early Life

Esther was born on the Isle of Skye to Francis Telfer and Jean Murray — the second of their three children. When she was four, the family sailed for South Australia aboard the *Prince George*, arriving at Port Adelaide on 26 December 1838. Her mother Jean died at the Emigration Depot barely a month after landing.

Esther grew up at Chain of Ponds in the Adelaide Hills, then Kersbrook, where her father Francis farmed and helped establish the Church of Christ.

### Marriage to John Smith

On **16 November 1864** at the **Wesleyan Parsonage, Kapunda**, Esther married **John Smith** — a man born in Copenhagen, Denmark in 1830, son of a Scottish Sea Captain and a Danish mother. John had bought a block of land on Gunningbah Creek, north of Nyngan, running sheep. Together they had six children.

### The Move to Victoria

The family set out for Victoria, but Esther, pregnant with her sixth child, found the journey by horse-drawn wagon with steel-rimmed wheels on dirt roads too much. She stayed in Millicent (South East) until after Elizabeth Anne was born in 1878, while John and some of the children pushed on to Natimuk, Victoria to set up a new home.

Their new home, called **"Ebenezer"**, was a pug-and-thatch construction at Sherwood Dam near Mount Arapiles. The children attended Arapiles School.

### The Trek to Nyngan

Towards the end of the 1880s, the two oldest boys — John James and Francis Telfer — rode pushbikes some 600 miles into the outback to Nyngan to scout land. They came back with glowing reports.

The family sold their Natimuk farm to the Lange family and set out on a weeks-long trek to Nyngan in a wagon drawn by four draught horses. Their diet: damper cooked in camp ovens, corned meat, and whatever rabbits and birds they caught along the way. Water bags hung from the side of the wagon in the shade to keep cool.

John bought the block on Gunningbah Creek and ran sheep there until his death on 5 May 1895.

### Later Life

After John died, Esther moved into Nyngan township — a brick home in Wambiana Street. She was described as a tiny person, just five feet tall, a devoted mother and grandmother, and a loyal church supporter.

Her home was still standing in good condition as of 1984.

She died on **12 March 1909**, aged 75, and was buried with her husband in Nyngan Cemetery.

## Family Stories

### The Bike Scouts

In the late 1880s, Esther's two boys — John James (about 17) and Francis Telfer (about 15) — rode pushbikes nearly 600 miles from Natimuk, Victoria into the wilds of outback New South Wales to scout land. They returned full of talk about Nyngan and the land opening up. It was their report that convinced the family to pull up roots and make the long trek north.

*(From the Borders to the Bush, pp.39–40)*

### Essie Ray — Esther's Granddaughter

Essie (Esther Jane Harper, granddaughter through Jane Sophie) grew up walking 2.5 miles to school, milking a cow before she left. At about age 11, her family moved from Miram, Victoria to Mullengudgery, NSW. Her mother died of pneumonia about three years later. At just 14, she kept house for six children in a big house with board floors she scrubbed weekly on hands and knees, made butter, did all the cooking, and looked after the lot.

Her brother rode a bike 27 miles into Nyngan to get the doctor — there were no telephones. Too late.

She later married Alex Stevenson (a "nice chap"), had two children. Alex died in his 30th year. She supported herself by dressmaking. Married second to Robert Ray, a widower with two grown daughters. Learned to drive a truck to take fruit from their orchard to the railway.

She celebrated her 90th birthday on 4 January 1989 and still attended Presbyterian Church and Guild, and had a life membership badge from the Orange Show.

*(From the Borders to the Bush, pp.40–41)*

### The Promise to a Dying Sister

Esther's namesake daughter, Esther Telfer Smith, married a Wesleyan minister named Thomas Henry Kent. Thomas died of consumption on 17 December 1895 — just eight months after their wedding. The younger Esther followed him to the grave five months later, also from consumption, on 5 May 1896.

On her deathbed, she asked her sister Margaret: *"If you ever go to Melbourne, will you visit Thomas's grave?"*

Forty-six years later, Margaret — then a widow herself — visited her daughter Ruby and son-in-law Roy Pearce at Bendigo. Roy drove her to Melbourne, and she fulfilled her sister's dying wish.

*(From the Borders to the Bush, pp.44–45)*

### The Eudora Merino Stud

Esther's youngest son, Francis Telfer Smith, drew a block at Mullengudgery (27 miles out of Nyngan) in 1898 and named it **"Eudora"**. He built a large weatherboard home surrounded by shade trees, a big garden with stone fruits and citrus, and a tennis court. He established the Eudora Merino Stud and took sheep to the Royal Sydney Show.

He was a keen pushbike rider in his youth — once rode from Eudora all the way to Mount Gambier with two friends. He also owned racehorses: "Pearl George" and "Pharalie" were sold and shipped to India during WWI.

His daughter Ena recalled: no refrigeration — a charcoal safe with a troublesome door and a green frog living in the water tray on top. Canvas water bags hanging on the verandah. Round galvanised tubs for bathing — knees under chin or legs over the side. Their first car was a T Model Ford; summer nights with the hood down, chugging along at about 20 mph.

When the 1955 flood hit the Bogon River, the Dubbo Aero Club dropped food parcels that burst hitting the water. The family fished tins out of two feet of floodwater — labels lost. They opened cat food for lunch once without realising.

*(From the Borders to the Bush, pp.47–57)*

### Jack Smith Saves Melrose

Esther's oldest son John James "Jack" Smith lived at "Brooklands" on Duck Creek and ran a Merino stud. When his sister Margaret Parkins' husband Thomas was killed in a sulky accident in 1917, Margaret struggled to keep their property "Melrose" going. Her son Dougal hit bad seasons and couldn't make ends meet. The bank threatened to foreclose.

Jack walked into the bank, threw his cheque book on the manager's desk, and said: *"Take what you want out of that, but don't you dare put Margaret Parkins — a widow — out of Melrose."*

Melrose stayed in the Parkins family for 61 years.

*(From the Borders to the Bush, pp.44, 46)*

## Life Summary

Esther Telfer Smith was born 27 Sep 1870 at Tungkillo, the third child of Esther Jane Telfer and John Smith. She married Thomas Henry Kent, a Wesleyan minister, on 9 Apr 1895; they had no children. She died of consumption on 5 May 1896 and is buried in the Methodist section of Nyngan General Cemetery, near her sister Jane Sophie.

Corrected — John Smith is the father, Esther Jane Telfer is the mother. Sources: WikiTree Telfer-591 (Esther Jane as daughter of Francis & Jean Murray), WikiTree Jorgenson-248 (Hans/Johann "John" Smith as husband of Esther Jane, d. 5 May 1895, Nyngan), FindAGrave memorials 60478615 (Esther) & 60478626 (John).

## Family Stories

🖊️ **Anecdote — as told in From the Borders to the Bush (book pp. 44–45):** It's a hard thing, the promise before she passed. Her daughter Esther — the namesake — fell in love with a Wesleyan minister named Thomas Henry Kent and married him in April 1895. But she hadn't even struck her first anniversary when that cruel consumption took Thomas, on the seventeenth of December 1895. And then, five months later to the day, Esther followed him. But before she went she made her sister Margaret promise something: that if ever Margaret found herself in Melbourne, she would go and stand at Thomas's grave. Forty-six years it weighed on Margaret. She lost her own husband too, and then one day, an old widow herself, she asked her son-in-law Roy Pearce to drive her all the way from Bendigo to Melbourne — just to keep that promise, to visit the grave of a man she'd barely known, because her dying sister had asked it of her. There's no explaining that except in blood and loyalty.

*(Anecdote only — family colour, told as the elders tell it. Does not establish any relationship, date or place.)*

Jean, as she was known, contributed "Some Childhood Memories" to the family history, a vivid first-hand account of growing up at Ungarra. # Florence Nicholas Telfer

**Role:** Wife of Rev. Ernest John Telfer — First Matron of Dulhi-Gunyah Orphanage

---

## Life Summary

Florence Nicholas married Rev. Ernest John Telfer on 24 February 1909 at Boulder City, Western Australia. The following day they began work together at Dulhi-Gunyah (meaning "little child's home") Orphanage in East Perth, where Florence served as the first Matron of the home. While Ernie travelled inland on missionary journeys to remote stations, Florence remained in charge of the orphanage, caring for Aboriginal children brought in from the far interior — some from as far as 900 miles inland.

In March 1911, Florence and Ernie resigned from the United Aborigines' Mission staff. Ernie subsequently entered the Baptist ministry, serving pastorates at Terowie (SA), in Tasmania, and in New South Wales. Florence likely accompanied him through these postings.

A photograph of Florence in academic regalia (mortarboard and gown) appears in Ernie's 1939 book *Amongst Australian Aborigines*, which she helped make possible by "supplying material" and supporting the work of the mission.

*(Details on Florence's parentage, birth year, and death date remain unverified — information needed from birth/marriage certificates or family records.)*

# Francis Adam Telfer (1875–1955)

**Role:** Son of Adam Francis Telfer and Margaret Dougal Telfer

**Spouse:** Clara Ann Millicent Dunn (m. 23 Oct 1899)

---

## Family

| Relation | Name |
|----------|------|
| **Father** | [[Adam Francis Telfer (1842–1925)]] |
| **Mother** | [[Margaret Dougal Telfer (1849–1936)]] |
| **Wife** | [[Clara Ann Millicent Telfer (1878–1966)]] (m. 23 Oct 1899) |

---

## Life Summary

Francis Adam (Frank) Telfer was born 17 August 1875 at Edgerston, Tantanoola, South Australia — the fourth of Adam Francis Telfer and Margaret Dougal Telfer's 12 children. He married **Clara Ann Millicent Dunn** (born 1 September 1878, Millicent, SA) on 23 October 1899 at the residence of Adam Telfer, Tantanoola. They had five children — Ronald Edgerston, Millicent Joyce, Dorothy Margaret Hope, Gordon Francis and Estelle May — and lived at "Pleasant Hill," Glencoe West. Frank died 28 May 1955; Clara continued to live in Mount Gambier until her death on 24 May 1966.

*(Relationship spine of Frank + his wife Clara (b. 1 Sep 1878, d. 24 May 1966) and the five children by name is confirmed in both "From the Borders to the Bush" and "A Telfer Family Tree — Supplement 2008.")*

---

**Source:** SA Death Registration (Book 826/Page 2940, district Grey, 28 May 1955) and *Border Watch* death notice, Tue 31 May 1955 p.6 (Trove article 296827265, "On May 28, at Hospital, Mount Gambier... aged 79") — confirm death **28 May 1955**. *From the Borders to the Bush* (pp. 286–297) + *A Telfer Family Tree — Supplement 2008* carry the 17 Aug 1875 birth, wife Clara Ann Millicent Dunn b. 1 Sep 1878 Millicent / d. 24 May 1966, marriage 23 Oct 1899 at residence of Adam Telfer, Tantanoola, and the five children — but gave the death day as 27 May, corrected here to 28 May on the two contemporaneous primary sources above. (FindAGrave memorial #215167931 "29 May" is the burial-transcription error.)

---

## Sources & Verification (28 May 1955)

Two independent source-groups confirm the death date **28 May 1955**:

1. **Official South Australian Death Register** — Genealogy SA member index: TELFER, Francis Adam; death **28-May-1955**; age 79; male; married; place of death Mount Gambier; district Grey; **Book 826 / Page 2940**. *(Accessed 6 Sep 2026 via Genealogy SA member login.)*
2. **Contemporary newspaper death notice** — *The Border Watch* (Mount Gambier, SA), **Tuesday 31 May 1955, p. 6**, Family Notices / DEATHS, Trove article [296827265](https://trove.nla.gov.au/newspaper/article/296827265): "TELFER — On May 28, at Hospital, Mount Gambier. Francis Adam, of Agnes Street, Mount Gambier, formerly of Glencoe, dearly beloved husband of Clara Ann Telfer... Aged 79 years. ... his remains were peacefully laid to rest in the Mount Gambier Cemetery on Sunday last."

The two family books recorded the day as 27 May; both contemporaneous primary records above give **28 May**, so the recorded date is corrected. The "29 May" on FindAGrave memorial #215167931 is a transcription of the *burial* day (Sunday 29 May), not the death.

---

## Family Stories

🖊️ **Anecdote — as told in From the Borders to the Bush (book pp. 286):** Frank was the plough-and-pencil farmer. He took up 'Pleasant Hill' down at Glencoe West, and for close on fifty years — 1908 to 1955 — he wrote his farming diary every blessed day. Weather, wool, the pigs, potatoes, the wheat and the barley; he kept the whole life of the place in those books, and his son Ronald kept them safe after him. They're a farm's heartbeat in ink. Sheep and cattle, crops, nothing too small to note. Five children grew up at Pleasant Hill around that steady, recording hand — and you get the feeling Frank believed if it wasn't written down, it hadn't properly happened.

*(Anecdote only — family colour, told as the elders tell it. Does not establish any relationship, date or place.)*

## Life Summary

Francis Charles Telfer — known as "Charlie" — was born at Kersbrook in the Adelaide Hills on 25 November 1875, the eldest son of John Telfer and Caroline Amelia Masters. He grew up in a farming family and later married Amy Ellen Provis on 6 April 1909 at Stokes, South Australia.

Charlie and Amy raised a large family of **ten children** — six boys and four girls — spanning from 1910 to 1933. Their ninth child was [[Murray John Telfer (1924–2009)]] (1924–2009), later a grazier on the Eyre Peninsula.

Charlie passed away on 20 March 1954 at Croydon, Adelaide, aged 78, and was buried at Enfield Memorial Park.

## Family Stories

### A Christmas Gift — Ernie's Book

Charlie's brother Ernie (Ernest John Telfer) wrote a book about his 40 years as a missionary with the United Aborigines' Mission, titled *Amongst Australian Aborigines*. A copy of this book was given to Charlie and Amy as a Christmas gift, inscribed "Charlie & Amy, with love & Christmas wishes, from Eva" — likely their cousin Eva Rowena Telfer. The book later passed to Murray John and Shirley Edna Telfer at Ungarra, and eventually found its way into the family history collection that preserved the story of Ernie's remarkable life. *(Inscription in front of "Amongst Australian Aborigines" by E.J. Telfer, 1939)*

Francis Charles Telfer — known as Charlie — was born at Kersbrook in the Adelaide Hills in 1875, the eldest son of John and Caroline Telfer. As a young man he drove his horses and wagon down from the family home at Willow Plains near Hawker to the Eyre Peninsula, where he took up 2,000 acres of virgin mallee scrub in the Hundred of Stokes (Ungarra). He had to cut his way into the block with an axe, tether his horses and set up camp. The first task was to dig a small dam with a pick and shovel to catch water for his horses, since the creek that flowed through the property was very salty. He later married Amy Ellen Provis, and they raised ten children in a four-roomed wood-and-iron house with clay floors. Charlie cleared the land using a scrub roller — a heavy log maybe a foot or more in diameter and eight to ten feet long, with chains around it hitched to horses — dragged through the scrub to knock it down before burning. He was a skilled blacksmith, making and mending nearly everything on the farm himself, including an improved stump-jump plough adapted to the tough mallee roots. By 1917 the family was established enough that Charlie could take on the soldiers' block next door when its original owner abandoned it during WWI. His son Edwin Roy remembered him as a great planner, working from daylight until dark, and a man who never let anyone leave his table hungry. *(From the Borders to the Bush, pp.130, 136–138)*

## Family Stories

### The Name That Continued

Francis Telfer was born around 1768 at Sorbietrees, Roxburghshire, the second son of James Telfer of Sorbietrees and Margaret Armstrong. His life is one of the pieces we can't fully recover — we know he was baptised, we know when he died, and his name is carved on the family headstone in Castleton Cemetery alongside his parents and siblings.

But that name carried weight. "Francis" appears regularly in succeeding generations — his nephew Francis Telfer (1809–1895) made the voyage to South Australia, and his great-grandnephew Francis Charles Telfer (1875–1954) carried it across the ocean. The stone is the record; the descendants are the story.

*(From the Borders to the Bush, pp.17-19)*

## Life Summary

Francis Telfer was born on 2 February 1809 at Blackburn Foot (the old Black Burn fort) in Liddesdale, Roxburghshire, Scotland — the seventh of eight children born to James Telfer and Elizabeth "Betty" Hutton. He grew up in the Castleton region of the Scottish Borders.

### The Voyage

Francis emigrated to South Australia aboard the *Prince George*, departing London in September 1838 and arriving at Port Adelaide on 26 December 1838. He travelled with his first wife Jean Murray and their three young children: James (6), Esther (4), and Elizabeth (2). A fourth child, John (the baby), died during the voyage.

### Three Marriages

Francis outlived his first two wives. Jean Murray died shortly after arrival at the Emigration Depot in Adelaide on 22 January 1839 — barely a month after landing. Her infant son John had died during the voyage.

Within months, Francis married **Dinah Flavel** (a young English immigrant from Northamptonshire) on 4 November 1839. They had one daughter, Jean (born at Chain of Ponds, 1840). Dinah died on 20 March 1844 at Chain of Ponds, aged only 22, and was buried at West Terrace Cemetery, Adelaide.

On 27 March 1845, Francis married **Margaret Wright**, with whom he had three more children: John (the main line ancestor), Margaret Dougal, and George Wright. Margaret Wright brought stability to the household and outlived Francis, dying in 1892.

### Later Life

Francis farmed at Chain of Ponds and Kersbrook in the Adelaide Hills before settling at **Hope Farm, Tarlee**, in the Clare Valley region. He became a respected local identity. By the time of his death at age 86, he had established the Telfer name across South Australia.

His obituary in *The Border Watch* (18 September 1895) recorded:
> "He leaves two sons — Mr. John Telfer, of Hawker, and Mr. G. W. Telfer, Willaston — and three daughters — Mrs. Farrow, of Hope Farm, Mrs. Smith, of Canouba, New South Wales, and Mrs. A. F. Telfer, of Edgerston, Tantanoola."

Francis died at Hope Farm, Tarlee on 2 September 1895. A memorial headstone was erected by the Telfer Family History Association in 1999, commemorating his three wives and his place as the founder of the Australian Telfer line.

## Family Stories

### The Lost Boy — James Telfer (1832–1845)

Francis's eldest son James, aged 13, disappeared while bringing in stray sheep during heavy rain in July 1844 near Chain of Ponds. Neighbours, police — they scoured the flooded countryside for days. Nothing. The *South Australian Register* ran a notice on 10 Jul 1844 asking for information. James was never seen alive again.

Around 1877, floodwaters receded near Adelaide and a human skeleton was found lodged against a tree in the river. A doctor said it was a boy about 13, probably there 20+ years. Whether Francis ever found out is unknown.

It was the fourth family member Francis lost in six years: infant John (died at sea, 1838), wife Jean (1839), wife Dinah (1844), and his eldest son James.

*(From the Borders to the Bush, pp.25–27; SA Register, 10 Jul 1844)*

### The Flavel Family and the Voyage of the *Prince George*

Francis sailed to South Australia on the *Prince George* alongside the Flavel family — Joseph and Mary Flavel and their seven kids. The Flavels became lifelong friends. William Flavel remembered arriving at Port Misery on 26 Dec 1838 and walking barefoot across the sandhills, where the summer sand was so hot he "had to run from one bush to another till I got clear of the sand." The Flavel baby, John Telfer, died during the voyage and was buried at sea.

The *Prince George* was a 482-ton, 118-foot, 3-masted barque under Captain Young. Francis applied for emigration on 9 August 1838, had just 26 days to prepare, and sailed from London on 4 September 1838.

*(From the Borders to the Bush, pp.22–24)*

### Francis and the Kersbrook Church of Christ

Francis was an intensely religious man. He regularly walked 22 miles from Kersbrook to Adelaide for the "Scotch Kirk" (Gouger Street United Presbyterian Church). In 1863, he became a founding trustee of the Kersbrook Church of Christ Chapel and served as Sunday School Superintendent. He was described as "the pastor's right hand" alongside John McMillan.

*(From the Borders to the Bush, pp.27–31)*

### Francis Elected as Church Elder — Gouger Street Church, 1845

Francis's faith wasn't a Sunday-only affair. On 1 December 1845, the congregation of the Gouger Street United Secession Church (the "Scotch Kirk") met to elect new Ruling Elders. The church minutes record that after a sermon by the Moderator, "Alexander Hay and Francis Telfer" were elected to the office — and after examination by the Session and being "found duly qualified," their induction took place on Friday 19 December 1845. Francis was just six years out from losing his first wife, and his second wife had died the year before. Yet here he was, being entrusted with spiritual leadership of Adelaide's first Presbyterian congregation.

*(From the Borders to the Bush, pp.25–26)*

### Francis's Last Letters — 1891

![Francis Telfer's 1891 letters — to granddaughter Jane Murray Farrow and to his wife Margaret (From the Borders to the Bush, p.33)](images/people/francis-telfer-letters-1891.jpg)

Two handwritten letters by Francis, both dated **October 1891** and written from Hope Farm, Tarlee — about **eleven months before the death of his wife Margaret** (who died 13 September 1892). One, dated **20 October 1891**, is addressed to "My Dear Jane Murray" — his granddaughter **Jane Murray Farrow (1857–1934)**, daughter of his daughter Elizabeth Hannah (Telfer) Farrow — and speaks of family matters and of his religious hope. The other, dated **21 October 1891**, is addressed to "Dear Wife," his third wife **Margaret Wright Telfer**, reflecting on their time together since their marriage in March 1845. They are among the few surviving documents in Francis's own hand — a direct connection to the man who founded the Australian Telfer line.

*(From the Borders to the Bush, p.33)*

### The House at Macoota

Francis's stone house at Section 6146, Kersbrook had walls 15 inches thick of local stone. Originally shingle-roofed (still preserved under later iron), it had a central passage, three bedrooms off the south side, a kitchen/dining room and drawing room with large fireplaces on the north, and a well about 50 yards from the back door. The land was so thick with wattle and banksia scrub you couldn't walk through it when first taken up.

*(From the Borders to the Bush, pp.31–33)*

### Margaret Wright and the Stirling Castle Legend

Family legend had it that Francis's third wife Margaret Wright was "born in Stirling Castle" — though which bit of the castle was left for debate. Problem is, the last king to actually live there was James VI (1567–1625), long before Margaret was born. Colourful story, suspect geography.

*(From the Borders to the Bush, p.27)*

## Life Summary

Francis Telfer Smith was born 14 Feb 1874, the fifth child of Esther Jane Telfer and John Smith. He married Ellie Valentine Forbes on 7 Oct 1908 at Mullengudgery, then Catherine Gibson. He died 9 Jul 1945 at Nyngan District Hospital, aged 71, and is buried in Nyngan General Cemetery. *(Birth place as Mt Gambier per vault + FamilySearch G4C5-KMQ; *A Telfer Family Tree* supplement p.12 lists "Reedy Creek" — see Leads.md discrepancy.)*

> ⚠️ **Verified correction (07 Aug 2026):** Previously the relationship fields in this file had Father and Mother reversed (listing Esther Jane Telfer as "Father" and John Smith as "Mother"). Corrected — John Smith is the father, Esther Jane Telfer is the mother. Sources: WikiTree Telfer-591 (Esther Jane as daughter of Francis & Jean Murray), WikiTree Jorgenson-248 ("Hans Hansen (Jorgenson) Smith", husband of Esther Jane), FindAGrave 60478615/60478626.

---

**Source:** *A Telfer Family Tree* (Supplement) p.12 · *From the Borders to the Bush* Ch.3 (pp.36–57) — accessed 07 Aug 2026. Parentage cross-verified via FindAGrave 60478615/60478626 + WikiTree Telfer-591 / Jorgenson-248.

---

## Family Stories

🖊️ **Anecdote — as told in From the Borders to the Bush (book pp. 39–40, 47–57):** Frank, the young one, got his own place in 1898. The family took up a block at Mullengudgery — about seven-and-twenty miles out from Nyngan — and Frank drew it and named it with a pretty name, Eudora. He put up a great big weatherboard home on it, and he didn't stop at a house. He planted an orchard, and set shade trees all around so you'd get away from that western sun, and built a tennis court — you could see they meant to live properly out there. And he stocked the place with sheep and built up the Eudora Merino Stud, and he was that proud of them he'd take his rams right down to the Royal Sydney Show to parade them. And it was Frank, barely a man, who'd climbed on his pushbike with his brother Jack and ridden six hundred miles to see the country — the very loop that brought the whole family west. Eudora wasn't just a farm to Frank; it was a kingdom.

*(Anecdote only — family colour, told as the elders tell it. Does not establish any relationship, date or place.)*

body_markdown:
# Frederick Parker (~1838–1928)

**Role:** Second husband of Jean Telfer
**Died:** 1928 — Wildes Meadow, New South Wales
**Buried:** Bowral Cemetery, NSW

Frederick Parker, son of George Parker, married Jean (who had by then adopted the name Jane) on Christmas Day 1871 at Kapunda. They lived at Finniss Point before moving to the far north of South Australia around Hawker and Oraparinna.

After Jane died in 1892 from heart disease, Frederick later went to live with his elder daughter Margaret and son-in-law Edward Liebich at Wildes Meadow, New South Wales. He died in 1928 and is buried in Bowral Cemetery.

**Source:** *From the Borders to the Bush* — Chapter on Jean/Jane Telfer

## Family Stories

After Jean Telfer, by then known as Jane, lost her first husband Richard Paynter to pleurisy in 1869, she remarried on Christmas Day 1871. Her new husband was Frederick Parker, described in the book *From the Borders to the Bush* as an itinerant farm labourer and bullock driver, son of George Parker. They were married at the Wesleyan Church in Kapunda, with Jane's brother-in-law Charles Farrow and niece Jane Farrow as witnesses. The family left Finniss Point and moved to the far north of South Australia, living around Hawker and Oraparinna. Their children — Margaret Eliza, Frederick George, Annie, Martha, Joanna Wittita Cordley, and Ethel May — were born at various places across that remote country. Frederick is believed to have worked as a railway ganger at Finniss during the later years. Jane died of heart disease on 15 July 1892 at Queens Own Town and was buried at Strathalbyn Cemetery. After many years, Frederick went to live with his eldest daughter Margaret and her husband Edward Liebich at Wildes Meadow, New South Wales. He died in Berrima Hospital on 12 August 1928 and is buried in Bowral Cemetery. At the time of his death, only three of his children — Margaret, Frederick (known as George), and Joanna — survived him.

*(From the Borders to the Bush, p.93)*

body_markdown:
# George Wright Telfer (1850–1913)

**Role:** Youngest child of Francis Telfer and Margaret Wright — the one who went west

**Born:** 22 November 1850 — Macoota, Kersbrook, South Australia
**Died:** 1913 — Nungarin, Western Australia
**Occupation:** Farmer, grocer, butter maker, steam laundry proprietor
**Spouse:** Ruth Penna (m. 17 Sept 1884, d. 1908)

---

## Family

| Relation | Name |
|----------|------|
| **Mother** | [[Margaret Wright Telfer (1810–1892)]] |
| **Father** | [[Francis Telfer (1809–1895)]] |
| **Spouse** | [[Ruth Penna (1863–1908)]] (m. 17 Sep 1884) |
| **Children** | [[William Francis Telfer (1885–1955)]], Olive Millie Telfer (1890–1890), [[Lesley Thomas Telfer (1891–1914)]], Olive Netta Telfer (1894–1986) |
| **Siblings** | [[John Telfer (1847–1929)]], [[Margaret Dougal Telfer (1849–1936)]] |

---

## Family Stories

### The Youngest Son

George Wright was the baby of the family — born at Macoota, Kersbrook on 22nd November 1850, the youngest son of Francis and Margaret. He grew up working his father's farm alongside brother John, learning the market gardening trade from the ground up. When he was old enough, he bought land of his own in the Kersbrook area and built himself a home. He wasn't one to stay in someone else's shadow. *(From the Borders to the Bush, p.180)*

### The Grocer Who Went the Distance

Long before road trains and highways, George ran a grocery van all the way to Port Augusta. That's a hell of a trip from Kersbrook — hundreds of miles of rough track, dirt roads, and outback settlements. He'd load up his van with supplies and make the journey north, peddling his goods to the scattered communities along the way. It was the kind of work that built character, or at least a strong back. *(From the Borders to the Bush, p.180)*

### The Land Speculator

George had an eye for a deal. He wasn't content with just farming — he bought and sold land like a man who could see which way the wind was blowing. He picked up blocks at Kensington that had once belonged to his mother, took out a mining lease at Kadina, and bought several sections at Hawker which he later sold to his brother John. He was always looking for the next opportunity, never one to sit still. *(From the Borders to the Bush, p.180)*

### Ruth Penna of Kersbrook

On 17th September 1884, at the age of 33, George married Ruth Penna. She was 21, the daughter of William and Ruth Penna, also market gardeners from Kersbrook. The wedding was in her parents' home, solemnized by the Rev. John Hall, Presbyterian minister. Ruth must have known what she was signing up for — life with George was never going to be quiet. *(From the Borders to the Bush, p.180)*

### The Salem Baptist Years

In December 1885, George and Ruth were welcomed into the fellowship of Salem Baptist Church at Gumeracha. George wasn't just a pew-warmer either — he was soon elected secretary of the church. This was the same faith that ran through the whole Telfer family, that same Baptist thread that had followed them from Scotland through Kersbrook and beyond. *(From the Borders to the Bush, p.180)*

### Three Children, Two Continents

While they were at Kersbrook, Ruth gave George three children: William Francis in August 1885, Olive Millie in March 1890, and Lesley Thomas in 1891. Little Olive only lived about two months — she was buried in the Gawler Cemetery on 5th May 1890, her parents' address listed as Mount Pleasant. It was a hard loss, the kind that marked a family. But life pushed on, and George kept moving. *(From the Borders to the Bush, p.180 — note: the Borders narrative gives 1892; the *A Telfer Family Tree* supplement p.160 gives "24 Sep 1891". See [[Lesley Thomas Telfer (1891–1914)]] Notes — birth year single-source, flagged.)*

### Father Francis Comes to Stay

After Margaret Wright died in 1892, old Francis came to live with George and Ruth. He was getting on by then, his health fading. In 1893 they all packed up and moved to Willaston, near Gawler, where George turned his hand to running a butter factory. It was a complete change from market gardening — but that was George, always ready to try something new. A year later, in June 1894, Ruth gave birth to another daughter, Olive Netta. *(From the Borders to the Bush, p.180)*

### The Westward Gamble

Some time in 1896, George made the biggest decision of his life. He packed up Ruth, the children, and the remnants of the household and moved the whole family to Western Australia. They lived in Albany for a few years first, then moved to Perth where they ran a boarding house overlooking the Swan River. From market gardener to butter maker to boarding house proprietor — George wasn't afraid to reinvent himself. *(From the Borders to the Bush, p.180)*

### The City Steam Laundry

From boarding house to laundry — George established the City Steam Laundry in Leederville, and by 1901 he was listed as manager. By 1902-03 it was "Telfer & Penna, proprietors," with his brother-in-law Thomas Penna as partner. Their ads boasted "Special quotations for Hotels" and a telephone number — number 464, which was something in those days. In 1908 they opened a branch on Hay Street in Perth, and the name changed to City Steam Laundry & Dye Works. The place was still operating as the Monarch Laundry as late as 1981, long after George was gone. *(From the Borders to the Bush, p.180)*

### The Loss of Ruth

1908 was a hard year. Ruth died, leaving George with three children to raise and a business to run. The laundry was split — son Frank took over Telfer's City Steam Laundry with two Hay Street branches, while George kept Telfer's Cleaning & Dye Works at Newcastle Street, Leederville. He pushed on, but something must have gone out of him with Ruth. *(From the Borders to the Bush, p.180-181)*

### The Merredin Years

Around 1912, George sold the laundry business and moved east along the railway line to Merredin. He opened a store there and bought a farming property at nearby Nungarin. He and his sons ran both for a year or so — a final attempt to build something in this new country. But George died in 1913, not long after they'd settled. The following year his younger son Lesley Thomas was killed in an accident on the same farm. Within two years, George and both his sons were gone from the land he'd tried so hard to work. *(From the Borders to the Bush, p.181)*

---

## Life Story

George Wright Telfer was the youngest child of Francis Telfer (1809–1895) and his third wife, Margaret Wright. He was born at Macoota, Kersbrook on 22nd November 1850.

He spent his early years working his father's farm at Kersbrook, then bought land of his own and built a home. He ran a grocery van to Port Augusta, speculated in land across Kensington, Kadina, and Hawker, and married Ruth Penna in 1884.

After his mother's death in 1892, his father Francis came to live with them, and in 1893 the family moved to Willaston where George ran a butter factory. In 1896 he moved the entire family to Western Australia — first Albany, then Perth, where he ran a boarding house before establishing the City Steam Laundry in Leederville.

After Ruth's death in 1908, George carried on the business, then sold up around 1912 and moved to Merredin where he opened a store and bought a farm at Nungarin. He died in 1913. His son Lesley was killed in an accident the following year.

**Source:** *From the Borders to the Bush* — pages 30, 180-181

---

## Sources

- **Source:** Donald Telfer, *From the Borders to the Bush* (ISBN 0 7316 6387 X), pp. 30, 180–181 — family narrative; laundry proprietor ~1901, business to Merredin/Nungarin by 1912
- **Source:** [Collections WA — HEAVY DUTY LAUNDRY IRON](https://collectionswa.net.au/items/9621843c-5e5d-4d6c-9100-aef622a545b3) — Merredin Railway Museum, registrar cwa-org-156-1994.638 — donor provenance corroborating GW Telfer's Leederville laundry (early 1900s) and the Olive Thomas / Frank Telfer sibling links — accessed 3 Sep 2026

Gilbert Melville Telfer (the book *From the Borders to the Bush* records his given names as Gilbert Melville, not Melvin McLeod — he was known as "Mel") was born in 1911, the third child of Mark Telfer (1877–1946) and Julia Matilda Seebohm (1876–1939) of Tantanoola, South Australia.

He married Jessie Allan and they had three children — Beth, who married Clive Lipscombe; Ian, who married Sally Taylor; and Allan, who married Christine Marshall.

Mel was a good footballer, playing at centre wing and proving formidable as a fast player and a good ball handler. He was an opening batsman for the Tantanoola Cricket team and made many centuries. He was a most useful member of the team and excelled as the wicket keeper. When his eyesight no longer permitted him to play football and cricket, Mel played bowls, both indoor and outdoor, and proved to be an excellent player.

Like his father and brothers, he was interested in local affairs and was a Life Member of the Tantanoola Pastoral, Agricultural and Horticultural Society.

In his father's obituary, he was listed as "Mel Telfer, Tantanoola".

## Family Stories

Mel was the third child of Mark and Tillie Telfer. The book *From the Borders to the Bush* describes him as a fine sportsman — a good footballer who played centre wing, fast and a good ball handler; an opening batsman for the Tantanoola Cricket team who made many centuries and excelled as wicket keeper. When his eyesight no longer allowed him to play football and cricket, he took up bowls, both indoor and outdoor, and proved an excellent player. Like his father and brothers, he was interested in local affairs and was a Life Member of the Tantanoola Pastoral, Agricultural and Horticultural Society. He married Jessie Allan and they had three children — Beth, Ian and Allan. *(From the Borders to the Bush, p.243)*

## Sources

- *From the Borders to the Bush* by Donald Telfer (1986) — page 243

---

## Life Summary

Hazel Rose Telfer was the youngest of twelve children of Adam and Margaret Telfer, born at Mount Gambier on 23 June 1891. She spent her early years at "Edgerston" in Tantanoola, attending Tantanoola School.

When the family moved to Waverley Park, Hazel worked in city offices performing secretarial duties. She was a valued member of the Knightsbridge Baptist Church choir — a soprano with an extensive collection of music. She played the piano, studied singing, and was much in demand as a soloist at various functions.

### Marriage

She married **Arnold Cuthbert Lawrie** (known as Cuth) on 28 June 1924. Cuth was the son of John and Elizabeth (née Nunan) Lawrie of Nelshaby near Port Pirie, a compositor in the printing trade and a skilled artisan.

During the early years of their marriage they lived in Adelaide, but the Great Depression forced them to leave the city and seek work in the country. They moved to Ceduna on the Far West Coast, where Cuth was employed at the gypsum works.

It was there, at the small bush nursing home in Ceduna, that their first child **Barbara June Lawrie** was born on 16 June 1928. Hazel's sister Elsie, a trained nurse, travelled to Ceduna to help her sister after the birth. Barbara was given the second name "June" because both her parents were born in June, they were married in June, and Barbara herself was born in June.

A second child, **Malcolm Roderick Lawrie** (known as Rod), was born at Rose Park Hospital on 24 February 1931.

As economic conditions improved, the family left the West Coast and moved to Murray Bridge, where Cuth resumed his trade as a compositor at the *Murray Valley Standard* newspaper. Both children started school at Murray Bridge Infant School, where Hazel was an enthusiastic member of the Mothers' Club.

*(From the Borders to the Bush, pp. 279, 331–333)*

---

## Sources

- Donald Telfer, *From the Borders to the Bush* (1986), pp. 279, 331–333
- *A Brief Account of the First Members of the Telfer Family to Settle in South Australia* (1986 reunion booklet)

## Life Summary

Isabella Lucieton Telfer was the third child of John Telfer and Martha Clara Henstridge. Born at Edgerston, South Australia on 17 July 1880, she married Alexander Brown Thomson on 12 July 1911. Together they had three children — [[Trevor Andrew Thomson (1914–1945)|Trevor]], Roma and Murray. She lived to the age of 83, passing on 30 June 1964 at Klemzig, South Australia. Her death place — Klemzig, a north-eastern suburb of Adelaide — suggests she may have moved closer to the city in her later years, possibly to be nearer to family.

**Note:** Her records must be distinguished from other Isabella Thomsons of the same era — an Isabella Thomson who died in Western Australia (Karrakatta) in 1936, and a Scottish Isabella Thomson who died in Polmont in 1935. The 1964 Klemzig death date is the correct match for the Tantanoola Telfer line.

## Family Stories

Isabella Lucieton Telfer was the eighth child of John and Martha Telfer. She married Alexander Thomson, and together they had three children — Roma, Trevor and Murray. Her life, like that of many of her siblings, was rooted in the Tantanoola district where the Telfer family had established themselves after arriving from Scotland.

body_markdown:
# Isobel Telfer (1798–?)

**Role:** Sister of Francis Telfer (1809–1895), stayed in Scotland

Isobel Telfer was born on 10 February 1798 at Greenholm, near Newcastleton, Roxburghshire, Scotland. She was the second child of James Telfer (1761–1845), a hand loom weaver, and Elizabeth "Betty" Hutton (1774–1853). Her name is also recorded as "Isabella".

She did NOT emigrate to Australia and stayed in Scotland.

The book *From the Borders to the Bush* states: *"We have no further information about four members of this family; namely Isobel, Adam, Margaret and William."* Like her younger siblings Adam, Margaret, and William, Isobel's fate after the family records is not documented.

## Family Stories

### The Sister Who Stayed

Isobel Telfer was born on 10 February 1798 at Greenholm, outside Newcastleton in the Scottish Borders. She was the second child and first daughter of James Telfer and Betty Hutton — the weaver and his wife raising a growing family in a cottage with its own cow.

Her baptism is there in the Old Parish Register for Castleton, clear as day. But after that? Nothing. The book *From the Borders to the Bush* says it plain: *"We have no further information about four members of this family; namely Isobel, Adam, Margaret and William."*

She was 39 when her brother Francis packed up and sailed for South Australia in 1838. She was 47 when her father died in 1845. And she was still in Scotland when her older brother James — the one who emigrated — passed away in 1863. After that, the record ends; her death date is unrecorded.

Some stories are lost because nobody wrote them down. Isobel's is one of them.

*(From the Borders to the Bush, pp.17-20)*

**Source:** *From the Borders to the Bush* — pages 17–20

# James Telfer (1761–1845)

**Role:** Scottish progenitor — father of South Australian immigrant [[Francis Telfer (1809–1895)]]
**Born:** ~1761 — baptised 14 Jul 1761, Castleton, Roxburghshire, Scotland
**Died:** 19 December 1845 — Castleton, Scottish Borders, Scotland
**Buried:** Old Castleton Cemetery, Newcastleton, Scottish Borders, Scotland
**Spouse:** [[Elizabeth Hutton Telfer (1774–1853)]] (m. ~1795)

> ⚠️ **Same-name note:** This James Telfer — **baptised 14 Jul 1761**, son of John Telfer of Castleton, father of SA immigrant [[Francis Telfer (1809–1895)]] — is a **distinct person** from several other Telfers also named James in the same Castleton parish. Do **not** merge him with the Sorbietrees Jameses: [[James Telfer (of Sorbietrees) (~1740–?)]] (m. Margaret Armstrong) and that family's son [[James Telfer (bap.1762)]] (bap. **24 Sep 1762** — a different, younger James born barely a year later). Also distinct: [[James Telfer (1829–1913)]] (South Australian pioneer). Public user trees routinely blend the 1761 and 1762 Jameses into one man — that is wrong (see Corrections Log, 30 Aug 2026).

## Photos

<!-- PORTRAIT REMOVED 2026-08-30: a sepia portrait was previously displayed here as "James Telfer (1761–1845) — portrait", but it has NO provenance in the Sources below (book pp.6/7, FindAGrave, WikiTree, OPR register) and James — an 18th-c. Borders shepherd/weaver — had no known photograph taken. The image fails the two-source/verified rule and the portrait is believed to be a different/unknown Telfer. File james-telfer-1761.jpg remains in Photos/ for future identification; it is no longer linked to this profile. -->

![Newcastleton and the Liddesdale Hills Roxburghshire Scotland p6](images/people/Newcastleton_and_the_Liddesdale_Hills_Roxburghshire_Scotland_p6.jpg)
*Newcastleton and the Liddesdale Hills — the valley home of James Telfer (1761–1845), in Roxburghshire in the Scottish Borders, Scotland. From the Borders to the Bush, p.6.*

![Liddesdale Hills Ancient Sheepfold Roxburghshire Scotland p7](images/people/Liddesdale_Hills_Ancient_Sheepfold_Roxburghshire_Scotland_p7.jpg)
*Liddesdale Hills — an ancient sheepfold in the Liddesdale valley, Roxburghshire, the Scottish Borders, Scotland; the "Ballad of Jamie Telfer of the Fair Dodhead" country. From the Borders to the Bush, p.7.*

![Blackburnfoot birthplace of Francis Telfer Roxburghshire Scotland p18](images/people/Blackburnfoot_birthplace_of_Francis_Telfer_Roxburghshire_Scotland_p18.jpg)
*Blackburnfoot — the site of the cottage in which son [[Francis Telfer (1809–1895)]] was born, in the Liddesdale valley, Roxburghshire, the Scottish Borders, Scotland (taken early 1980s). From the Borders to the Bush, p.18.*

## Family

| Relation | Name |
|----------|------|
| **Spouse** | [[Elizabeth Hutton Telfer (1774–1853)]] — Elizabeth "Betty" Hutton (m. ~1795) |
| **Son** | [[James Telfer (1796–1863)]] — m. Elizabeth Beattie |
| **Daughter** | Isobel/Isabella Telfer (1798–?) — m. Hunter |
| **Son** | Adam Telfer (bap. 18 Oct 1799) |
| **Daughter** | Margaret Telfer (bap. 17 Jul 1801, d. 1884) — m. Armstrong |
| **Son** | Robert Telfer (bap. 23 Apr 1803, d. 1878) — m. Elizabeth Oliver |
| **Son** | John Telfer (bap. 20 Mar 1805, d. 3 Mar 1839) — unmarried |
| **Son** | [[Francis Telfer (1809–1895)]] (bap. 2 Feb 1809, d. 1895) — emigrated to SA |

| **Father** | John Telfer (of Castleton) (~1731–?) |
| **Mother** | Elspeth Young (~1722–?) |

## Life Summary

James Telfer was born around 1761 in the Liddesdale/Castleton area of Roxburghshire, Scottish Borders. He was baptised at Castleton on 14 July 1761, the son of John Telfer of Castleton. He married Elizabeth "Betty" Hutton around 1795.

James and Betty raised at least eight children in the Castleton parish, Roxburghshire, near the English-Scottish border. Their son Francis emigrated to South Australia in 1838 aboard the *Prince George*, establishing the Australian Telfer branch.

According to Donald Telfer's *From the Borders to the Bush* (1989), James was known as a hard-working farm man in the Liddesdale region. His descendants in Scotland continued farming the same area.

James died on 19 December 1845 at Castleton and was buried at Old Castleton Cemetery, Newcastleton. His wife Betty outlived him by eight years.

## Timeline

| Date | Event |
|------|-------|
| 14 Jul 1761 | Baptised — Castleton, Roxburghshire, Scotland |
| ~1795 | Married Elizabeth "Betty" Hutton |
| 1796–1811 | Eight children born at Castleton |
| 1838 | Son Francis emigrated to South Australia |
| 19 Dec 1845 | Died — Castleton, Scottish Borders |
| | Buried — Old Castleton Cemetery, Newcastleton |

## Family Stories

### The Newcastleton Valley

![Newcastleton and the Liddesdale Hills — From the Borders to the Bush, p.6](images/people/Newcastleton_and_the_Liddesdale_Hills_p6.jpg)

The Telfer name reaches back deep into the Scottish Borders, to the Liddesdale valley in Roxburghshire — the country around Newcastleton. It is a landscape of rounded hills, small sheep farms and winding valley roads, and it is the ground the family stood on long before Australia was ever a twinkle. Newcastleton sits where the Liddel Water runs, ringed by the Liddesdale hills. In the photo above, the village is seen from the hillside on the property of Mrs. Margaret Henrs, the clustered roofs and chimneys among the trees with the fields climbing toward the hillsides.

This was the world James Telfer was born into and never left. He and his wife Betty farmed the little holdings at Greenholm and later Blackburnfoot in the same valley, weaving wool on home looms as their neighbours did. Historians trace the family's presence here before the Jacobite upheavals of 1745; generation after generation lived and died within sight of these hills. When his son Francis eventually crossed the world to South Australia in 1838, he carried this valley with him — it is the wellspring of the Australian branch of the Telfers.

*(From the Borders to the Bush, p.6)*

### The Ballad of Jamie Telfer of the Fair Dodhead

![Liddesdale Hills — an ancient sheepfold. From the Borders to the Bush, p.7](images/people/Liddesdale_Hills_Ancient_Sheepfold_p7.jpg)

The same Liddesdale hills that James Telfer farmed carried a much older Telfer story. The hill country had been raided back and forth across the English border for centuries — "worked over many times by the English (with fire and sword)". The *Ballad of Jamie Telfer of the Fair Dodhead*, written about the middle of the 16th century, tells of one such raid: the English under the Captain of Bewcastle rode up into the valley to drive off the herds, and were met on the way back. It is the oldest trace of the Telfer name in the Borders, and the book spells out what it means for the family: "The Telfers must have been affected by the constant wars and skirmishes which took place all about them." The old stone sheepfold in the plate above is exactly the kind of dry-stone enclosure the valley's herds were kept in in those centuries.

*(From the Borders to the Bush, p.7)*

### Douglas Square — Sheep Through the Main Street

![Newcastleton Douglas Square main street Roxburghshire Scotland p9](images/people/Newcastleton_Douglas_Square_main_street_Roxburghshire_Scotland_p9.jpg)
*Newcastleton's main street as it passes through Douglas Square, with a flock of sheep being herded — Newcastleton, Roxburghshire, the Scottish Borders, Scotland, on the Liddel Water. From the Borders to the Bush, p.9.*

The same hills and village streets feature a third plate: the main street of Newcastleton as it passes through **Douglas Square**, with a flock of sheep being driven along it under the eye of several men, between the traditional stone buildings and mature trees. It is the very street of the village that grew up where Castleton had stood — the lane the Telfers would have walked, herding and trading and attending the kirk. Douglas Square is the old heart of Newcastleton, and a flock of sheep on its cobbles is the Borders made visible — the world the book describes when it says the Telfers "were shepherds for several generations, hard working, but not well monied." The photograph gives that line a face: this is what the shepherd's life looked like on the home ground, not in the abstract hills but right along the main street of the family's own town.

*(From the Borders to the Bush, p.9)*

### The Greenholm Years

James Telfer didn't start out in Castleton itself. He and Betty lived first at Greenholm, a little farming area in Liddesdale where their first five children were baptised between 1796 and 1805 — James, Isobel, Adam, Margaret, Robert, and John. Life was simple and hard. The Telfers were sheep farmers and hand-loom weavers, like most of their neighbours in the Scottish Borders. They worked their small land holdings with the seasons, shearing and weaving wool to make ends meet.

### The Move to Blackburnfoot

Sometime between 1805 and 1809, James moved the family from Greenholm to Blackburnfoot — another farmstead in the same Liddesdale valley. It was there that their last two sons were born: Francis in February 1809, and William in April 1811. Francis would go on to become the one who crossed the world. But back then he was just another bairn in a packed cottage in the Borders, learning the shepherd's trade from his father.

### A Hand Loom Weaver's Life

In those days the Telfers of Roxburghshire were what the old parish records call "hand loom weavers" — men who worked wool at home on their own looms, spinning and weaving the fleece from the sheep that grazed the Cheviot Hills. It was honest, calloused-hand work that paid just enough to keep a family fed. The Industrial Revolution was already reshaping Scotland, but up in Liddesdale, the old ways held on a little longer. James lived and died in that world, never leaving the valley he was born in.

*(From the Borders to the Bush, pp.17–20)*

James Telfer was born in 1796 at Castleton, Roxburghshire, the eldest of eight children of James Telfer and Elizabeth "Betty" Hutton. He married Elizabeth Beattie around 1825 and stayed in Scotland when his younger brother Francis emigrated to South Australia in 1838.

James and Elizabeth farmed in the Liddesdale/Castleton area, where they raised at least five children. Their descendants continued in the Scottish Borders region.

## Children

The headstone inscription at Southdean Churchyard lists seven children by name (Elizabeth, James, Margaret, Jean, Robert, John, Adam). The 1841 Scotland Census adds Isabella (age ~4 in 1841). Vault records suggest up to 11 children total — the remaining may have died in infancy.

## Family Stories

James Telfer was the first child of James and Betty Telfer, born at Greenholm in 1796. He married Elizabeth Beattie around 1830 and stayed in Scotland as the eldest brother, while Francis set off for South Australia. Four of James's sons and one daughter would eventually follow their uncle across the world in later years.

Getting reliable records of James and Elizabeth's family has been a challenge. The children — with the exception of the youngest, Adam — were apparently never baptised, which suggests the family attended a non-conformist church during those years. Many births simply weren't registered because of a government tax of one shilling, which was a significant amount of money at the time.

The 1851 Jedburgh Census shows James as a 52-year-old agricultural labourer born in Roxburghshire, living with his wife Betty (48), and their children Ellen (19, servant), Bellie (14, servant), John (13, scholar) and Adam (9, scholar). Also in the household were Robert Beattie, a 77-year-old widower labourer (likely Elizabeth's father), and a nephew also named Robert Beattie, aged 11. James, Robert, Elizabeth and Margaret were already out of the home by then. The same census lists a Robert Telfer, aged 16, agricultural labourer, born Newcastleton, living at Falside Stable — this would have been James and Elizabeth's son Robert.

James Telfer died at 4pm on 9th December, 1863, at his dwelling house at Falside, Southdean, Roxburghshire. The cause was injuries he received from being squeezed between the shafts of a cart and a granary wall. His youngest son Adam reported the death. Elizabeth died on 28th December, 1891, at the age of 89, from "natural decay" — a quiet end after a long life.

*(From the Borders to the Bush, pp. 188)*

## Life Summary

James Telfer was the eldest son of James Telfer and Elizabeth Beattie. Born at the ruins of Hermitage Castle in Liddesdale, he emigrated to South Australia at age 25 on the ship "Oliver Lang", arriving in Melbourne in 1854 with his brother Robert and sister Elizabeth. He went on to manage Koppio Station near Port Lincoln for 39 years and became one of the colony's leading wool experts.

## Family Stories

James Telfer was born on 3rd September, 1829 at Hermitage Castle, Liddesdale, Roxburghshire, Scotland — the eldest son of James Telfer and Elizabeth Beattie. He came to Australia at the age of 25 on the ship "Oliver Lang", in company with his brother Robert and sister Elizabeth.

According to the official shipping list, the "Oliver Lang" departed Liverpool on 25th July, 1854, and arrived in Melbourne on 25th September, 1854. The Master was Henry Manning, tonnage 1736, and the ship carried 445 passengers. James, Robert and Elizabeth were listed as "adults" and "English" — though they were of course Scots — but with so many folks emigrating, officials weren't fussy about accuracy.

After landing in Melbourne, the three made their way to South Australia where they made contact with their Uncle Francis Telfer at Kersbrook in the Adelaide Hills.

James was under contract to Mr. Alexander Borthwick Murray and worked as a shepherd at Tungkillo for five years. While still there, he married Janet Welsh, the daughter of John and Margaret Welsh of Nisbet, Scotland. The marriage took place at "the Manse", Wakefield Street, on 6th November, 1855, according to the rites of the Church of Scotland, conducted by the Rev. Robert Haining. The witnesses were Robert and Elizabeth Telfer — his brother and sister.

After his five years at Tungkillo, James took over the management of Koppio Station near Port Lincoln for Dr. John Harris Browne. He managed Koppio for 39 years and in addition looked after "Talia", "Kalka" and "Pondanna" Stations in the Gawler Ranges. This meant many miles of arduous travel over unmade roads in all weathers.

James was recognised as one of the State's leading experts in wool production. Koppio Station carried 25,000 sheep, and the wool produced there and on the West Coast and Gawler Ranges stations was noted for its very high quality.

James and Janet's family of seven children grew up at Koppio Station. Two gum trees that still stand near the entrance were named "James" and "Janet" after the twins.

Janet died in 1885 after a long illness. James wrote a letter to his son James that described her last hours — it's preserved in the family records.

*(From the Borders to the Bush, pp. 189–192)*

# James Telfer (1832–1845)

**Role:** Eldest son of [[Francis Telfer (1809–1895)]] and Jean Murray — vanished at age 13
**Born:** 1832 — Scotland
**Disappeared:** July 1844 (aged 13) — Chain of Ponds area, South Australia
**Declared dead:** ~1845 (presumed)

## Family

| Relation | Name |
|----------|------|
| **Father** | [[Francis Telfer (1809–1895)]] |
| **Mother** | [[Jean Murray (1810–1839)]] |
| **Stepmother (1)** | [[Dinah Flavel (1821–1844)]] | 
| **Stepmother (2)** | [[Margaret Wright Telfer (1810–1892)]] |
| **Sister** | Esther Jane Telfer (1834–1909) — m. John Smith |
| **Sister** | Elizabeth Hannah Telfer (1836–1916) — m. Charles Farrow |
| **Half-sister** | Jean Telfer (1840–1892) |

## Life Summary

James was born in Scotland in 1832, the eldest of Francis and Jean's kids. He made the voyage on the *Prince George* with his parents and two younger sisters, docking at Port Adelaide on 26 December 1838. His mother died just 27 days later — leaving Francis with three kids under 7.

James grew up in the Adelaide Hills frontier on his father's farm near Chain of Ponds. By 13 he was working as a shepherd on the family sheep station.

## Family Stories

### The Disappearance of James Telfer

In July 1844, during a week of heavy rain, James left the sheep station on the River Torrens near Chain of Ponds to round up stray sheep. He never came home.

Francis raised the alarm that night. Neighbours searched for days but the creeks were flooded and rain hadn't let up. Nothing was found. The general feeling was the flood took him. People figured when waters dropped, his remains would turn up in the riverbed or the Reedbeds. They didn't.

The *South Australian Register* printed this on 10 July 1844 (p.3):

> **"BOY MISSING** — On Tuesday last, during the heavy rain then falling, a youth named Telfer, thirteen years old, left his fathers sheep station on the River Torrens, near Chain of Ponds, to recover some stray sheep, but up to Saturday last had not been heard of. The surrounding country has been searched, but no trace of the wanderer has been found: and from the late inclemency of the weather, there is too much reason to believe that he has perished."

Family stories over the years threw up different theories — killed by aborigines, step-mother troubles, ran away. The most detailed version came from William Flavel: one morning someone walked twelve miles to tell Francis, who rounded up every man in the district. They searched for days, then got the police from Adelaide. Nothing.

Then around 1877 — 33 years later — a newspaper article reported that recent floods had washed away logs and debris lodged against a tree in the river near Adelaide. Amongst the debris was a human skeleton. Police took charge. A doctor said the bones were a boy about 13, probably there for more than 20 years.

Whether Francis ever learned his son had been found is unknown.

Tragically, James was the fourth family member Francis had lost in six years — wife Jean (1839), infant son John (died at sea 1838), second wife Dinah (1844), and now his eldest boy.

*(Based on Donald Telfer, From the Borders to the Bush, pp.25–27, and the SA Register, 10 Jul 1844)*

## Sources

- Donald Telfer, *From the Borders to the Bush* (ISBN 0 7316 6387 X), pp. 25–27 — story reference, not verbatim
- South Australian Register, 10 July 1844, Page 3, Col. A — public domain newspaper quote

## Life Summary

James Telfer was the first child and eldest son of [[John Telfer (1840–1913)]] and his first wife [[Martha Allen (1840–1876)]]. Born at Honeysuckle Flat, South Australia on 18 October 1866, James was the first of four children from this marriage and carried his paternal grandfather's name.

In 1895, James—then living at Tantanoola—was listed in the *Border Watch* Almanac as a newspaper agent for the district, suggesting he operated a local agency for the Mount Gambier newspaper. The 1894 Tantanoola Show concert featured him as a performer, and Border Watch advertisements from 1898 and 1900 confirm his newspaper agency at Tantanoola.

He married Alma Ida Sporer (1880–1965) on 24 October 1917 at the Lutheran Church, Mount Gambier — James was 49, Alma was 37. Their only child, Vida, was born on 8 March 1919. James became a prominent community figure in Glencoe West: he was appointed a Justice of the Peace in 1924, served as District Council Auditor (re-elected 1927), and acted as Secretary of the Glencoe District Hall in 1929.

He died on 28 August 1946 at Glencoe West, South Australia, aged 79. His obituary in The Advertiser (2 Sep 1946) and The Chronicle (5 Sep 1946) described him as the beloved husband of Alma and loving father of Vida.

## Family Stories

James was the first of John and Martha Telfer's four children, born at Honeysuckle Flat on 18 October 1866. He moved with the family to Tantanoola as a young boy and quickly became involved in community life. He served as the first Secretary of the Tantanoola Agricultural and Floral Society and was also Secretary of the committee formed to organise the building of a Presbyterian Church in the town.

In 1917 he married Alma Ida Sporer at Mount Gambier, and together they established a general store at Glencoe West that also housed the local Post Office and sold groceries, hardware, drapery and anything else the farming community might need. James was an Elder at the local Presbyterian Church — a quiet, gentle soul who loved reading, especially poetry. He was Patron of the Glencoe West Tennis Club, served as its Auditor, and was an enthusiastic supporter of the Cricket Club. Always ready to lend a hand, James was a pillar of the community until his death in 1946. He and Alma had one daughter, Vida.

*(From the Borders to the Bush, pp.235–236)*

title: James Telfer (of Sorbietrees) — Family & Biography
body_markdown:
# James Telfer (of Sorbietrees) (~1740–?) — Scotland

James Telfer of Sorbietrees (also recorded as *Sorbytrees*) is the earliest confirmed Telfer ancestor in the Scottish branch of the family. He was born around 1740 — the exact date is lost — and spent his life in the rolling border country near Newcastleton, Roxburghshire. He married Margaret Armstrong, and together they raised a family at Sorbietrees, a smallholding in a region marked by centuries of cross-border raiding, reiving, and hard pastoral life.

Though no portrait or personal writings survive, James almost certainly worked the land as a shepherd or farmer. The Border hills were sheep country, and a man living at a place called Sorbietrees would have been intimately tied to the rhythms of lambing, shearing, and the seasonal drives to market. Life in eighteenth-century Liddesdale was rugged and self-reliant — a world away from the cities, and one that shaped the generations to come.

> ⚠️ **Same-name note:** This James Telfer — of **Sorbietrees**, husband of Margaret Armstrong, father of [[James Telfer (bap.1762)]] (bap. 24 Sep 1762) — is a **distinct person** from [[James Telfer (1761–1845)]] (bap. 14 Jul 1761, son of John of Castleton, father of SA immigrant Francis) — a *different, older* James born barely a year earlier. Also distinct: [[James Telfer (1829–1913)]] (South Australian pioneer). Do not merge them; public user trees routinely blend the Sorbietrees and Castleton Jameses into one man — that is wrong (see Corrections Log, 30 Aug 2026).

## Family Stories

### The Sorbietrees Connection

Sorbietrees — sometimes spelled *Sorbytrees* in older records — was a small farm or croft in the parish of Castleton, Roxburghshire, not far from the modern village of Newcastleton (formerly Copshaw Holm). The name likely refers to a stand of sorb (rowan) trees, a common feature of the Border landscape. It was here that James Telfer and Margaret Armstrong made their home, and here that their known children were baptised in the local kirk.

The first clear documentary trace of James appears in the parish registers. His son James was baptised at Castleton on 24 September 1762, followed by a daughter, Jean, on 24 June 1764. These entries, brief as they are, anchor the family in time and place. For a man of humble station — unlikely to have left a will, a land deed, or a tombstone of his own — a baptismal record is the closest thing to a signature.

### The Headstone Evidence

Beyond the baptismal entries, a second piece of evidence fills out the family picture. In Castleton Cemetery, a headstone commemorates several individuals who are almost certainly children or close relatives of James and Margaret. While the stone does not name the parents directly, the combination of names, dates, and location makes the connection persuasive:

- **Francis Telfer** (1768–1836)
- **Jenet Telfer** (1770–1842)
- **Adam Telfer** (1771–1846)

If these three are added to James (bap. 1762) and Jean (bap. 1764), the family grows to five children born over roughly a decade — a typical span for a Border farming family. Francis, Jenet, and Adam would have been young adults during the turbulent years of the Napoleonic Wars, a time when many Scots from the border counties began to look abroad for opportunity, setting the stage for the family's later emigration.

*(From the Borders to the Bush, pp. 17–18)*

## Sources

- Parish baptismal registers, Castleton, Roxburghshire: James Telfer (24 Sep 1762), Jean Telfer (24 Jun 1764).
- Castleton Cemetery headstone inscriptions, recorded by Hope Simmons.

## Life Summary

Jane Murray Farrow was born **17 April 1857** at **Chain of Ponds**, in the Adelaide Hills of South Australia, the daughter of **Charles Farrow** and **Elizabeth Hannah Telfer**. Through her mother she is a direct descendant of the first-generation Telfer immigrants **Francis Telfer** and **Jean Murray**, who arrived in South Australia aboard the **Prince George on 26 December 1838** — making Jane a key anchor connecting the Farrow line into the Telfer family tree.

She married **Alfred George Stribling** around **1885**. The couple had three recorded sons: **Arthur Clifford "Cliff"** (1890–1918), **Lindsay Ellis** (1893–1979), and **George Charles** (1898–1988). The family was associated with the **Tarlee / Finniss district** and later lived at **Rutland Avenue, Brighton, South Australia** (the residence recorded for son Cliff's WWI service record).

### Death

Jane died on **14 March 1934** at **Brighton**, Holdfast Bay City, South Australia, aged 76, and was buried at **North Brighton Cemetery** on a joint family headstone with her husband Alfred, who had predeceased her in January 1928.
