## Life Summary

Maria Clara Telfer was the second child of John Telfer and his second wife Martha Clara Henstridge, born around 1878. She was the elder sister of ten siblings from this marriage and was named with the middle name Clara after her mother. She died young, on 22 December 1903 at Tantanoola, South Australia, at approximately 25 years of age, never having married. She predeceased both her mother (who died in 1921) and father (who died in 1913) by ten and eight years respectively — an unusually early passing that cut short a life that might have continued long enough to see the family's later expansion.

## Family Stories

Maria Clara Telfer was the seventh child of John Telfer and the second child of his marriage to Martha Clara Henstridge. She died young at just 25 years of age, never having married. Her memorial card — printed in black with gold lettering — bore her photograph circled with the poignant words "Though lost to sight, To memory dear." Below the photograph was inscribed: "In Loving Memory of Maria Clara Telfer." Her early passing in December 1903 at Tantanoola was a sadness visited upon the family well before her mother's death in 1921 and her father's in 1913.

*(From the Borders to the Bush, pp.242, 248–249)*

## Life Summary

Mark Telfer was born on 12 April 1877 at Up and Down Rocks, South Australia, the first biological child of John Telfer (1840–1913) and his second wife Martha Clara Henstridge. He was the eldest of eleven children from the second marriage.

He married Julia Matilda Seebohm on 9 July 1902. Together they had seven children: Floris Ethel Victoria (1904–1951), Kenneth William John (1904–?), Gilbert Melville known as Mel (1911–1978), Jean Maryann Martha (1910–1984), Joyce Elizabeth (1912–2012), Maifie Beryl (1913–1948), and Lindsay Roland (1920–1976).

The book *From the Borders to the Bush* confirms all seven, listing them as: Floris, Ken, Mel, Jean, Joyce, Maifie and Lindsay.

Mark died on 23 July 1946 in Adelaide, South Australia, at age 69. His death location (Adelaide, not Tantanoola) suggests he may have moved from the family's Tantanoola home base later in life.

## Family Stories

Mark Telfer was John Telfer's sixth child — the first born to his second wife, Martha Clara Henstridge. He married Julia Matilda Seebohm (known as Tillie) in the Tantanoola Public Hall on 9 July 1902, with the Rev. James Davies officiating. Both Mark and Tillie were active in Sunday School teaching at the Tantanoola Presbyterian Church, and the congregation presented them with a large family Bible on their Silver Wedding anniversary.

Mark took over his father's farm, "Brackenridge", when John retired, growing crops and running sheep and cattle. He lived there until about 1940, then purchased a house in Millicent and retired with two of his daughters, Jean and Maifie. Mark was a fine sportsman — he played football and cricket, served as Timekeeper for the football club when his sons took the field, and was a capable batsman and slow bowler who won a medal for the highest batting average in the Tantanoola Cricket Club. He and Tillie raised seven children: Floris, Ken, Mel, Jean, Joyce, Maifie and Lindsay.

*(From the Borders to the Bush, pp.240–241)*

## Life Summary

Martha Allen married John Telfer on 10 January 1865 at the Residence of Robert Boyd, Adelaide, South Australia. She bore four children between 1866 and 1873 — three daughters and one son — before dying young at German Flat, near Mount Gambier, on 9 March 1876, aged approximately 36.

Her death left John Telfer a widower with four young children (the youngest, Martha, was barely three). John remarried seven months later to Martha Clara Henstridge on 28 December 1876.

**Place of origin, parents, migration, and burial location are all unknown.** She may have arrived in South Australia aboard the *Morning Star* (departed Liverpool 28 November 1862, arrived Port Adelaide 13 February 1863) as an unmarried servant, but this is unconfirmed.

## Timeline

|---|---|

## Family Stories

Martha Allen married John Telfer on 19th January 1865. The ceremony took place at the private residence of Mr Robert Boyd in Synagogue Place, Adelaide. On the marriage certificate John was described as a Shepherd of "full age" and Martha as a spinster, also of "full age". Martha was the daughter of William Allen, born in 1842, and her parents are believed to have come from Glenmaquin, County Donegal, Ireland.

John and Martha had four children — James, Elizabeth, Susan and Martha. The family moved to the South East of the state in 1874 and settled at Tantanoola, then known as Lucieton.

Sadly, Martha died on 9th March 1876 at German Flat, leaving John with four children aged 10, 8, 5 and 3. Her death was recorded in the Border Watch on 11th March 1876 with a brief and blunt notice: "Death in Hospital: On Thursday morning, Martha Telfer, wife of Mr. John Telfer, of German Flat, died in Hospital in Mount Gambier from cancer. She had not been there long. She was 34 years of age."

It's a stark statement, and we can only imagine the pain and suffering Martha endured before her untimely death.

*(From the Borders to the Bush, p.234)*

body_markdown:
# Martha Henstridge (~1854–1921)

**Role:** Second wife of John Telfer (1840–1913)

After the death of his first wife Martha Allen (1840–1876), John Telfer (1840–1913) married Martha Clara Henstridge on 28 Dec 1876 at the Residence of J. Telfer, Tantanoola Creek, South Australia.

**Born:** 22 Jan 1854, South Australia
**Died:** 13 Nov 1921, Adelaide, South Australia (aged 67)
**Buried:** Tantanoola Cemetery, Tantanoola SA

Martha was the daughter of Frederick Henstridge Sr. and Maria Smith. She had 10 children with John Telfer: Mark, Maria Clara, Isabella Lucieton, John Roland, Clara Blanche, Robert Freddy, Douglas, Colin Roy, Alan Dale, and Alma Tressy.

**Sources:**
1. **WikiTree:** [Martha Clara Henstridge (Henstridge-4)](https://www.wikitree.com/wiki/Henstridge-4) — birth 22 Jan 1854, marriage 28 Dec 1876, death 13 Nov 1921 (GenealogySA records)
2. **FindAGrave:** [Martha Clara Telfer (memorial 186972464)](https://www.findagrave.com/memorial/186972464/martha-clara-telfer) — burial at Tantanoola Cemetery
3. **GenealogySA:** Death record Ade sym H B 450 P 228 — Martha died 13 Nov 1921, aged 68, widow, of Tantanoola
4. **Book:** *From the Borders to the Bush*

## Family Stories

After the death of his first wife, John Telfer married for the second time on 28th December 1876. His second wife was Martha Clara Henstridge, daughter of Frederick Henstridge. The marriage took place at John's private residence at Tantanoola Creek, officiated by the Rev. Charles Tresize. John was described as a "Stockholder", aged 34, and Martha as a Spinster, aged 23.

Martha came from a family with a remarkable history. An old letter preserved in the family tells the story: "When John Telfer took Martha Henstridge to wife, he married into a family with a great historic heritage." The Henstridge family is descended from the Viking Hengest, who came to England as a mercenary to assist King Vertigen of Kent, but overthrew him and ruled Kent for a number of years. His descendants fought the Normans in Sherwood Forest with Robin Hood. The heir to Hengest-Ridge Castle was given a baroncy by King John, and the barons kept the manuscripts to Magna Carta secretly in Hengestridge Castle until the King was forced to sign them.

Martha was very supportive of her husband in all his activities. She was an active member of the Tantanoola Red Cross, and served as Postmistress at Tantanoola from 1919 to 1921 after her daughter Tressic. Martha died in 1921 and is buried alongside John at Tantanoola Cemetery, where her headstone reads: "Blessed are the dead who die in the Lord."

*(From the Borders to the Bush, pp. 238–240)*

## Life Summary

Martha Telfer was born on 18 April 1873 at Black Heath (also recorded as Blackheath), Tungkillo, South Australia, the fourth child and third daughter of John Telfer (1840–1913) by his first wife [[Martha Allen (1840–1876)]]. The family lived at Honeysuckle Flat and Black Heath during her early years before moving to the Tantanoola district in the South East.

On 29 March 1899 at Tantanoola, SA, Martha married Malcolm Duncan Cameron (1873–1935), a farmer. They had at least one known child: a son, Malcolm Murray Cameron, born 2 August 1905 at Mount Gambier SA.

Martha died on 4 August 1964 at Mount Gambier, South Australia, aged 91, and was predeceased by her husband by 29 years. Her burial location has not been positively identified — no FindAGrave record has been found, and her 1964 death was too late for Trove newspaper death notices.

## Family Stories

Martha — known as Mattie — was the fourth and youngest child of John Telfer and his first wife Martha Allen, born on 18 April 1873 at Black Heath. She married Malcolm Duncan Cameron on 29 March 1899 at Tantanoola. Malcolm was a man of public affairs: during his time in Parliament he served on the Works Committee, eventually becoming its Chairman, and was a lifelong member of the Liberal Party. He was also an Elder of the Presbyterian Church for thirty years.

Mattie and Malcolm raised five children — Murray, Ivan, Lorna, Mavis and Jack — in the South East district. Malcolm died on 1 March 1935, and Mattie lived on for another twenty-nine years, passing away at Mount Gambier in 1964 at the age of 91.

*(From the Borders to the Bush, pp.238–239)*

body_markdown:
# Murray John Telfer (1924–2009)

**Lifespan:** 1924–2009

**Role:** Ninth child and youngest son of Francis Charles and Amy Telfer; husband of Shirley Edna Parker; father of Daryll William, John Robert, Grantley Keith, Timothy Neil, Kathryn Mavis and Susan Shirley.

![Murray ruth telfer duchess horse 1936](images/people/murray-ruth-telfer-duchess-horse-1936.jpg)
*Murray John Telfer and sister Ruth Telfer (aged 6) on Duchess the horse with family dog, circa 1936*

![Murray shirley telfer wedding 1950](images/people/murray-shirley-telfer-wedding-1950.jpg)
*Murray John Telfer and Shirley Edna Parker on their wedding day, 18 February 1950, in the car after the ceremony at Prospect Church of Christ*

![Murray shirley telfer wedding portrait 1950](images/people/murray-shirley-telfer-wedding-portrait-1950.jpg)
*Murray John Telfer and Shirley Edna Parker formal wedding portrait, 18 February 1950, at Prospect Church of Christ — Shirley in her lace-trimmed gown, veil, and round glasses beaming; Murray in double-breasted suit with boutonnière, an older woman watching in background*

---

## Family

| Relation | Name |
|---|---|
| **Father** | [[Francis Charles Telfer (1875–1954)]] |
| **Mother** | [[Amy Ellen Telfer (1884–1951)]] |
| **Spouse** | [[Shirley Edna Telfer (1929–2017)]] |
| **Children** | [[Daryll William Telfer]], [[John Robert Telfer]], [[Grantley Keith Telfer]], [[Timothy Neil Telfer (1959–?)]], [[Kathryn Mavis Telfer (1961–1965)]], [[Susan Shirley Lawrie (?–living)]] |

---

## Life Summary

Murray was a **grazier and farmer** on South Australia's Eyre Peninsula — a man of the land whose life spanned the great transition from horse power to mechanisation. He worked **horse teams of twelve to fourteen horses**, ploughing 30 acres a day with a twenty-row combine. He drove **tandem Fordson tractors** for extra traction on the hills of Karulga. He cut chaff with a Hornsby oil engine, later a McCormick Deering tractor.

His **Christian faith was the defining thread of his life**. At an early age he made his commitment to the Lord, remembering a sermon from his father: "let your yes be yes and your no be no." He lived that out faithfully — in business, in family, in every interaction. He served as **elder at Ungarra and Tumby Bay Churches of Christ**, **secretary of Tumby Bay Church of Christ for over 20 years**, **Sunday School teacher**, **lay preacher**, taught **Religious Education at Ungarra and Mt Hill schools**, completed a **Christian Counselling course**, and later became a member of **Gideons International** placing Bibles in motels and hospitals. He also helped build the **Stokes Methodist Church**.

A **loving son, brother, husband, father, father-in-law, grandfather, great-grandfather**, caring friend, counsellor, helper and mentor — his deep trust in God was evidenced in all he did and said. His quiet humour was always to the fore.

---

## Family Stories

Murray was the ninth child of Francis Charles and Amy Telfer, the youngest of the boys. As a small boy he held out his finger to his brother Reg and said "cut it" — and Reg did, with a pair of scissors. He later married Shirley Edna Parker and together they raised four sons — Daryll William, John Robert, Grantley Keith and Timothy Neil — and two daughters, Kathryn Mavis and Susan Shirley. *(From the Borders to the Bush, pp.139, 175)*

---

## Stories & Memories

### Childhood at Ungarra & Saddleworth

The Telfer family arrived at Ungarra in 1904. Murray's father took up scrub land and batched (lived alone as a bachelor) for years before marrying Amy Provis in April 1909. Their equipment was basic: horses, a wagon, and a plough. Sometimes he carted water for soak at Wilkins' property.

From the farm near Saddleworth, the children walked **three miles to school** regardless of weather. Murray was nearly six when he started — he completed grades 1 and 2 at Saddleworth, then grade 3 back at Ungarra on the new scrub block.

**Transport:** The family travelled in a Nash Tourer car with a canvas top and side curtains (top speed 25–30 mph / 40–50 km/h). Leaving Saddleworth early, they reached Port Augusta after dark, stayed overnight at a hotel, and continued the next day. The windscreen wiper was operated by a handle inside the car!

### Horses — The Heart of Farm Life

> "Horses were a part of everyday life. We had one old pony called **Duchess** that you could run up behind while it was standing in the yard and leap frog onto its back if you were agile enough, and she wouldn't move."
>
> — Murray & Ruth (aged 6) on Duchess, circa 1936 *(photo in gallery)*

**Daily horse team routine:** They were up before breakfast to feed chaff. Each horse was harnessed with its own winkers and collars, coupled in the correct working order — six or seven horses in the front row, the same behind. Long leather reins ran through to the leaders. Nosebags of chaff (half-filled Hessian bags) hung on the harness until they reached the paddock.

**Knock-off time:** Chains dropped, they walked behind holding the reins. Reversed the harnessing at the shed. Horses went to the dam for a drink — some would roll if they were sweaty. Back to the manger in the straw-roofed stable (walls built of mallee stumps). After tea, hurricane lantern in hand, more chaff. Twenty horses lined up munching — "an era that has passed."

**Chaff cutting (once a week):** Sheaved hay fed into a chaff cutter driven by a Hornsby oil engine, later by a McCormick Deering 15–30 petrol-kerosene tractor (started on petrol, switched to kerosene once warm).

**Horse names (front row):** Ranji, *[unknown]*, Lon, Tiger, Clyde, *[unknown]*, Lola — plus Ruby (Murray's riding horse) and Duchess (the family pony).

### A Tribute *(from the memorial book)*

Murray was a man of **integrity, humility, and generosity**. His word was his bond. He never sought recognition, only to serve. He married **Shirley Edna Parker** on 18 February 1950 at Prospect Church of Christ — a partnership lasting 59 years.

He served in the **RAAF during WWII as a radar mechanic** — a role demanding precision and trust. After the war, he managed **"Glen Alvie"** at Karulga, running sheep and wheat on 2,000 acres. He served as **elder at Ungarra and Tumby Bay Churches of Christ**, **secretary of Tumby Bay Church of Christ for over 20 years**, **Sunday School superintendent**, **lay preacher**, and taught **Religious Education** at local schools.

His **love of horses** never faded — from the great teams of his youth to the pony Duchess that carried his grandchildren. He was a **gentle man with a quiet chuckle**, always ready with a story.

### The Early Years: Horse-Stealing at Military Camp

During military training, Murray and his mates **Jack, Stan, and Bob** decided to "borrow" a horse from a nearby property. They snuck out after lights out, led the horse back to camp, and hid it in the lines. Next morning the horse was discovered — **Murray had injured his neck** in the escapade. **Stan got chewed out by the Sergeant** while Murray tried to look innocent. The horse was returned, but the story became legend among the mates.

### The Cows' Tails

Reg and Murray were milking about 10 jersey-cross cows, aged 11–12. One day Murray said, "We ought to tie their tails together." He tied a reef knot in the tail hair. The cows walked side by side, gradually parted, and a tug-of-war ensued — the first joint broke off one tail. They cut off the broken piece and disposed of it. Dad never saw it, or didn't say. That cow had a docked tail that **stung like a whip** at milking time ever after.

### River Swimming Challenge

At the river, the boys would challenge each other to swim across the deep waterhole — a test of courage. Murray, never one to back down, took the challenge. He made it across, emerging with his **typical chuckle** at the bravado of youth. "We were all mad," he'd say later, shaking his head with that grin.

### A Good Scare

Murray and his brother **Mantle** loved a good prank. One day Murray placed a **fake snake** on Mantle's path, expecting a laugh. But Mantle spotted it, picked it up, and **chased Murray with it** — the tables turned! Murray's own trick backfired, and he got the scare of his life. He told this story with a grin: "Mantle got me good that day."

### Rabbit Trapping

School holidays meant 30–40 traps set along the creek on Monday afternoon. Thirty to forty rabbits the first night, progressively fewer after that. Saturday: pull the traps, fill the holes. Skins drying by the dozen. Sold for ~1 penny per skin (8–9 pence per pound) — pocket money. The place smelled of rabbits "from one end of the holidays to the other." Mum cooked rabbit that tasted "equal to chicken."

### Triumph Motorcycle & the Sidecar

Teen years: Murray bought a second-hand Triumph motorcycle, borrowed £10 from Mum, and paid it back. He fitted a sidecar. Evenings were spent rabbit hunting with a half-whippet, half-greyhound bitch in the sidecar — she'd run them down in the headlight. They chased foxes too, but the foxes turned too sharply. He also rode the motorbike to and from Long Plains courting Shirley.

### Sliding Down Culverts

They wore the seats of their pants out sliding down cement culverts between home and school at Saddleworth. A handful of sand helped the slide. Mum was in hospital, with May looking after them. Rather than tell May about the holes in their trousers, they went to school with holey pants — **double trouble**.

### Bed Without Tea

May sent them to bed hungry for misbehaviour. Eddie sneaked out and found cake. May felt sorry and brought food later. "Challenging days for small boys who had to make their own fun (no television or radio). But they were happy days with little thought or care for what lay ahead."

### A Message to His Grandchildren *(from the memorial book)*

> "What would you do if you had no electricity, or no running water on tap? Perhaps no telephone. Maybe no car, or truck, or tractor, and you lived 30 or more kilometres from a town where you could get groceries, or see a doctor, or dentist, or chemist. That's what it was like when I was born.
>
> Families were usually large — I was ninth in a family of ten. Mother had **Bake Day on Friday** — big loaves of bread and trays of buns, us waiting for a hot bun. Never went hungry.
>
> **No electricity:** wood stove (fire lit every morning — nice in winter, added heat in summer, often in an iron house). Big kettle always on. Wash days: wood-fired copper, scrubbing board (corrugated wood or glass). Hand-ringer or wring by hand. **Bath night: Saturday only**, big tub in kitchen near stove, same water for all children.
>
> **Workshop:** forge and anvil. Children worked the bellows. Hammer and chisel. **Lighting:** kerosene lamps or candles — sometimes read so long the lamp ran out of kerosene (what a smell when the wick burned).
>
> **Refrigeration:** none until kerosene fridges. The **Cool Safe** — hessian/cork sides, tray of water on top dripping down to keep sides damp, kept butter from melting. Dad killed a sheep weekly. Salted meat in a wooden wine keg.
>
> **Everything was labour intensive.** The changes were gradual over many years."

### Always Remember *(poem from the memorial book)*

> **Always remember the things that are true**  
> **The love of the Lord and His love for you**  
> **The love of a family that's loyal and kind**  
> **The friends that are faithful, the ties that bind**  
>   
> **Remember the laughter, the fun and the joy**  
> **The memories shared, like a favourite toy**  
> **The lessons of life, both bitter and sweet**  
> **The strength to go on when the pathway is steep**  
>   
> **Remember the horses, the land and the sky**  
> **The days that were long, as the years wander by**  
> **The faith that sustained through the storm and the calm**  
> **The peace that is found in the Saviour's palm**  
>   
> **So when you look back on the life that I've known**  
> **Remember the seed that was faithfully sown**  
> **Not in the things that will rust and decay**  
> **But the love that endures, come what may**

---

## Family & Community

- **1929 Family Picnic at Christensen Park, Clare** — Fran, Walter, May, Bert, Gladys, Albert, Charlie, Sylvia, Doris, Joyce, Melville, Jean; Reg, Hope, Nellie, Beattie, Amy, Murray, Millie, Doug; Ralph, Bill, Eddie, Keith
- **Siblings & families:** Reg & Elma (50th anniversary), Frank & Merle, Jean & Eric McMurtrie (Murray & Pamela Ruth as attendants), May & Dick Fatchen, Eddie & Lola, Milly & Fred Barton, Les & Gladys Pedler
- **Grandchildren:** James & Alexa, Kristin & Ben Stefanoff (Nairne SA — music teacher, theatre performer, writer), Nicholas, Jonathan, Andrew, Gerrie, Helen, Rex
- **Faith community:** Ungarra Church of Christ 75th Anniversary (15 Nov 1986) — Family Day Bag Sewing Competition at Provis Park, Stokes
- **2007:** Unveiling the Telfer Memorial Plaque at Pioneer Park, Ungarra — commemorating Telfer settlers

---

## Final Years

Last trip to the farm: 22 April 2009. Special moments in his final weeks. Passed peacefully 1 May 2009. "We thank God for Murray's life and the effect that he had on so many lives. Our lives are so much the richer for him being a part."

---

## Timeline

| Date | Event |
|------|-------|
| 24 Mar 1924 | Born, Tumby Bay, South Australia |
| ~1926 | Family moved briefly to Clare (fruit block) |
| 1933 | Moved back to Ungarra |
| 1930s | Farm life at Ungarra & Saddleworth; school 3 miles walk |
| ~1936 | Photo on Duchess the horse with sister Ruth (aged 6) |
| 1940s | Teen years: horse teams, rabbit trapping, Triumph motorcycle; military service |
| 18 Feb 1950 | Married Shirley Edna Parker at Prospect Church of Christ *(wedding photos in gallery)* |
| 1950s-60s | Grazier at Garravale, Karulga — horse teams, Fordson tractors |
| 1964 | Last crop at Garravale |
| 1970s-80s | Active in Church of Christ: Elder, Secretary (20+ yrs), Sunday School, RE teacher |
| 1980s-90s | Gideons International member |
| 15 Nov 1986 | Ungarra Church of Christ 75th Anniversary — Family Day |
| 1999 | Shearing ewes with Steve Rogers at wool classing table |
| 2007 | Telfer Memorial Plaque unveiled, Pioneer Park, Ungarra |
| 22 Apr 2009 | Last trip to the farm |
| 1 May 2009 | Passed away peacefully, aged 85 |

---

## Sources

- **Primary:** *Celebrating the life of Murray John Telfer — 24 March 1924 – 1 May 2009* (family memorial book, compiled with photos & memories from Daryl, Grantley, Auntie Pam, Shirley). Full commemorative book archived in the vault: [[Celebrating the life of Murray John Telfer - 24th March 1924 - 1st May 2009.pdf]]
- **Oral History:** "Murray's Memories" as told to son Grantley Keith Telfer
- **Wikipedia-style note:** The rich biography is preserved from the earlier family record; see the memorial note [[Celebrating the life of Murray John Telfer]] for the fuller account.
- **WikiTree:** [Murray John Telfer (1924–2009)](https://www.wikitree.com/wiki/Telfer-403) — confirms birth location Tumby Bay, SA
- **Geni:** [Francis Charles Telfer (1875–1954)](https://www.geni.com/people/Francis-Telfer/6000000037272985511) — confirms Murray as son of Francis Charles
- **WikiTree:** [Amy Ellen (Provis) Telfer (1884–1951)](https://www.wikitree.com/wiki/Provis-64) — confirms Murray's mother's identity

# Rev. Ralph Drummond (1792–1872)

**Role:** First Presbyterian minister in South Australia; arrived 1839 with his wife and eight children; minister of the United Presbyterian congregation, Gouger Street chapel, 1839–1855.

**Born:** 1792
**Died:** 1872
**Denomination:** United Presbyterian Church of Scotland

## Context (Telfer connection)

Francis Telfer and his wife arrived in South Australia in December 1838, in the same wave of Scottish emigration that brought Ralph Drummond's Presbyterian ministry to the young colony. Drummond was one of the **three founding Presbyterian ministers of South Australia** (with Rev. Robert Haining and Rev. John Gardner) whose ministry anchored the colonies' early congregations and, significantly, performed the marriages that shaped the Telfer line. His Gouger Street chapel ministry predated Haining's arrival in 1841.

## Life Summary

Ralph Drummond came to South Australia in 1839 and established the first Presbyterian congregation in the colony. With Robert Haining (Church of Scotland) and John Gardner (Free Church of Scotland), he represented one of the three branches of Scottish Presbyterianism that would be brought together at the formation of the Presbytery of South Australia in 1865.

title: Rev. Robert Haining (1802–1874) — Church of Scotland Minister, Adelaide
roles: Church of Scotland minister at Adelaide; performed the marriage of Francis Telfer to Margaret Wright on 27 March 1845 at North Adelaide.
body_markdown:
# Rev. Robert Haining (1802–1874)

**Role:** Church of Scotland minister at Adelaide; performed the marriage of Francis Telfer to Margaret Wright on 27 March 1845 at North Adelaide.

**Born:** 14 August 1802 — Maxton, Roxburghshire, Scotland
**Died:** 26 April 1874 (aged 71) — Glenelg, South Australia
**Ordained:** 31 March 1841, Edinburgh
**Arrived Adelaide:** 20 November 1841, aboard the *Orissa*

## Context (Telfer connection)

Robert Haining performed the second marriage central to the Telfer line: the wedding of **Francis Telfer** to **Margaret Wright** on **27 March 1845** at North Adelaide. He was one of the **three founding Presbyterian ministers of South Australia** (with Rev. Ralph Drummond and Rev. John Gardner).

## Life Summary

Born at Maxton, Roxburghshire on 14 August 1802, son of Rev. John Haining and Wilhelmina (née Wilson). Educated at Sir John Watson's Hospital and Edinburgh University (1818–25). Appointed by the Church of Scotland's Committee on Colonial Churches on 5 February 1841 as minister at Adelaide, ordained 31 March 1841, and married Jessie, daughter of bookseller Robert Grant of Edinburgh, on 1 June 1841 before voyaging to South Australia on the *Orissa*, arriving at Port Adelaide on 20 November 1841.

He held his first service in Adelaide on 28 November 1841. After worship in rented quarters, a small church, **St Andrew's, Grenfell Street**, was erected for him and opened 14 July 1844 — succeeded by a larger St Andrew's in Wakefield Street, opened 13 February 1859. It was from this ministry that he performed the Francis Telfer–Margaret Wright marriage in March 1845.

Haining accepted state aid for the Church of Scotland in 1846–51, was a principal participant at the union of the Presbyterian denominations on 10 May 1865 creating the Presbyterian Church of South Australia, and was described as "a clergyman of broad sympathies, allied with strict orthodoxy, of genial temperament and unassuming disposition." His Adelaide ministry ended in 1871; he died at Glenelg on 26 April 1874.

## Sources

- **Australian Dictionary of Biography (J. McLellan),** [Haining, Robert (1802–1874)](https://adb.anu.edu.au/biography/haining-robert-2142), Vol 1, 1966, online 2006 — full life summary verified — accessed 7 Aug 2026
- **SA History Hub (John Love),** [Presbyterian Church](https://sahistoryhub.history.sa.gov.au/organisations/presbyterian-church/) — names Haining (with Drummond and Gardner) as one of three founding Presbyterian ministers — accessed 7 Aug 2026

*Verified against two independent source groups (ADB + SA History Hub) by the review gate, 7 Aug 2026. Matches the 27 Mar 1845 marriage performed for Francis Telfer and Margaret Wright.*

title: Richard Paynter — Family & Biography

body_markdown:
# Richard Paynter (1838–1869)

**Role:** First husband of Jean Telfer
**Born:** ~1838 — Cornwall, England
**Died:** 7 February 1869 (aged 30) — St. Kitts Creek, pleurisy
**Buried:** Kapunda area

Richard Paynter was born in Cornwall, England, the son of Richard Paynter of Calstock. He emigrated to South Australia where he worked as a labourer at Chain of Ponds.

He married Jean Telfer on 12 September 1859 at the Chain of Ponds Parsonage, solemnised by John Kither and witnessed by her father Francis Telfer and Henry Whiting. Jean was several months pregnant at the time.

After their first child Thomas was born, the family moved to Koppio near Port Lincoln where Richard worked as a shepherd for Jean's cousin James Telfer. They later returned to the Chain of Ponds area and then to St. Kitts between Kapunda and Truro, where Richard became the local school teacher — a change brought on by his failing health.

Richard died of pleurisy at the age of 30, leaving a widow and five children unprovided for.

**Source:** *From the Borders to the Bush* — Chapter on Jean/Jane Telfer

## Family Stories

Richard Paynter was born in Calstock, Cornwall, the son of Richard Paynter, who died in January 1856 aged 39 after "a protracted affliction." Richard the younger emigrated to South Australia and worked as a labourer at Chain of Ponds. On 12 September 1859, at just 19 years old, Jean Telfer married 21-year-old Richard Paynter at the Chain of Ponds Parsonage — a different setting from her sisters, who were married in their father Francis's home. Jean was several months pregnant at the time. After their first son Thomas was born, the family moved to Koppio near Port Lincoln, where Richard worked as a shepherd for Jean's cousin James Telfer. They later returned to the Chain of Ponds area and eventually settled at St. Kitts, between Kapunda and Truro. There, as Richard's health began to fail, he made an unusual career change — from shepherd to school teacher. The book *From the Borders to the Bush* records that he died of pleurisy on 7 February 1869 at St. Kitts Creek, aged just 30, leaving his widow and five children unprovided for. An in memoriam notice was placed in a local newspaper. His first child Dinah was born at Finniss Point five months after his death.

*(From the Borders to the Bush, p.16)*

Robert Dunlop Lawrie was born at Craigman, New Cumnock, Ayrshire, Scotland on 23 May 1850, the son of John Lawrie (1810–1888) and Janet Dunlop (?–1902). His father farmed at Craigman before emigrating to South Australia in 1853 aboard the *Ann Dashwood*, arriving in Melbourne on 10 November 1853. Robert Freddy Telfer was the sixth child of John Telfer and Martha Clara Henstridge, born 4 January 1886 at Rosaville, South Australia. He remained geographically anchored within his home state. body_markdown:
# Robert Telfer (1803–1878)

**Role:** Son of the Scottish patriarch — stayed in Castleton, Roxburghshire his entire life  
**Born:** 25 April 1803 — Castleton, Roxburghshire, Scotland  
**Died:** 1878 (aged 74) — Castleton, Scottish Borders, Scotland  
**Buried:** Likely Old Castleton Cemetery, Newcastleton, Scottish Borders, Scotland  
**Occupation:** Farm servant / agricultural labourer

---

## Family Stories

### The Brother Who Stayed — A Life in Castleton

Of all the children of James Telfer and Betty Hutton, Robert was the one who lived and died within a few miles of where he was born. While his younger brother Francis crossed the world to South Australia, and his older brother James followed years later, Robert stayed put in the Liddesdale valley.

He married Elizabeth "Betty" Oliver around 1828 and they set up house in Castleton. The 1841 census shows them with four young children — Elizabeth, James, Jean, and John — living alongside an older John Telfer (64), Violet Telfer, and William Telfer. Extended family sharing a roof, as folks did in those days.

Robert worked as an agricultural labourer, the kind of life his father had lived as a hand loom weaver — hard work, modest means, family close. By 1851, things had changed. Robert was 46 and living with only two of his children still at home. His wife Betty was gone — whether she'd died or left, the records don't say.

He died in 1878 at age 74, in the same parish where he was born. The statutory death registration records his mother's maiden name as Hutton, confirming his place in the family.

Robert never saw Australia. Never sailed on a ship across the ocean. But his story matters too — the brother who stayed, kept the old name in the old country, and lived the quiet life that his more adventurous siblings left behind.

*(From the Borders to the Bush, pp.17-20; 1841 and 1851 Scotland Censuses)*

---

## Family

## Life Summary

Robert Telfer was born in 1803 in Castleton, Roxburghshire, the fifth child and third son of James Telfer and Betty Hutton. He was baptised on 25 April 1803 in the Church of Scotland at Castleton parish, the same Liddesdale valley where the Telfer family had lived for generations.

Unlike his younger brother Francis, who emigrated to South Australia in 1838, Robert remained in the Scottish Borders his entire life. He married Elizabeth "Betty" Oliver around 1828. The 1841 census shows the couple living in Castleton with their young family, alongside Robert's older brother John Telfer (64), Violet Telfer (25), and William Telfer (22) — likely extended family sharing a household.

By 1851, Robert (now aged 46) was living in Castleton with only his daughters Elizabeth (17) and John (11) still at home. His wife Betty is absent from the 1851 census household — she may have died between 1841 and 1851, though her death has not been traced.

Robert's death at age 74 was registered in 1878 in the Castleton district. The statutory death registration records his mother's maiden surname as Hutton, confirming his parentage.

## Life Summary

Ruth Telfer was the **youngest** of the ten Telfer children born to Francis and Amy Telfer. She was born at **Saddleworth**, South Australia, on 26 October 1931 — her birth name was **Pamela Ruth Telfer**, but the family called her Ruth.

Her sister Jean McMurtrie wrote in her memoir:

> \"Our youngest sister Ruth was born while we were at Saddleworth, mother was 48, and that was very hard for her, but Ruth being so much younger than the rest of us has been a real blessing to us all.\"

Ruth appears in a cherished family photograph circa 1936 at approximately age 6, riding the family horse **Duchess** with her brother Murray (then aged ~12), accompanied by the family dog.

The photograph captures a tender moment of rural childhood on the Eyre Peninsula — Ruth beaming with joy in her bob haircut and light summer top, bare legs dangling, while Murray holds the reins responsibly. Duchess, a bay with distinctive white blaze and four white socks, was clearly a beloved family horse.

Further details of Ruth's life — marriage, children, later residence — are currently being researched.

## Life Summary

Shirley Edna Telfer (née Parker) was the matriarch of the Telfer family — wife of [[Murray John Telfer (1924–2009)]] for over 50 years, and mother of six children. She lived her life on the family farm in the Ungarra/Tumby Bay region of South Australia's Eyre Peninsula.

She was the youngest child of [[William Henry Parker (1893–1968)]] and [[Caroline Edna Lawrie (1890–1957)]], born at the family farm at Long Plains, South Australia, and married Murray in 1950, uniting the Parker and Telfer families. Her mother, Caroline Edna, was the daughter of Robert Dunlop Lawrie and Caroline Hosking, connecting Shirley to the **Lawrie family** — Scottish pioneers who emigrated from Ayrshire to South Australia in the 1850s and helped establish the Alma Church of Christ.

Shirley raised her family in a strong Christian home. The Church of Christ was central to the Telfer family's life — Murray served as an elder and secretary at both the Ungarra and Tumby Bay Churches of Christ for decades, and Shirley was a steadfast partner in that faith journey.

She was the grandmother of [[Mark Kenneth Telfer (1986–?)]] through her son [[Timothy Neil Telfer (1959–?)]].

Shirley passed away peacefully at Tumby Bay Hospital on Thursday, 23 February 2017, aged 87. Her funeral was held at the Church of Christ, Tumby Bay, on Wednesday, 1 March 2017, followed by burial at Tumby Bay Cemetery. In lieu of flowers, the family requested donations to the Tumby Bay Hospital Auxiliary.

- **Funeral Notice** — *Centralian Advocate*, 25 February 2017: Funeral conducted at Church of Christ, Tumby Bay, 1 March 2017 at 11:00am. Cortege proceeded to Tumby Bay Cemetery. Donations to Tumby Bay Hospital Auxiliary.

## Family Stories

Shirley Edna Parker married Murray John Telfer, the ninth child of Francis Charles and Amy Telfer. Together they raised three sons — Darryl William, John Robert and Grantley Keith — carrying on the farming tradition of the Telfer family on the Eyre Peninsula. *(From the Borders to the Bush, p.175)*

## Life

Sophia Webster was born on 18 June 1803 in Tuttington, Norfolk, England, the daughter of William Webster (1777–1816) and Susanna Hewett (1781–1850).

On 31 October 1825, she married Joseph March at St Michael's Church, Aylsham, Norfolk. Joseph was a carpenter and wheelwright from Aylsham.

Sophia and Joseph emigrated to the Colony of South Australia with their children aboard the ship **Canton**, departing London and arriving at Port Adelaide on 31 July 1846. The family settled in the Prospect area, north of Adelaide.

Joseph March died on 30 October 1883 at Prospect, South Australia, and was buried at North Road Cemetery, Nailsworth.

Sophia died on 6 October 1892 at Prospect, South Australia, at the age of 89. She was buried at North Road Cemetery, Nailsworth, City of Prospect, South Australia — the same cemetery as her husband.

Sophia was born in Aylsham, Norfolk in 1829, the daughter of [[Joseph March (1797–1883)]] and [[Sophia (Webster) March (1803–1892)]].

She emigrated to the Colony of South Australia with her parents and siblings aboard the ship **Canton**, arriving at Port Adelaide on 31 July 1846 (Bound for South Australia database). Her death notice states she was "a colonist of 50 years" but also says she arrived on the Canton in "August, 1845" — likely a memorial error by the family; the Bound for SA database and contemporaneous passenger lists confirm 1846.

She married [[William John Baker (1831–1919)]] on **9 March 1853** in Adelaide, South Australia (Genealogy SA Marriage Index, District Adelaide, Book 15, Page 73). The couple settled at Francis Street, Hyde Park, Unley, where they raised nine children. William had emigrated from Devon, England aboard the *Stag* in 1850.

Sophia died at her residence, Francis Street, Hyde Park on **1 December 1901** at the age of 72 and was buried at West Terrace Cemetery, Adelaide.

## Life Summary

Susan Burton married Robert Telfer and settled in the Mount Gambier district of South Australia. Her husband Robert worked as stock manager at Moorak, one of the large pastoral estates near Mount Gambier. When Dr. Browne subdivided the Woodlands estate, Robert purchased a farm there and the family moved to that property at Yahl, near Mount Gambier.

They raised seven children — three sons and four daughters. Susan was widowed in 1907 when Robert died, but she continued living on the Woodlands property until her death.

Her obituary in the Border Watch (Mount Gambier, 7 Oct 1924) described her as "another old and highly respected resident of this district." The funeral was conducted by Rev. A. H. Ballinger, with Mr. W. Pearce carrying out the arrangements.

> Another old and highly respected resident of this district in the person of Mrs. Susan Telfer, of Yahl, passed away on Sunday last. The deceased lady was the wife of the late Mr. Robert Telfer, who for many years was employed on Moorak as stock manager. When Dr. Browne cut up Woodlands Mr. Telfer purchased a farm there and when he retired from Moorak he went there to reside with his family. Mr. Telfer died several years ago, but Mrs. Telfer continued to reside on the property until her death. Mrs. Telfer had a family of seven—three sons and four daughters. The sons are Messrs. Jas., Mount Gambier; W., Yahl; and Robert, N.S.W. The daughters are Mesdames George B. Renfrey, St. Kilda; Rowbotham, North Adelaide; and the Misses S. and E. Telfer. There are several grandchildren. The funeral was held this afternoon, the Rev. A. H. Ballinger conducted the service, and Mr. W. Pearce carried out the funeral arrangements.

## Life Summary

Susan Telfer was the third child of John Telfer and [[Martha Allen (1840–1876)]]. Born at Black Heath, Tungkillo, South Australia on 9 May 1871, she married Robert Agnew on 21 December 1892. She passed away on 29 July 1952 in Mount Gambier, South Australia at the age of 81, having outlived all her siblings from Martha Allen's line except Martha Cameron, who died twelve years later.

## Family Stories

Susan was the third child of John and Martha Telfer, born on 9 June 1871. She married Robert Agnew, a farmer, and they made their home first at Millicent and later at Glencoe in the South East of South Australia. Robert served on the Mt. Muirhead School Board of Advice alongside Adam Telfer. Together they raised a large family of eight children — two sons, Keith and Gilbert, and six daughters, Myrna, Gladys, Doreen, Thelma, Marjorie and Betty.

Susan lived to 81 years of age and died on 29 July 1952 at the home of her eldest daughter Myrna (Mrs. Arthur Goodes) at Glencoe West. Her descendants carried the Telfer line into the next generation across the South East and beyond.

*(From the Borders to the Bush, pp.237–238)*

🖊️ **Anecdote — as told in From the Borders to the Bush (book pp. 272):** Ray — you'll smile at this one. He was the one with the old buggy and the good heart, and when there was a dance anywhere within reachable distance, he was the chauffeur. He'd pile his sisters aboard and drive them off, and then the trouble began — getting them home. One sister would have her eye on the next dance, then another, and before Ray could round the whole lively lot of them up it was light, and milking time. More than one morning came up as Ray steered that buggy back to Edgerston with the girls still humming the last waltz. He ended his days farming out at Scotts Creek, and he died in 1960 — but the family never forgot who got the girls home on dance mornings.

🖊️ **Anecdote — as told in From the Borders to the Bush (book pp. 318–320):** Everyone's Aunt Vi. She never married — she was too busy mothering the whole tribe. When the family moved down to Rochester Street in Adelaide, Violet ran that big house, and it was the boarding house for every niece and nephew who came to the city for Teachers College — they'd land on her doorstep with their trunks and she'd feed them and send them out clean. A fine cook and gardener, the settled one, the respected one. When her mother went blind with cataracts, Violet was the one by her side. After Margaret passed, Violet and her sister Elsie took over a small private hospital in Rochester — the pair of them running the wards. ## Life Summary

William Henry Parker was born on 13 April 1893 at Long Plains, South Australia, the seventh child and third son of Scottish-born William Humphrey Parker (1850–1926) and Hannah Baker (1855–1948). His father had migrated from Mossblown, Ayrshire, Scotland, to South Australia. His older sister Sophia Parker (1886–1918) married into the Lawrie family (Frank Lindsay Lawrie), creating a double connection between the Parker and Lawrie families.

William married Caroline Edna Lawrie on 29 March 1917 at the residence of R. D. Lawrie, Long Plains, solemnised by Pastor Ross Goodwin. They had five children: Avis (b. 1918), Howard (b. 1920), Sydney Hugh (b. 1922), William Humphrey (b. 1926), and Shirley Edna (b. 1929).

He was a farmer at Long Plains for most of his life. He died on 16 December 1968 near Owen, South Australia, aged 75, and was buried at Shannon Cemetery (Calomba Methodist Cemetery), SA, alongside his wife Caroline Edna (who predeceased him in 1957).

# William James Telfer (1880–1880)

**Role:** Infant son of John Telfer and Caroline Amelia Masters
**Born:** 15/16 September 1880 — Hawker / Willow Plains, South Australia
**Died:** 7 November 1880 (aged 7 weeks) — Arkaba, South Australia
**Buried:** Telfer Road Lone Graves, near Hawker, South Australia
**Parents:** [[John Telfer (1847–1929)]] & [[Caroline Amelia Telfer (1842–1929)]]
**Siblings:** Francis Charles, John Ernest, Ernest John, Albert George, Walter William, Edwin Gilbert

---

William James Telfer was the fourth son of John Telfer and Caroline Amelia Masters, born at Willow Plains (near Hawker) in September 1880. He lived only seven weeks, dying on 7 November 1880. He was buried by the side of the road at Telfer Road Lone Graves, near Hawker — a testament to the family's early hardships on the land.

**Source:** *From the Borders to the Bush* (body text); FamilySearch MF8B-PND; FindAGrave memorial 200328442.

---

## Family Stories

🖊️ **Anecdote — as told in From the Borders to the Bush (book pp. 117):** William came too soon after the one before him — born in September 1880 and gone by November, just two months old. They couldn't get him to a proper churchyard in time, so they laid him where they had to, in a lonely grave right beside Telfer Road, and the family kept the spot marked. Years later, when the stone house was up and the homestead stood proud, they still had a picture taken of that small roadside grave, looking back towards the house and the windmill and the hill they called Windy — a reminder that this was a place built in blood and salt and loss, not just sweat.

*(Anecdote only — family colour, told as the elders tell it. Does not establish any relationship, date or place.)*

- **FindAGrave:** [Memorial 200328442](https://www.findagrave.com/memorial/200328442/william-james-telfer) — burial at Telfer Road Lone Graves, Hawker, SA; death 7 Nov 1880 aged 7 weeks

**Baptised:** 24 Apr 1831 at Bickleigh, Devon (parish register)

**Buried:** West Terrace Cemetery, Adelaide, South Australia

## Life

William was born in Bickleigh, Devon in 1831. According to the Ship *Stag* passenger manifest (1850), he was a mason by trade. His parents were **James and Jane Baker** of Bickley, Devonshire, England, as stated by the Playford's Past community history resource (single source — not independently verified).[^playford]

He emigrated to the Colony of South Australia aboard the ship **Stag**, departing Plymouth on 22 February 1850 and arriving at Port Adelaide on 11 June 1850. He travelled as a young single man aged 18-19 seeking opportunity in the new colony.[^playford]

After arriving in South Australia, William initially worked carting goods by bullock team to the Burra copper mines. He later took up farming.

He married [[Sophia Baker (1829–1901)|Sophia (March) Baker]] (née March) on **9 March 1853** in Adelaide, South Australia (Genealogy SA Marriage Index, District Adelaide, Book 15, Page 73). Sophia was the daughter of [[Joseph March (1797–1883)]] and [[Sophia (Webster) March (1803–1892)]], who had emigrated from Norfolk, England in 1846.

William and Sophia raised a large family of nine children at Hyde Park, Unley. After Sophia's death in 1901, William continued living in the family home.

He died at Hyde Park on 3 June 1919 at the age of 88 and was buried at West Terrace Cemetery, Adelaide.

title: William Telfer (1802–1850) — Australian Pioneer
body_markdown:
# William Telfer (1802–1850)

**Born:** 7 October 1802 — Oxnam Parish, Roxburghshire, Scotland  
**Died:** 16 September 1850 — Tamworth, New South Wales  
**Mother:** [[Janet Nichol]]  
**Father:** [[William Telfer (shepherd)]]  
**Spouse:** Margaret (surname unknown) — m. unknown, before 1841

## Life Summary

William Telfer was born on 7 October 1802 in the Parish of Oxnam, Roxburghshire, Scotland, the fourth child of William Telfer, a shepherd, and his wife Janet Nichol. From an early age, William and his older brother Andrew worked as shepherds in the Cheviot Hills region, herding sheep through hard winters and bad seasons when work was difficult to obtain.

In 1825 William and Andrew signed on as Indented Servants — "Free People" — with the newly formed Australian Agricultural Company. William's agreement was dated 10 February 1825, with an annual salary of £30. He sailed on the "York" which arrived in Sydney Harbour on 13 November 1825. His brother Andrew arrived two days later on the "Brothers".

William rose through the ranks of the Company over the next two decades. He was Shepherd in Charge at Booral from 1827, supervising up to 1,877 sheep. By 1828 he was Master Shepherd at three stations, supplying shepherds with fresh meat three times a week on horseback. In 1832 he accompanied Sir Edward Parry (the Arctic explorer turned Company Commissioner) on the expedition to the Liverpool Plains to assess land for the Company's new stations at Warrah and Goonoo Goonoo. Parry selected William as Manager of the new sheep stations, writing that William was "an intelligent, sober, industrious man, and as careful of the Co.'s property as if it were his own."

William moved 6,000 lambing ewes from Port Stephens to Warrah with the loss of only one sheep — a remarkable feat. In 1835 he was put in charge of the Goonoo Goonoo sheep station on the Peel River near Tamworth. He left the Company's employ in 1844.

In 1844 William purchased the leasehold of a store and accommodation house in Quirindi on the Liverpool Plains. Sir Thomas Mitchell, the famous explorer and Surveyor-General, spent Christmas Day with the Telfers in 1845. In 1846 William built the first public house in Quirindi, known as "The Squatters Home". In 1848 both W.C. Wentworth and the Rev. John Dunmore Lang stayed at Telfer's inn on the same night — both members of the newly formed Legislative Council.

William died in Tamworth on 16 September 1850 and was buried in the old cemetery. He died without leaving a will, and his widow Margaret applied for administration of the estate, as published in the NSW Government Gazette on 29 August 1851.

## Family Stories

William Telfer was born into shepherd life in the Scottish Borders and grew up knowing hard winters and scarce work. When the Australian Agricultural Company was formed in London in 1824 to develop the fine wool industry in New South Wales, William and his brother Andrew signed on as Indented Servants. They sailed on separate ships from Cowes in June 1825, arriving in Sydney Harbour in November after calling at Rio de Janeiro. The passengers remained on board for days while arrangements were made to transport them to "Retreat", a temporary property thirty miles west of Sydney. Twenty carts were hired, but they needed another twenty. Their first night on land ended in a heavy thunderstorm and miserable conditions.

William's skill with sheep was evident from the start. When Sir Edward Parry took over as Commissioner, he personally selected William for the task of establishing new sheep stations on the Liverpool Plains. Parry's despatches to London speak of William in the highest terms — "an intelligent, sober, industrious man" with "strict honesty in the case of stores committed to his charge." When the Company needed to move 6,000 lambing ewes from Port Stephens to Warrah, William and his brother Andrew did the job with the loss of only one sheep. Parry preferred William over the Company's surveyor, Henry Dangar, for the position of Manager — a significant show of confidence in a former indentured servant.

After leaving the Company in 1844, William bought a store and accommodation house at Quirindi. He built the first public house in town — "The Squatters Home" — on 200 acres leased from the government. The pub sat on the flat near Jacob and Joseph Creeks, where the Kamilaroi people camped. It played host to some of the colony's most notable figures: Sir Thomas Mitchell arrived on Christmas Eve 1845 and spent Christmas Day with the family. In 1848, W.C. Wentworth and the Rev. John Dunmore Lang stayed on the same night — both members of the newly formed Legislative Council. Lang, a powerful orator and true patriot, was having financial difficulties at the time, and William was among those who subscribed to keep him in the House.

William returned to Tamworth in 1850, but died later that year on 16 September. He was buried in the old cemetery. He left no will and little provision. His eldest son William, the "oldest native of West Tamworth" born in 1841, was working for a magistrate by age 10. His wife Margaret must have faced hard years after his death.

William and Andrew sailed aboard chartered hand-me-downs, not new ships. The Australian Agricultural Company hired the "York" (429 tons) and the "Brothers" (425 tons), both of them former convict transports. The pair slipped out of Cowes on 26 June 1825, struck across the Atlantic to call at Rio de Janeiro for supplies, and dropped anchor in Sydney Harbour on 13 November 1825 — William's flagship was reported first, with Andrew's "Brothers" coming in two days behind. The long passage claimed its own losses too: eighteen sheep died on board before the New South Wales coastline hove into view.

West Tamworth's early settlers paid a brutal price for their frontier diet. On little more than salt meat and damper, men sickened and died young, carried off by liver complaints and heart disease. The old cemetery filled quickly, and in those rough years grief allowed little ceremony — as many as four coffins could be lowered into a single grave.

William's eldest son, born on 26 July 1841, was put to work under a magistrate while still a boy of ten, and spent his teenage years droving and shepherding across the colony's runs. Then in 1859 he attempted an epic droving odyssey, pushing a mob of stock over the great divide into the Maranoa district of Queensland — a long, punishing trek that would have tested even the hardest bushman.

William's son David fared little better. His father's death in 1850 cut his schooling short almost before it began, and by 1851 — still only ten years old — David was already out earning for the family, working under a magistrate.

*(From the Borders to the Bush, pp.364–371)*

body_markdown:
# William Telfer (1811–?)

**Role:** Brother of Francis Telfer (1809–1895), youngest of the siblings

William Telfer was born ~1811 at Blackburnfoot, Newcastleton, Roxburghshire, Scotland. He was the youngest child and son of James Telfer (1761–1845), a hand loom weaver, and Elizabeth "Betty" Hutton (1774–1853).

He did NOT emigrate to Australia and stayed in Scotland.

The book *From the Borders to the Bush* states: *"We have no further information about four members of this family; namely Isobel, Adam, Margaret and William."* Like his siblings Isobel, Adam, and Margaret, William's fate after the family records is not documented.

**Source:** *From the Borders to the Bush* — pages 17–20

---

## Family Stories

### The Youngest Brother

William Telfer was born around 1811 at Blackburnfoot, Newcastleton — the youngest child of James Telfer and Elizabeth Hutton. He was seven years younger than his brother Francis, who would go on to build a new life in South Australia.

William never made the voyage. He stayed in Scotland, the youngest of the siblings who remained behind. Like Adam, Isobel, and Margaret, his life after the family records ends is undocumented — one of the four the book *From the Borders to the Bush* has no further information on. He's the bookend of that generation, the youngest, the one who stayed.

*(From the Borders to the Bush, pp.17-20)*

# Charles Masters (1809–1866)

**Lifespan:** 30 June 1809 – 4 June 1866

**Branch:** Masters (father of Caroline Amelia Telfer)

**Role:** Caroline Telfer's father; SA pioneer farmer at Wroxton Grange, Angaston

## Biography

Charles Masters was born 30th June 1809 at Brownsover, Warwickshire, England. He married **Martha Williams** on 6th August 1835 at Aston le Walls, Northamptonshire.

# Beatrice Rowe Telfer (1877–1951)

**Lifespan:** 12 October 1877 – 29 June 1951

**Branch:** Rowe → Telfer (married into)

**Role:** Wife of Albert George Telfer; mother of his six children

## Biography

Beatrice Rowe was born 12th October 1877 at Kadina, South Australia. She was a school teacher in the Warcowie district, and boarded with the Telfer family for a year or two before being transferred to Moolawurtie.

She married **[[Albert George Telfer (1881–1970)]]** at Warcowie and they farmed there from 1903 before moving to Hill River (near Clare) in 1923 so their children could attend High School. Their children — **Rita Joyce, Beatrice Sylvia, Douglas Ivan, Melville Bruce, John Alick Ralph and Murray Keith** — were all born while the family lived at Warcowie.

Beatrice died 29th June 1951 and is buried at Clare Old Cemetery, beside her husband Albert.

# James Alexander Alcorn (1915–1942)

**Role:** Dillon-branch descendant — RAAF sergeant lost over the North Sea, WWII
**Born:** 2 December 1915 — Adelaide, South Australia
**Died:** 16 July 1942 (aged 26) — North Sea (aircraft accident, no remains recovered)
**Father:** Leslie Alcorn
**Mother:** Rebecca Elizabeth Alcorn
**Branch:** Tantanoola/Dillon line of Elizabeth Beattie Telfer

## War Service

Sergeant **James Alexander ALCORN** (Service No. 407886), Royal Australian Air Force (RAAF), Air Gunner. Enlisted 3 February 1941. Unit: **No. 27 Operational Training Unit (RAF), RAF Lichfield, Staffordshire.**

Died in an aircraft accident when **Wellington P9285** of No. 27 OTU, on a cross-country training exercise, crashed into the **North Sea on 16 July 1942** (RDF plot faded at 1230 hrs; aircraft did not return). Aged 26. **Body never recovered.**

Commemorated at the **Runnymede Memorial, Surrey, England**. Names on the AWM Roll of Honour panel.

Son of Leslie and Rebecca Elizabeth Alcorn; husband of Rona Mary Alcorn, of Henley Beach, South Australia.

## Life Summary

James Alexander Alcorn, born Adelaide 2 December 1915, was an RAAF Air Gunner during the Second World War. Attached to the RAF's No. 27 Operational Training Unit at Lichfield for training, his Wellington bomber disappeared over the North Sea on 16 July 1942 and his body was never recovered. He is commemorated at the Runnymede Memorial in England.

## Anecdote

🖊️ **Anecdote — as told in *A Telfer Family Tree* (Supplement 2008, p.198):** RAAF sergeant James Alcorn was lost when his Wellington crashed into the North Sea during RAF training at Lichfield in July 1942. His body was never recovered; Runnymede remembers him.

## War Service

Flight Sergeant **Trevor Andrew Thomson** (Service No. 436777), **No. 460 Squadron RAAF** (RAF Binbrook, Lincolnshire). Killed in action **2 March 1945** when his Lancaster bomber was lost on a raid toward Cologne during the Allies' push to the Rhine.

Commemorated at **Hotton War Cemetery, Hotton, Wallonie, Belgium.** Name located in the Commemorative Area at the Australian War Memorial (Second World War, Air Force).

Son of Alexander and Isabella Thomson; husband of Ethel Winifred Thomson, of South Perth, Western Australia.

## Life Summary

Trevor Andrew Thomson was born at Thebarton, South Australia on 20 October 1914, delivered into the Telfer line through his mother Isabella Lucieton Telfer, daughter of John Telfer (1840–1913) and Martha Clara Henstridge. Isabella married Alexander Brown Thomson in July 1911; the couple raised three children — Roma, Trevor and Murray.

Trevor enlisted in the RAAF and served as a Flight Sergeant with No. 460 Squadron. He died on 2 March 1945 when his aircraft went down on a mission over Germany, aged 30. He has no marked local grave; he is commemorated at Hotton War Cemetery in Belgium and on the AWM Roll of Honour.

## Anecdote

🖊️ **Anecdote — as told in *A Telfer Family Tree* (Supplement 2008, p.264):** Trevor Andrew Thomson, Flight Sergeant, RAAF 460 Squadron, was killed 2 March 1945 when his bomber went down on a Cologne raid during the Allied push to the Rhine. Son of Alexander & Isabella Thomson; buried Hotton War Cemetery, Belgium.

# Colin Lindsay Beaton (1915–1944)

**Born:** 24/25 March 1915 — Tantanoola, South Australia
**Died:** 14 May 1944, aged 29 — whilst a Prisoner of War (Burma Railway / Siam)
**Buried:** Kranji War Cemetery, Singapore
**Mother:** [[Elizabeth Beattie Bessie Telfer (1871–1948)]]

## Family

| **Maternal Grandfather** | [[Adam Francis Telfer (1842–1925)]] |
| **Maternal Grandmother** | [[Margaret Dougal Telfer (1849–1936)]] |
| **Siblings** | Ivy, Margaret, Bill (William), Olive, Harold & Frank (twins), Ken |

## Life Summary

Colin Lindsay Beaton was the youngest of the eight children of Bessie (Elizabeth Beattie) Telfer and William John Beaton of Tantanoola, South Australia. He was the grandson — through his mother Bessie — of Adam Francis Telfer (1842–1925) and Margaret Dougal Telfer (1849–1936), placing him squarely in the Telfer family's South-East SA line.

Colin and his brother Ken rode a pony five miles each way to school and both won exhibitions (scholarships) in the Qualifying Certificate examinations — Colin scored 677 out of 700. They boarded at Mount Gambier High School. A keen sportsman, Colin played most of his football for Tantanoola, represented the Inter-Association teams on several occasions, and was a useful cricketer for Tantanoola.

## War Service & Death

At the outbreak of the Second World War, Colin enlisted with his brothers Harold and Frank. He served as a Private with the Australian Army (service number **SX10061**, enlisted 7 August 1940). He was taken prisoner and held at **Changi prison in Singapore**, then forced onto the **Burma Railway** with his captors, where he died while on the project — **14 May 1944, aged 29**.

He is buried at **Kranji War Cemetery, Singapore**. His name also appears on his parents' memorial at the Tantanoola cemetery, which reads:

> **Colin L. Beaton, Died whilst Prisoner of War 14th May, 1944, Aged 29 years Lest We Forget.**

# Robert Telfer (1835–1907)

**Role:** Second son of [[James Telfer (1796–1863)]] to emigrate — manager of Moorak Station
**Born:** 1835 — Jedburgh, Roxburghshire, Scotland
**Died:** 12 January 1907 — Yahl, South Australia *(FindAGrave headstone gives 14 Jan 1907 — day conflict, see Sources)*
**Spouse:** Susan Burton Telfer (1844–1924) (m. 1865)
**Father:** [[James Telfer (1796–1863)]]
**Mother:** Elizabeth Beattie (1802–1891)

## Family

| Relation | Name |
|----------|------|
| **Spouse** | Susan Burton Telfer (1844–1924) |
| **Father** | [[James Telfer (1796–1863)]] |
| **Mother** | Elizabeth Beattie |
| **Brother** | [[James Telfer (1829–1913)]] |
| **Sister** | [[Elizabeth Beattie Telfer (1832–1896)]] — m. Dillon |
| **Brother** | [[John Telfer (1840–1913)]] |
| **Brother** | [[Adam Francis Telfer (1842–1925)]] |

## Life Summary

Robert Telfer, the second son of James and Elizabeth, was born at Jedburgh in 1835. He came to Australia at sixteen on the "Oliver Lang" with his brother James and sister Elizabeth. He spent his entire working life in the employ of Dr. J.W. Browne and his successor, eventually becoming manager of Moorak Station near Mount Gambier.

## Family Stories

*Stories drawn from the family book, *From the Borders to the Bush*, pp. 225–227.*

**The young emigrant.** Robert was only sixteen when he left the old family town of Jedburgh behind and set out for the far side of the world. Travelling as the second son alongside his brother James and sister Elizabeth, he sailed for Australia on the *Oliver Lang* and reached Melbourne in 1854. Rather than settle in the colony of Victoria, the young party pushed overland into South Australia, where Robert made contact with his uncle Francis Telfer at Macoota, Kersbrook, before pressing on to the South East with the promise of land and work ahead of him.

**The rise at Moorak.** Robert's working life began under Dr J.W. Browne, who first sent him to the Gawler Ranges in the remote north of the colony. From there he moved south to Browne's Moorak Station near Mount Gambier and steadily climbed the ranks — trusted first with the German Creek section, then raised to overseer, and finally made manager of the whole station. He was living at Moorak when he married Susan Burton on 11 April 1865; Susan was twenty, the daughter of James Burton of Claraville, and the ceremony was performed at her family home by Reverend Needham. The marriage certificate is almost illegible now. The couple had five sons and four daughters — James Robert, William, Lindsay Burton, Robert Allan Burton and Francis John Burton; and Elizabeth, Helen, Susan and Edith Mary Kathleen. After more than fifty years' service to the Browne family, ill health at last forced Robert to resign, and he went on to build his own home, which he named *Carlowrie*, at nearby Yahl.

**Taken too soon.** Robert spent his last months confined to bed at Carlowrie, his strength worn down by a series of paralytic strokes. He died there on a Saturday evening at the age of seventy-two, having been a colonist for fifty-two years. He left his widow and nine children to mourn him. His obituary in *The Chronicle* of 19 January 1907 recorded that he was "72 years of age and was highly respected," a colonist of fifty-two years standing; he was described as "a man of sterling worth, of a quiet and unassuming disposition, who had made a host of friends." His funeral was conducted by Reverend Caldwell of the Presbyterian Church, and a long cortege followed him to the Mount Gambier Cemetery.

Susan Burton Telfer lived on until 1924, outliving her husband by seventeen years.

## Sources

- **Source:** Donald Telfer, *From the Borders to the Bush* (ISBN 0 7316 6387 X), pp. 34
- **Source:** The Chronicle, 19 January 1907 — obituary (age 72)

title: Clara Blanche Telfer/Lane (1883–1974)
body_markdown:
# Clara Blanche Telfer (1883–1974)

**Born:** 19 November 1883 — Tantanoola, South Australia  
**Died:** 5 June 1974 — South Australia  
**Father:** [[John Telfer (1840–1913)]]  
**Mother:** [[Martha Henstridge (~1854–1921)]]  
**Spouse:** Francis Edward Lane (m. 6 April 1903, d. 1940)

## Life Summary

Clara Blanche Telfer was born on 19 November 1883, the tenth child of John Telfer (1840–1913) and his second wife Martha Clara Henstridge. She married Francis Edward Lane on 6 April 1903 at the Tantanoola Presbyterian Church. The marriage certificate listed Francis's occupation as "Hotel Keeper" — he was the Licensee of the Tantanoola Tiger Hotel from 1902 to 1905, together with his brother William Lane.

Clara and Francis had ten children, though three died in infancy: Edna Elizabeth Lane (lived nine months), Brenda Olive Lane (lived three months), and Francis Lane (lived two days). The seven who survived were Nina Amy, Ethel Jean, Derrice Elma, Edna Mary, Doris Elizabeth, Albin Edward John and June.

Clara had a very close relationship with her brothers and sisters and often visited Tantanoola. In her 90th year she made a special request to be driven to the Presbyterian Church where she had been married, and to other places which held very special memories. She died five months after this visit, on 5 June 1974.

Francis Edward Lane died in 1940 at the age of 74.

## Family Stories

Clara Blanche was the tenth child of John Telfer — the last of his daughters — born in 1883 at Tantanoola. At nineteen she married Francis Edward Lane, a hotel keeper who ran the Tantanoola Tiger Hotel with his brother. The wedding took place at the Tantanoola Presbyterian Church on 6 April 1903.

She raised seven surviving children through hard times. Her brother Roland never married and was a great friend of Clara and her family, spending every Good Friday and Christmas Day with them for decades.

In her 90th year, Clara returned to Tantanoola for a visit and asked to be driven to the Presbyterian Church where she had been married all those years before, and to other places that held special memories. She died five months later, on 5 June 1974 — ninety years old, and the last surviving child of John and Martha.

*(From the Borders to the Bush, pp.249–251)*

## Life Summary

Charles Telfer was the fifth child of [[John Telfer (1840–1913)]] and the first child of his second wife [[Martha Henstridge (~1854–1921)]]. Born at Mount Gambier, South Australia on 13 January 1875, he was the eldest of Martha Clara Henstridge's children. He married Amelia Curkpatrick James at Naracoorte, South Australia on 26 February 1902. They had six children — three sons and three daughters. Like several of his siblings he moved to the mid-north of the state, and he died at Port Augusta, South Australia on 1 September 1954, aged 79.

**Note — two Charles Telfers (do not merge):** This is the Tantanoola-branch Charles Telfer (1875–1954), son of John Telfer & Martha Henstridge, who died at Port Augusta. He must be distinguished from the OTHER Charles Telfer who also died in 1954 — Francis Charles "Charlie" Telfer (1875–1954) [[Francis Charles Telfer (1875–1954)]], the son of John Telfer & Caroline (John 1847–1929 branch), who died at Croydon. Two different men, same given name, same death year, different branches.

**Note — spouse surname discrepancy:** The family history book (*From the Borders to the Bush*, p.240) records his wife as "Amelia **Fitzpatrick**"; FamilySearch gives "Amelia **Curkpatrick** James." These share a common root and are almost certainly the same person under a transcription/OCR variance, but the exact form is not authoritatively resolved — recorded, not silently chosen.

**Note — birth year variance:** FamilySearch records birth 13 Jan **1875**; the Lehmann/Henschke genealogical sheet records **1874**. Age-79 at death (1 Sep 1954) is consistent with either. File titled 1875 per FamilySearch's precise birth date; variance noted.

> "Charles Telfer was the fifth child of John and Martha (nee Henstridge), who married Amelia Fitzpatrick. They had six children, Charles died at Port Augusta in 1954."

# Hugh Parker (1859–1861)

**Born:** Nov 1859, Virginia, South Australia | **Died:** 13 Dec 1861 (aged ~2), Peachy Belt, South Australia | **Father:** [[David Parker (1822–1888)]] | **Mother:** [[Isabella Kelly (~1825–1867)]]

## Family Stories

### The First Name in the House

Hugh came first — the eldest son David and Isabella gave the name of David's own father, Hugh Parker of Ayrshire. But this boy only lived to about two, dying in December 1861 on the family farm country near Peachy Belt. Rather than lose the name, the family gave it again to a son born three Octobers later, in 1864 — the practice of the time. Two short-lived boys, one much-loved name, passed down twice in a row.

*(Research-compiled story, 26 Aug 2026 — see Sources.)*

## Family

## Life Summary

Hugh Parker was born in November 1859 at Virginia, South Australia, the son of David Parker (1822–1888) and Isabella Kelly (c. 1825–1867). He was the first son his father named Hugh, in honour of David's own father Hugh Parker.

Hugh died on 13 December 1861, aged about 2, in the Peachy Belt area of South Australia — not long after his mother Isabella, born to the family near Virginia and Two Wells in the Adelaide Plains district. His death record is registered in the Port Gawler district. After his death, the family gave the name Hugh again to a son born in 1864.

## Note on Name

This Hugh Parker is distinct from his brother **Hugh Parker (1864–1891)**, born after this child's death. Both sons were named after David Parker's father, Hugh Parker.

## Evidence Note

> **Verification status:** This profile is a **lead, not a fully-verified fact.** The parent link (son of David & Isabella) rests on one source group (WikiTree, user-contributed). A matching burial record exists (FindAGrave, Two Wells Cemetery, died 13 Dec 1861 — exact date match) but is **not** name-linked to this family and lists no parents. The exact SA birth/death registration could not be pulled (paywalled). Per the Telfer vault standard, the parent link should be re-confirmed against the SA BDM death registration (Port Gawler district, ~1861) when accessible.

# Hugh Parker (1864–1891)

**Born:** 31 Oct 1864, Virginia, South Australia | **Died:** 23 Nov 1891 (aged 27), Hundred of Pirie, South Australia | **Father:** [[David Parker (1822–1888)]] | **Mother:** [[Isabella Kelly (~1825–1867)]] | **Buried:** Port Pirie Cemetery, SA

## Family Stories

### A Name Carried On

Hugh was the second son his parents named Hugh. His elder brother, also Hugh, had died in December 1861 at barely two years old — and in an era when families didn't waste a good name, David and Isabella gave it again to this son born in October 1864. The name honoured David's own father, Hugh Parker, back in Ayrshire. Hugh himself died young, at 27, in 1891 — never marrying or leaving children of his own, but his short life is how the name travelled through the tree twice.

*(Research-compiled story, 26 Aug 2026 — see Sources.)*

## Family

## Life Summary

Hugh Parker was born on 31 October 1864 at Virginia, South Australia, the son of David Parker (1822–1888) and Isabella Kelly (c. 1825–1867). He was one of two sons his father named Hugh — he carried the name after his elder brother Hugh (1859–1861), who had died in infancy.

Hugh died on 23 November 1891, aged 27, at Hundred of Pirie, South Australia, and was buried at Port Pirie Cemetery — near his father David, who had died three years earlier. His early death at 27 meant he did not appear among the sons listed in his father's 1888 death notice.

## Note on Name

This Hugh Parker is distinct from — and lives alongside, in the records — his elder half-decade brother **Hugh Parker (1859–1861)**, who died aged two. David Parker named both a son Hugh in honour of his own father, Hugh Parker (christened David at Tarbolton, Ayrshire, 1822; father Hugh Parker, mother Christian Fulton). Reusing the name after an infant death was a common practice of the period.

# Olive Mary Lillecrapp (1899–1993)

**Role:** Eldest daughter of Alfred Edward Lillecrapp and Mary Bayes Farrow (Mary Bayes Farrow was a daughter of Charles Farrow and Elizabeth Telfer)

**Born:** 10 June 1899, Finniss Point near Tarlee, South Australia
**Died:** 10 September 1993, South Australia; buried Mitcham General Cemetery

**Father:** [[Alfred Edward Lillecrapp (1869–1934)]]
**Mother:** Mary Bayes Farrow (1875–1938) *(profile pending — see Corrections Log)*
**Husband:** Cyril Thomas Piper (1902–1961) *(profile pending — see Corrections Log)*

---

## Family

| Relation | Name |
|----------|------|
| **Father** | Alfred Edward Lillecrapp (1869–1934) |
| **Mother** | Mary Bayes Farrow (1875–1938) |
| **Husband** | Cyril Thomas Piper (1902–1961) (m. 2 Jun 1928) |

---

## Life Summary

Olive Mary Lillecrapp was born on **10 June 1899** at Finniss Point near Tarlee, SA. She married **Cyril Thomas Piper** on **2 June 1928** at the Baptist Church, Adelaide. She died on **10 September 1993** and is buried at Mitcham General Cemetery, SA.

> **Correction note:** Earlier research guessed Olive's marriage took place ~1916–1920. The verified record is **2 June 1928** to Cyril Thomas Piper. (See Corrections Log — Olive Lillecrapp.)

---

## Story — Marriage into the Piper Family (in-law context)

*This is the story of Olive's husband's family — the name she married into. It is cultural/contextual colour, NOT blood-Telfer lineage. All details verified against the sources cited below.*

Olive married into the **Piper family of South Australia**, a family with a striking rise from modest English origins to the upper ranks of the colonial legal world.

Her father-in-law, **Arthur William Piper** (1865–1936), was born in Kent, England, the son of Thomas Piper (1835–1928), a Bible Christian minister who came out to Adelaide in 1870. Arthur won a scholarship to Prince Alfred College, was admitted to the Bar at just **21** (1886), became **King's Counsel in 1911**, and was appointed a **Justice of the Supreme Court of South Australia in 1927**. The ADB praises him as "a prodigious worker," erudite enough to handle any case with ease.

He was a **Federationist** — an official guest at the 1901 Federation ceremonies in both Melbourne and Sydney — a **Grand Master of the Freemasons of South Australia** (1919–1924), and he drafted the constitution of the forerunner to the modern Liberal Party. He died in 1936 and, like Olive, is buried at **Mitcham Cemetery**.

Her husband **Cyril Thomas Piper** (1902–1961) was a **doctor (physician)** and an **officer in the Australian Army Medical Corps during World War II** (service record held by the National Archives of Australia). The couple lived in **Bute, South Australia**.

The legal line carried on through two of Arthur's sons — **Harold Bayard Piper** (1894–1953) and **F. E. Piper** — who were brought into the family firm (then **Bakewell, Stow & Piper**, which became **Piper, Bakewell & Piper**) as it passed to the next generation. Bayard was appointed a **Judge of the Commonwealth Court of Conciliation and Arbitration in 1938** and served as its **Chief Judge from 1941 to 1947** — so the family genuinely spanned a courtroom dynasty across two generations (per the ADB and Wikipedia).

## Life Summary

Rose Isabel Margaret Paynter was born 8 August 1900 at a Quorn nursing home in the Pichi Richi district, South Australia; the family farmed at Arden Vale. *(From the Borders to the Bush, p.88)*

Around 1918 she married John Hunter Rankin of Koolunga. The couple worked the property owned by the Fosters of Arden Vale for about 23 years, then moved into Quorn in 1942. John became semi-invalid before a stroke; the couple later lived at Port Augusta, where Rose died 8 July 1988. She is buried at Quorn Town Cemetery. *(From the Borders to the Bush, p.88; FindAGrave headstone)*

## Life Summary

Margaret Wright Telfer was the first of Adam and Margaret's twelve children, born at Koppio in the Port Lincoln region in 1869. She died at Tantanoola in April 1890, aged about twenty, unmarried, of pneumonia. Her mother's biography records that Margaret was to receive a piano as a present for her twenty-first birthday but never lived to see it — a loss that, by family account, never left her mother.

Her name is the same as her aunt, [[Margaret Wright Telfer (1810–1892)]], which has repeatedly caused confusion in record transcription; they are separate people.
